items.titleOriginal: Massive 262.5 MWh battery with 42 containers could power 21,000 homes for hours
items.description: Ο γερμανικός ενεργειακός γίγαντας RWE μόλις έσπασε το έδαφος με μια κολοσσιαία μπαταρία 262,5 μεγαβατώρων (MWh) που είναι ικανή να τροφοδοτήσει περίπου 21.000 νοικοκυριά με ηλεκτρική ενέργεια κατά τις βραδινές ώρες αιχμής. Η μπαταρία των 62,5 μεγαβάτ (MW) είναι το πρώτο σύστημα αποθήκευσης ενέργειας μπαταρίας της RWE (BESS) στην Ιταλία. Βρίσκεται στην πόλη Ragusa στη Σικελία, θα είναι…
items.descriptionOriginal: German energy giant RWE has just broken ground on a colossal 262.5-megawatt-hour (MWh) battery that is capable of supplying roughly 21,000 households with electricity during peak evening hours. The 62.5-megawatt (MW) battery is reportedly RWE’s first battery energy storage system (BESS) in Italy. Located in the city of Ragusa in Sicily, it will be fitted with 42 containers housing lithium-ion batteries. RWE representatives revealed that the system will have a total storage capacity of 262.5 megawatt-hours (MWh). It will be capable of delivering its maximum output for four hours. This will be enough to cover the evening peak electricity demand of around 21,000 Italian households. The company expects to commission the project by the end of 2027. “The start of construction of our Ragusa battery storage marks an important milestone,” Sopna Sury, CEO of RWE Renewables Europe & Australia, said. “We have been operating in Italy for many years, using the energy from the wind and the sun.” Power for peak demand Sury explained that the battery will support the balance between electricity supply and demand . “In a world of growing renewable energy, battery storage systems are crucial for stabilizing the grid and ensuring that electricity is used when it is needed most,” Sury continued. Unlike conventional power plants, renewable energy sources depend on weather conditions. Battery storage systems can store excess electricity when production is high and release it when the demand increases. RWE said its new battery will provide balancing energy to stabilize the electricity grid . It will also feature technology capable of delivering grid-forming services such as instantaneous reserve, also known as inertia. Apart from installing the batteries, RWE will build the necessary grid infrastructure, including a high-voltage transformer that will link the system to the 150-kilovolt (kV) electricity grid. “[The] Ragusa battery will be capable of covering the evening peak demand of around 21.000 households for four hours,” Sury added. More battery capacity With the project, RWE aims to expand its battery storage business across Europe and other parts of the world. The company currently operates approximately 1.7 gigawatts (GW) of battery storage capacity worldwide. At the same time, another three GW are under construction. Additionally, RWE has established a strong presence in Italy’s renewable energy market. It currently operates 18 onshore wind farms, one solar power plant, and three agrivoltaic facilities. Together, these projects have an installed capacity of approximately 670 MW. This is enough to supply renewable electricity to more than 550,000 Italian households. The company is also constructing 200 MW of additional wind and solar capacity across the country. The Ragusa project will complement these renewable energy operations. Meanwhile, RWE plans to develop further battery storage capacity in Italy alongside its existing wind and solar projects. “We look forward to establishing further battery storage capacity in Italy soon – in addition to wind and solar power – in order to support Italy in building a resilient energy system,” Sury said in a press release . He explained that the expansion will make Italy’s electricity grid more reliable.

items.descriptionOriginal: New technology could allow wearables to one day rely less on batteries and more on vibrations generated by the user. The model, developed by the University of Surrey and its spinoff company Z-PULSE, predicts how much electricity small generators can make from vibrations. The work is published in the journal Advanced Energy Materials.

Αυτό μετατρέπει την προφορική γλώσσα σε ομαλή…
items.descriptionOriginal: Characters may be able to pronounce each word correctly but may appear to lack realism in their body movements, such as hand, facial and bodily movements. This issue has been tackled by researchers from Tohoku University and the University of Hong Kong with their creation of a new system named DynaConTalk . This converts spoken language into smooth 3D movements. The system works by creating realistic body movements. It creates fluid movements with parts of the body instead of just hand movements. This allows for smoother movements, such as changing posture, finger and facial movements, to create a much more realistic character. However, getting these movements to be realistic can be difficult. Big body movements and small facial and hand movements occur at different speeds and if the animation system isn’t in sync you may get repetitive movements, stiff postures or sudden changes in movements. This issue has been addressed by dividing movements into slow and fast elements. This ensures that movements are in sync as big movements won’t clash with smaller ones. The system takes into account the rhythm, vocal qualities and words being spoken to decide what movements to produce. Making AI-generated movements more natural Additionally, movements are kept smooth by using previous movements to guide the next set of movements. This means there aren’t any sudden changes in movements as the character is continuing to speak. You can also specify the initial posture of the body or provide reference movements. This level of control could be useful for artists and developers who want the character to be a certain style or move in specific ways. This system will manage the link between the spoken words and the movements. The system was tested with two public data sets (BEAT2 and SHOW) and a human evaluation was organized with 30 participants. Participants were shown videos created by three different systems with 15 examples of speech. The system scored the highest average across all four categories. The movements created were more similar to the distribution of human movements recorded in the evaluations. This was based on naturalness, relevance to the spoken words, synchronization and variety. AI could transform animation and virtual learning The results could be interesting for developers creating video games, films, virtual presenters and online learning. An instructor could have hand and facial movements that match the rhythm and meaning of a spoken explanation. Similar technology could be used to make virtual characters appear more realistic during online presentations. However, there are still issues with getting the system to be realistic. There are not many examples of large scale body movements within current data sets. The spoken words alone don’t give enough information for the animation system to know exactly where to move the person. Whilst a sentence may indicate someone’s emotions or intentions it doesn’t show if they should be moving forwards, turning around or going somewhere else. The team wants to look into larger movement data sets and adding extra information about the path of the movements. They also want to expand this to activities such as walking. This research will also be presented at SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 which will be held in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia between the 1st and 4th December. The findings were published in ACM Transactions on Graphics .

items.descriptionOriginal: Researchers at UCLA Health have shown in lab-grown human brain cells that boosting the activity of a healthy gene copy can offset the effects of a mutation linked to autism. The findings, published in Nature Neuroscience, suggest a new direction for treating autism and related neurodevelopmental conditions, though the work is still at an early stage.

items.descriptionOriginal: Researchers at the Institute of Metal Research, part of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, picked dopants by two measurable properties to design a cobalt-free, nickel-rich lithium-ion cathode, according to a Nature Synthesis paper and an academy release. They report high capacity at fast discharge and at minus 4 degrees Fahrenheit (minus 20 degrees Celsius). A cathode is a battery’s positive electrode, which takes in and releases lithium ions as the cell charges and discharges. Removing cobalt lowers cost and raises capacity, the release said, but it also slows lithium-ion movement and destabilizes the crystal structure, including its oxygen framework. Doping, or adding small amounts of other elements, is a common fix, but the release said dopants are usually chosen by experience and repeated testing. The team, led by professors Feng Li, Hui-Ming Cheng and Chunyang Wang, instead used two descriptors: how concentrated an ion’s charge is (ionic charge density) and metal-oxygen bond strength. Picking dopants with two descriptors The team gave each descriptor a job. Magnesium and calcium have low ionic charge density, which the release said weakens electrostatic constraints on the lithium ions moving through the material. Titanium and zirconium form strong metal-oxygen bonds, which the release said reinforce the oxygen framework, the lattice of oxygen atoms that holds the metal ions in place. The resulting cathode was tested at high discharge rates and in the cold. The release said it improved rate performance and structural stability together. The paper’s abstract reports a specific capacity, the charge stored per gram of material, of 130.9 milliamp-hours per gram at 25 C. A C rate compares current with capacity, so 25 C means a full discharge in 1/25 of an hour, about 2.4 minutes. The cathode kept 82.4 percent of its capacity after 350 cycles at 10 C. At minus 4 degrees Fahrenheit it delivered 112.2 milliamp-hours per gram at 1 C. Pouch-cell result and open questions The release also reported a 5.74-ampere-hour pouch cell, a battery sealed in a flexible foil case, that reached 278.6 watt-hours per kilogram at minus 20 degrees Celsius. It said multimodal characterization, meaning several analysis techniques used together, showed faster lithium-ion transport and fewer harmful phase changes. The pouch-cell figure comes only from the release, which doesn’t give its discharge rate or say whether the 350-cycle test used a coin cell or a pouch cell. The release also gives no comparison cathode, no dopant amounts and no cost figures. The release calls the approach a new design paradigm, but it describes results for one four-dopant composition, so how well the descriptors guide other choices isn’t shown there. Other labs are also dropping cobalt, including Caltech’s lithium iron phosphate cathode and McGill-led disordered rock-salt cathodes that need neither cobalt nor nickel. Another Chinese Academy of Sciences team reported a single-use lithium-metal battery that kept 447 watt-hours per kilogram at minus 40 degrees Fahrenheit. The study appeared Oct. 1 in Nature Synthesis.

items.descriptionOriginal: Researchers at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST) built a lip-reading AI that decodes clear words first and uses them to resolve ambiguous ones, in a paper that won an Outstanding Paper Award at a 2026 language-processing conference. It reached a 19.4 percent word error rate on the LRS3 benchmark, which the authors call the best among methods using only LRS3 as labeled training data. Lip reading is hard because English’s 40 sounds map to only 10 to 13 distinguishable mouth shapes, the paper said, so /p/, /b/ and /m/ look nearly identical. AI models write sentences from first word to last, so an early wrong guess can affect later words, KAIST said. Word error rate counts wrong, missing or added words against a correct transcript, so lower is better. KAIST said the technology could turn noisy speech into text or help deaf and hard-of-hearing people follow conversations. The paper tests only recorded benchmark videos. Filling in the clear words first The system uses a diffusion large language model, a text generator that starts with every word position blank and fills them in over repeated passes instead of writing left to right. According to the paper , the model commits early to positions it is confident about, then uses these words as context on both sides to refine uncertain ones. In the paper’s example, confident words such as “bags” and “trip” help correct “back” to “pack.” The team, led by Professor Yong Man Ro, trained the model in two stages, KAIST said. It first learns to match lip movements in video to text, then learns to model sentence length. When decoding, it estimates several plausible lengths from the video’s duration, generates a candidate sentence for each and picks the best scorer on length likelihood and model confidence. The team trained on LRS3, 433 hours of labeled TED and TEDx video, the paper said. Using the same visual encoder, error fell from 25.8 percent for a baseline the authors reproduced themselves to 19.4 percent. Where the results stop The authors’ claimed record applies only to methods using LRS3 as their only labeled training data. The paper’s table lists systems trained on far more labeled video with lower error, including 12.8 percent for a 2024 model trained on 100,000 hours. On WildVSR, an out-of-domain test set, the same model scored 39.9 percent. Tests covered English only, and results haven’t been checked across speaker or demographic subgroups. Testing sentence lengths adds decoding time: 0.87 times the video’s duration on one RTX 3090 graphics card, versus 0.14 without it, the paper says. They also flag privacy risks, since speech could be inferred from silent video without consent. KAIST said the team plans to reduce the model’s size and computing cost, aiming for real-time use on wearables and robots without an internet connection. Ro said the work would lay the foundation for physical AI (machines that sense and act in the real world) that people can reliably use on varied devices in daily life. The study appeared in the conference’s October proceedings in Budapest.

items.descriptionOriginal: Scientists from the Institute of Metal Research (IMR) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences have developed an ordered patterning strategy that integrates p-type and n-type BiVO₄ stripes on a conductive substrate. This strategy enables efficient Z-scheme charge separation and significantly enhances the photocatalytic overall water-splitting process. The research is published in the journal Advanced Energy Materials.

items.title: Ρωτήσαμε τους ανθρώπους τι τους αρέσει που οι άλλοι δεν καταλαβαίνουν. Μια απάντηση τους κυρίευσε όλους.
items.titleOriginal: We asked people what they enjoy that other people don’t understand. One answer ruled them all.
items.description: Μερικοί άνθρωποι έχουν ιδιόμορφα χόμπι και ενδιαφέροντα που άλλοι μπορεί να βρουν περίεργα, οπότε όταν ρωτήσαμε το κοινό μας στο Upworthy στο Facebook , "Τι είναι κάτι που σας αρέσει πραγματικά και οι άλλοι άνθρωποι δεν φαίνεται να καταλαβαίνουν;" και πάνω από 1.700 άτομα ζύγισαν, δεν ήταν και πολύ περίεργο. Μερικοί άνθρωποι μοιράζονταν πράγματα όπως οι δουλειές του σπιτιού, η καθαριότητα και το πλύσιμο ρούχων, τα οποία πολλά o…
items.descriptionOriginal: Some people have quirky hobbies and interests that others might find odd, so when we asked our Upworthy audience on Facebook , “What’s something that you really enjoy that other people can’t seem to understand?” and over 1,700 people weighed in, it wasn’t too surprising. Some people shared things like housework , cleaning and laundry, which a lot of people see as chores. Others shared different puzzles or forms of art they like doing, and still others shared things like long car rides or grocery shopping . But what was surprising was the one answer that dominated the list of responses. It came in various wordings, but by far the most common answer to the question was “silent solitude.” A man sits quietly by the water. Photo credit: Canva Here are a few examples: “Feeling perfectly content, when I’m all alone.” “Being home. Alone. In silence.” “That I enjoy being alone and my soul is at peace in the silence. I don’t need to be around others to feel content, and it takes me days to recharge from being overstimulated after having an eventful day surrounded by others.” “Enjoying your own company. Being alone isn’t isolating oneself. It’s intentional peace and healthy… especially for deep feelers/thinkers.” Spending time by ourselves is something some of us relish, while some of us hate being alone. Naturally, this points to the common theory of introversion vs. extraversion , but in some ways, that’s overly simplistic. Even the most peopley people among us can enjoy some quality alone time, and not all introverts see time alone as truly enjoyable. (It might be necessary for an introvert’s well-being, but not necessarily something they truly revel in.) The surprising psychology of loners Interestingly, studies have found that people who enjoy being alone are not any more or less extraverted than those who don’t, though they do tend to be less “sociable.” They are also much less likely to be neurotic (tense, moody, worrying types) and more likely to be open-minded than people who don’t enjoy being alone. “If our stereotypes about people who like being alone were true, then we should find that they are neurotic and closed-minded. In fact, just the opposite is true,” writes Bella DePaulo, PhD. There may be lots of reasons some people like to spend time by themselves while others don’t. We are naturally social creatures and need social interaction, but some of us find ourselves overstimulated by being around other people all the time. When alone time feels uncomfortable On the flip side, some people find being alone not just unenjoyable, but extremely uncomfortable, which can be a problem. “Ideally, we should be comfortable with ourselves, alone or with others,” writes psychologist Tara Well Ph.D. “If you are uncomfortable being alone, it means you are uncomfortable being with yourself without distraction, engagement, or affirmation from others. This can be a liability in life. If you cannot be alone, you may stay in situations or make life choices that aren’t good for you in the long run, like staying in a job or a relationship, mainly because you can’t tolerate being alone while transitioning to a better situation.” An older woman dances alone while listening to headphones. Photo credit: Canva How to make the most of solitude Dr. Well also points out that people can make the most of their alone time, even if it’s not something they naturally enjoy. One way is to make it purposeful, setting aside a little time daily to write in a journal, meditate, go for a walk or otherwise engage your mind and body in some form of reflection. Another is to pay attention to self-judgments that might make alone time uncomfortable and challenge them with some compassionate confrontation and counteraction with positive thoughts about yourself. Alone time can be refreshing and rewarding, especially if it’s something you naturally crave. Some people even like to take themselves out on dates or enjoy traveling by themselves. That kind of self-care can be just as important as connecting with others for our overall health and well-being. Being alone doesn’t mean being a loner and it doesn’t mean being lonely. Some of us genuinely like having quality time with ourselves, whether it makes sense to other people or not. This article originally appeared last year. It has been updated. The post We asked people what they enjoy that other people don’t understand. One answer ruled them all. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Το 1973, οι Bee Gees τραγούδησαν ένα unplugged medley αφιέρωμα στους Beatles. είναι πανέμορφο.
items.titleOriginal: In 1973, the Bee Gees sang an unplugged medley tribute to the Beatles. It’s gorgeous.
items.description: Μέχρι το 1973, η καριέρα των Bee Gees είχε φτάσει στα χαμηλά. Μετά από μια σειρά επιτυχιών στα τέλη της δεκαετίας του 1960 και στις αρχές της δεκαετίας του 1970, συμπεριλαμβανομένων των "To Love Somebody", "How Can You Mend a Broken Heart" και "I Started a Joke", το συγκρότημα βρισκόταν σε τέλμα. Το τελευταίο τους άλμπουμ, Life in a Tin Can, και το single "Saw a New Morning" πωλήθηκαν ελάχιστα και η δημοτικότητα του συγκροτήματος μειώθηκε. Στις 10 Αυγούστου,…
items.descriptionOriginal: By 1973, the Bee Gees ’ career had hit a low. After a series of hits in the late 1960s and early 1970s, including “To Love Somebody,” “How Can You Mend a Broken Heart,” and “I Started a Joke,” the band was in a rut. Their latest album, Life in a Tin Can , and single “Saw a New Morning” sold poorly, and the band’s popularity declined. On August 10, 1973, the Gibb brothers (Barry, Robin, and Maurice) appeared on The Midnight Special, a late-night TV show that aired on Saturday mornings at 1 a.m. after The Tonight Show with Johnny Carson. Given the lukewarm reception to their recent releases, the Bee Gees decided to change things up and play a medley of hits from their idols, The Beatles, who had broken up three years before. The performance, which featured five of the Fab Four’s early hits, including “If I Fell,” “I Need You,” “I’ll Be Back,” “This Boy,” and “She Loves You,” was a stripped-down, acoustic performance that highlighted the Bee Gees’ trademark harmonies. “When you’ve got brothers singing, it’s like an instrument that nobody else can buy. You can’t go buy that sound in a shop. You can’t sing like The Bee Gees because when you got family members singing together, it’s unique,” Noel Gallagher, who sang with his brother Liam in Oasis, said according to Far Out . From folk harmonies to disco kings A year later, the Bee Gees performed in small clubs , and it looked like their career had hit a dead end. Then, at the urging of their management, the band began to move in a new direction, incorporating soul, rhythm and blues, and a new, underground musical style called disco into their repertoire. Barry also adopted a falsetto singing style popularized by Black singers such as Curtis Mayfield and Marvin Gaye. This unlikely change for the folksy vocal group catapulted them into the stratosphere and they became the white-satin-clad kings of disco. In the late ‘70s, the band had massive hits, including songs featured on the 40-million-selling Saturday Night Fever soundtrack: “Stayin’ Alive,” “How Deep is Your Love,” “More Than a Woman,” Jive Talkin’,” and “Night Fever.” A Beatles tribute that flopped hard In 1978, the band made a significant misstep , starring in a musical based on The Beatles’ music called Sgt. Pepper’s Lonely Hearts Club Band , produced by Robert Stigwood , the man behind Saturday Night Fever and Grease . The film was a colossal bomb, although the soundtrack sold well. The Beatles’ George Harrison thought the Bee Gees film was about what happens when you become successful and greedy. “I just feel sorry for Robert Stigwood, the Bee Gees, and Pete Frampton for doing it because they had established themselves in their own right as decent artists,” Harrison said . “And suddenly… it’s like the classic thing of greed. The more you make the more you want to make, until you become so greedy that ultimately you put a foot wrong.” Even though the Bee Gees’ Beatle-themed musical was a flop, former Beatle John Lennon remained a fan of the group. He sang their praises after the public’s growing distaste of disco resulted in a significant backlash. “Try to tell the kids in the seventies who were screaming to the Bee Gees that their music was just the Beatles redone,” he told Playboy magazine in 1980. “There is nothing wrong with the Bee Gees. They do a damn good job. There was nothing else going on then.” A sound that couldn’t be replaced The Bee Gees historic career ended when Maurice passed away in 2003 at 53. Robin would follow in 2012 at 62. Barry, who turned 80 in September 2026, is the final surviving member of the band. That unmistakable, family-blood harmony they built together is something no lineup change or tribute act has ever quite managed to replicate. From a stripped-down Beatles tribute to disco immortality, the brothers Gibb spent decades proving that some sounds really can’t be bought in a shop, they can only be sung by people who grew up singing together. This article originally appeared last year. It has been updated. The post In 1973, the Bee Gees sang an unplugged medley tribute to the Beatles. It’s gorgeous. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Μια απλή λέξη κάνει τα παιδιά 30 τοις εκατό περισσότερες πιθανότητες να συνεργαστούν. Λειτουργεί και σε ενήλικες.
items.titleOriginal: One simple word makes children 30 percent more likely to cooperate. It works on adults, too.
items.description: Η ανθρώπινη ψυχολογία δεν είναι πραγματικά τόσο περίπλοκη, αν το σκεφτείς. Όλοι θέλουν να δουν τον εαυτό τους με θετικό πρίσμα. Αυτό είναι το κλειδί για να κατανοήσετε την απλή τακτική του Jonah Berger που κάνει τους ανθρώπους 30% πιο πιθανό να κάνουν αυτό που ζητάτε. Ο Μπέργκερ είναι καθηγητής μάρκετινγκ στο Wharton School του Πανεπιστημίου της Πενσυλβάνια και το μπεστ σέλερ…
items.descriptionOriginal: Human psychology really isn’t that complicated, if you think about it. Everybody wants to see themselves in a positive light . That’s the key to understanding Jonah Berger’s simple tactic that makes people 30% more likely to do what you ask . Berger is a marketing professor at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania and the bestselling author of “Magic Words: What to Say to Get Your Way.” Berger explained the technique using a Stanford University study involving preschoolers. The researchers messed up a classroom and made two similar requests to groups of children ages 3 to 6 to help clean up. One group was asked, “Can you help clean?” The other was asked, “Can you be a helper and clean up?” The kids who were asked if they wanted to be a “helper” were 30% more likely to want to clean the classroom. The children weren’t interested in cleaning but wanted to be known as “helpers.” Turning actions into identities Berger calls the reframing of the question as turning actions into identities . “It comes down to the difference between actions and identities. We all want to see ourselves as smart and competent and intelligent in a variety of different things,” Berger told Big Think (video below). “But rather than describing someone as hardworking, describing them as a hard worker will make that trait seem more persistent and more likely to last. Rather than asking people to lead more, tell them, ‘Can you be a leader?’ Rather than asking them to innovate, can you ask them to ‘Be an innovator’? By turning actions into identities, we can make people much more likely to engage in those desired actions.” Berger says that learning to reframe requests to appeal to people’s identities will make you more persuasive. “Framing actions as opportunities to claim desired identities will make people more likely to do them,” Berger tells CNBC Make It . “If voting becomes an opportunity to show myself and others that I am a voter, I’m more likely to do it.” It works both ways, good and bad This technique doesn’t just work because people want to see themselves in a positive light. It also works for the opposite. People also want to avoid seeing themselves being portrayed negatively. “Cheating is bad, but being a cheater is worse. Losing is bad, being a loser is worse,” Berger says. The same tactic can also be used to persuade ourselves to change our self-concept. Saying you like to cook is one thing, but calling yourself a chef is an identity. “I’m a runner. I’m a straight-A student. We tell little kids, ‘You don’t just read, you’re a reader,’” Berger says. “You do these things because that’s the identity you hold.” Berger’s work shows how important it is to hone our communication skills. By simply changing one word, we can get people to comply with our requests more effectively. But, as Berger says, words are magic and we have to use them skillfully. “We think individual words don’t really matter that much. That’s a mistake,” says Berger. “You could have excellent ideas, but excellent ideas aren’t necessarily going to get people to listen to you.” This article originally appeared two years ago. It has been updated. The post One simple word makes children 30 percent more likely to cooperate. It works on adults, too. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Ο συγγραφέας Aubrey Hirsch ρώτησε τι είναι ένα «καθολικό πράγμα που αρέσει στους άντρες» και πήρε ξεκαρδιστικές απαντήσεις
items.titleOriginal: Writer Aubrey Hirsch asked what’s a ‘universal thing men like’ and got hilarious answers
items.description: Η συγγραφέας και εικονογράφος Aubrey Hirsch ρώτησε αστειευόμενος τους followers της στο X (πρώην Twitter) τι είναι ένα «καθολικό πράγμα που αρέσει στους περισσότερους άντρες;» επειδή έγραφε ένα κόμικ και «μόλις συνειδητοποίησα ότι στην πραγματικότητα δεν ξέρω κανέναν άντρα στην πραγματική ζωή». Το tweet ενέπνευσε μια χιονοστιβάδα αστείων απαντήσεων. Ο Hirsch είναι ο συγγραφέας του βιβλίου «Γιατί δεν μιλάμε ποτέ για τη ζάχαρη»…
items.descriptionOriginal: Writer and illustrator Aubrey Hirsch jokingly asked her followers on X (formerly Twitter) what’s a “ universal thing that most men like ?” because she was writing a comic and “just realized I don’t actually know any men in real life .” The tweet inspired an avalanche of funny responses. Hirsch is the author of “Why We Never Talk About Sugar,” a collection of short stories, and her work has appeared in The New York Times, Vox, American Short Fiction and TIME Magazine. The interesting thing about the responses is that they weren’t the typical stereotypes about men. She didn’t get a ton of people talking about sex, sports or toxic masculinity. Instead, there were a lot of folks who mentioned very specific male behaviors as if they were talking about a bizarre species they discovered in the wild. What’s a universal thing that most men like? I’m making a comic but I just realized I don’t actually know any men in real life. — Aubrey Hirsch (@aubreyhirsch) March 21, 2022 The two things that dominated the thread There were, undeniably, two things that got the most comments on her post. First, men enjoy watching construction sites. Evidently, the habit is so well known in Italy that there’s a word for these men: umarell . Watching construction sites, "just in case." https://t.co/5En64Rwrm3 — Wrath Of Gnon (@wrathofgnon) March 22, 2022 When asked why men enjoy watching construction sites so much, a poster on Reddit had the perfect response. “I just find it really satisfying and interesting to see the process behind things being built,” he wrote. The other beloved male activity is throwing heavy objects into bodies of water. Preferably, as large a rock as possible, and as deep a body of water as possible, and getting to throw from the highest vantage point possible. Throwing big rocks off cliffs into lakes https://t.co/hQ1vM0FW9d — Michael (@mcmorrise) March 22, 2022 pic.twitter.com/33W9wqOYP4 — Uhtred Ragnarson (@Iskander861) March 22, 2022 Gotta say, as a man, I have seen dudes do this and I have done it plenty of times myself. A few more that rang true Here are some more fun ones: If a guy walks under a low hanging sign he will jump up and try to tap the bottom of the sign as he passes. Guys like being asked to open jars. Power tools. Give a guy a new drill and he'll wander around looking for stuff that needs holes. — Alan Morgan BLUECHECKMARK (@lettersndigits) March 21, 2022 (When we do this 99% of the time we’re pretending that the sign is 10 feet high and that we have the ability to dunk a basketball. There are two types of men: those that can dunk and mere mortals.) Memorizing favorite lines from their favorite movies, then reciting them with their friends (or even strangers) who’ve also memorized them, doing entire scenes. Extra points for using accents. A true source of unparalleled amusement & male bonding. — Bewildered (@bjcallee) March 22, 2022 This one is near and dear to my heart. I can’t tell you the number of hours I have spent with my friends just throwing lines from “ The Big Lebowski ” back and forth. “Nice marmot.” “The Dude abides.” “Say what you want about the tenets of National Socialism, Dude. At least it’s an ethos.” Another dude-buddy flick that has cemented its place among the most quotable is “ Once Upon a Time … in Hollywood .” “All right, that’s too hot. Anything we can do about that heat?” … “Rick, it’s a flamethrower.” Lastly, we’ll never pass up the opportunity to say hello to a complete stranger wearing our exact same hat, or re-live some sports-related glory days. Right, no-one else has posted this yet, I know my duty: pic.twitter.com/HPwd8qwgUP — Katie (@ZiziFothSi) March 22, 2022 Talking about their athletic glory days pic.twitter.com/9LmaG2oEiD — Ben Ross (@BenRossTweets) March 21, 2022 Okay, everyone is an individual human , but there is certainly a lot to laugh at, and connect to, with this list. This story originally appeared two years ago. It has been updated. The post Writer Aubrey Hirsch asked what’s a ‘universal thing men like’ and got hilarious answers appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Ένας άντρας που ήθελε να «βλέπει μουσική» συνδύασε ένα πιάνο με βιοφωταύγεια φύκια. Είναι μαγικό να το παρακολουθείς.
items.titleOriginal: A man who wanted to ‘see music’ paired a piano with bioluminescent algae. It’s magical to watch.
items.description: Η μουσική προορίζεται να ακούγεται και να μην φαίνεται, σωστά; Σίγουρα, μπορούμε να παρακολουθήσουμε μουσικούς να παίζουν όργανα και μπορούμε να δούμε τη μουσική σημειογραφία σε χαρτί. Αλλά αυτό δεν είναι το ίδιο με το να βλέπεις την ίδια τη μουσική. Ένας νεαρός άνδρας ονόματι He Tongxue από το HTX Studio, μια ομάδα καινοτόμων DIY από το Hangzhou της Κίνας, ήθελε να μπορεί να «βλέπει μουσική». Είχε μόλις αρχίσει να μαθαίνει πιάνο και…
items.descriptionOriginal: Music is meant to be heard and not seen, right? Sure, we can watch musicians play instruments , and we can see music notation on paper . But that’s not the same as seeing music itself. A young man named He Tongxue from HTX Studio, a team of DIY innovators from Hangzhou, China, wanted to be able to “see music.” He had just started learning piano and felt like the visible dimension was missing. There are plenty of computer programs that create digital visual effects with music, of course. But the goal was to make music visible in real life. View this post on Instagram It took the studio three years, four prototypes, and endless tests to come up with just the right combination of elements. They wanted something that would rise from the piano and light up when the keys were pressed. Their first idea went up in smoke “Our first thought was smoke,” he said. They figured they could line up smoke machines that would be triggered by the piano keys and use lasers to light up the smoke as it rises. The studio built a prototype, and at first, it looked pretty cool. But after a few minutes of playing, the cool factor wore off. He later described it as “a disaster.” “The smoke drifts everywhere,” he said. “You can’t tell which light matches which note. It feels like a genie is coming out. And after a while, it feels like someone is barbecuing inside the piano.” They wanted the smoke to rise in chunks, like solid musical notes, instead of spreading out. That led them to the idea of vortex rings. Essentially, they could make smoke rings that would give the visible “notes” more structure. A vortex ring of smoke floats through the air. Photo credit: Canva A second prototype was made to test out this idea. And it did look really cool at first. The vortex rings worked, but there was too much extraneous smoke that eventually built up and made it hard to see the rings. The contraptions that made the rings were also too large to make separate ones for every key on the piano, and making them smaller rendered them unusable. Back to the drawing board again. From smoke rings to paint and water Since a vortex ring is essentially rotating fluid, they shifted to different fluids: water and paint. They created yet another piano prototype that would shoot paint vortex rings into water. Yet again, cool at first, but soon the water simply clouded up as the paint rings dissipated. They tried using oil paints, which wouldn’t dissolve in water, but that also disappointed. Oil paint didn’t form rings, but rather broke apart into small spheres in the water. When smoke didn’t work, the studio turned to water. Photo credit: Canva However, the spheres gave them the idea of simply using droplets. They created a piano that would push up a droplet of colored glycerin into the water tank with each note played. Lights would illuminate them. The idea was solid, but the execution left something to be desired. The beauty of the lit-up droplets didn’t extend throughout the tank. The droplets drifted, and attempts to rein them in with glass tubes ruined the magical effect. “By this point, the project had dragged on for two years,” he said. “We had tried everything we could think of. I honestly didn’t know what I was to do. We’ve abandoned projects before. But never one that consumed this much time, energy, and effort from almost everyone in the studio.” Then disaster struck. One night, the glass tank shattered under the water pressure, destroying the entire system. Watch the full story here: Then nature gave them the answer “If the universe was telling me to stop, this felt like the sign,” he said. But in the midst of significant setbacks and creeping self-doubt, the idea of turning to nature arose. What if they used bioluminescent algae, which light up all on their own? “Around the world, you can see this blue glow in coastal waters,” he said. “It’s caused by a reaction between luciferin and luciferase when the algae are stimulated. We didn’t spray algae into water. We filled the entire tank with them, then disturbed them with bubbles so they would glow all the way to the surface.” He and his studio mates did it. No AI. No digital effects. Real-life, 3D visible music with an assist from nature. They named it the Blue Tears Piano. Here’s German pianist Oskar Roman Jezior playing “Golden Hour” on it: You can follow HTX Studio on YouTube for more incredible innovations. Sometimes the answer was already glowing What makes this story land isn’t just the science, it’s the sheer stubbornness behind it. Two years into a project that kept failing in increasingly spectacular ways, most people would have called it a lesson learned and moved on. He Tongxue and his team didn’t. They kept chasing an image they couldn’t quite build, through a shattered tank and a whole lot of ruined water, until the answer turned out to be something nature had been doing quietly in coastal waters the entire time. That’s really the quiet magic of the Blue Tears Piano. It’s not AI, and it’s not a screen. It’s real light, made by living things, responding to real music in real time. Sometimes the most impressive innovation isn’t inventing something new at all. It’s noticing what was already there and finding a way to let it shine. This article originally appeared in April. It has been updated. The post A man who wanted to ‘see music’ paired a piano with bioluminescent algae. It’s magical to watch. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Οι επιστήμονες προτείνουν ένα πρότυπο σχεδίασης που βασίζεται σε περιγραφείς για υλικά καθόδου μπαταρίας
items.titleOriginal: Scientists propose descriptor-driven design paradigm for battery cathode materials
items.description: Επιστήμονες από το Ινστιτούτο Έρευνας Μετάλλων (IMR) της Κινεζικής Ακαδημίας Επιστημών έχουν δημιουργήσει ένα νέο πρότυπο για το σχεδιασμό υλικών καθόδου οξειδίου. Έχουν προχωρήσει πέρα ​​από τις εμπειρικές δοκιμές και σφάλματα προς το σχεδιασμό προσανατολισμένο στο στόχο χρησιμοποιώντας φυσικοχημικούς περιγραφείς.
items.descriptionOriginal: Scientists from the Institute of Metal Research (IMR) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences have established a new paradigm for designing oxide cathode materials. They have moved beyond empirical trial and error toward goal-oriented design using physicochemical descriptors.

items.title: Ένα κοινό σήμα για ανθρώπους και ρομπότ: Η ευέλικτη οθόνη χρησιμοποιεί χρώμα και εγγύς υπέρυθρες για επικοινωνία
items.titleOriginal: A shared signal for humans and robots: Flexible display uses both color and near-infrared to communicate
items.description: Μια κοινή ερευνητική ομάδα από το Προηγμένο Ινστιτούτο Επιστήμης και Τεχνολογίας της Κορέας (KAIST) και το Πανεπιστήμιο Yonsei έχει αναπτύξει μια ευέλικτη οθόνη που μπορεί να μεταφέρει πληροφορίες τόσο σε ανθρώπους όσο και σε ρομπότ. Οι εργαζόμενοι μπορούν να ερμηνεύσουν πληροφορίες μέσω ορατών χρωματικών αλλαγών, ενώ τα ρομπότ μπορούν να ανιχνεύσουν μοτίβα κοντά στο υπέρυθρο αόρατα στο ανθρώπινο μάτι.…
items.descriptionOriginal: A joint research team from the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST) and Yonsei University has developed a flexible display that can communicate information to both humans and robots. Human workers can interpret information through visible color changes, while robots can detect near-infrared patterns invisible to the human eye. The technology could serve as an "electronic tag" attached to products or equipment, allowing humans and robots to monitor work status using the same display.

items.descriptionOriginal: Ένα διαφορετικό μοντέλο λειτουργίας των data centers επιχειρεί να παρουσιάσει η Σουηδία , με χαρακτηριστικό παράδειγμα την εγκατάσταση της EcoDataCenter στην πόλη Φάλουν. Κατασκευασμένη από ξύλο, τροφοδοτούμενη αποκλειστικά από ανανεώσιμες πηγές ενέργειας και σχεδιασμένη με γνώμονα τις ανάγκες της τοπικής κοινωνίας, φιλοδοξεί να αποδείξει ότι η ψηφιακή ανάπτυξη δεν χρειάζεται να γίνεται εις βάρος του περιβάλλοντος. «Ήταν αρκετά εντυπωσιακό όταν το κατασκευάζαμε. Έμοιαζε με ένα τεράστιο ΙΚΕΑ», περιγράφει ο Τζον Βέρνβικ, στέλεχος της EcoDataCenter, κατά την ξενάγησή του στις εγκαταστάσεις της εταιρείας στη Φάλουν της Σουηδίας. Η πρώτη εντύπωση είναι πράγματι ασυνήθιστη. Σε αντίθεση με τα παραδοσιακά data centers , που κατασκευάζονται κυρίως από χάλυβα και σκυρόδεμα, το συγκεκριμένο κτίριο έχει ξύλινο σκελετό. Μεγάλα πάνελ από συγκολλητή ξυλεία διασταυρούμενων στρώσεων (CLT) έφτασαν στο εργοτάξιο ήδη κομμένα στις απαιτούμενες διαστάσεις και συναρμολογήθηκαν με τη βοήθεια γερανών, σχεδόν όπως τα έπιπλα επίπεδης συσκευασίας. Το αποτέλεσμα θυμίζει έναν τεράστιο, άδειο εκθεσιακό χώρο ΙΚΕΑ, με ψηλά ταβάνια και πεντακάθαρους διαδρόμους. Ωστόσο, η επιλογή του ξύλου δεν έγινε μόνο για αισθητικούς λόγους. Σύμφωνα με τον Βέρνβικ, διευθυντή εξωτερικών σχέσεων και βιωσιμότητας της εταιρείας, η χρήση ξυλείας μειώνει κατά τρεις φορές τον ενσωματωμένο άνθρακα της συνολικής κατασκευής σε σύγκριση με ένα αντίστοιχο κτίριο από χάλυβα και σκυρόδεμα. Παρά το γεγονός ότι απαιτούνται μεγάλες ποσότητες ξύλου για μια εγκατάσταση στο μέγεθος γηπέδου ποδοσφαίρου, ο ίδιος υποστηρίζει ότι τα σουηδικά δάση χρειάζονται μόλις 10 έως 15 λεπτά για να αναπληρώσουν την ποσότητα ξυλείας που χρησιμοποιείται σε ένα data center της εταιρείας. 100% ανανεώσιμη ενέργεια και εξαιρετικά χαμηλές εκπομπές Οι εγκαταστάσεις της EcoDataCenter στη Φάλουν της Σουηδίας. Φωτογραφία: EcoDataCenter Τα data centers βρίσκονται ολοένα και συχνότερα στο επίκεντρο αντιδράσεων σε πολλές χώρες. Η τεράστια κατανάλωση ηλεκτρικής ενέργειας και νερού, η κατάληψη μεγάλων εκτάσεων γης, αλλά και οι περιορισμένες θέσεις εργασίας που συχνά δημιουργούν, έχουν προκαλέσει έντονες αντιπαραθέσεις με τις τοπικές κοινωνίες. Στη Φάλουν, όμως, η εικόνα είναι διαφορετική. Η ηλεκτροδότηση της εγκατάστασης προέρχεται αποκλειστικά από ανανεώσιμες πηγές, με το 75% της ενέργειας να προέρχεται από υδροηλεκτρικά έργα και το υπόλοιπο 25% από αιολικά πάρκα. Η Σουηδία διαθέτει ένα από τα λιγότερο ανθρακικά ενεργειακά μείγματα στην Ευρώπη, καθώς μόλις το 1% της ηλεκτρικής της ενέργειας προέρχεται από ορυκτά καύσιμα. Το αντίστοιχο ποσοστό στην Ευρωπαϊκή Ένωση ανέρχεται στο 29%, ενώ στις ΗΠΑ φτάνει το 55%. Μάλιστα, σε ορισμένες αγροτικές περιοχές της Σουηδίας, όπου η παραγωγή από υδροηλεκτρικά, ηλιακά και αιολικά συστήματα μπορεί να ξεπερνά την τοπική ζήτηση, τα ενεργοβόρα data centers συμβάλλουν στην εξισορρόπηση του ηλεκτρικού δικτύου. Η εγκατάσταση στη Φάλουν έχει ισχύ 80 MW, ποσότητα που αντιστοιχεί περίπου στην κατανάλωση 60.000 κατοικιών. Παρά το μεγάλο ενεργειακό της αποτύπωμα, οι δείκτες λειτουργίας της παρουσιάζουν σημαντικές διαφορές σε σχέση με τους μέσους όρους άλλων περιοχών. Ένας από τους βασικούς δείκτες είναι η αποτελεσματικότητα χρήσης άνθρακα (CUE), η οποία μετρά τις εκπομπές διοξειδίου του άνθρακα ανά κιλοβατώρα ενέργειας που καταναλώνεται. Ενώ ο μέσος όρος των data centers στις ΗΠΑ ανέρχεται σε 414 γραμμάρια CO₂ ανά κιλοβατώρα και στην Ευρωπαϊκή Ένωση σε 263 γραμμάρια, η EcoDataCenter καταγράφει μόλις 1,17 γραμμάρια. Αντίστοιχα, στον δείκτη αποτελεσματικότητας χρήσης ενέργειας (PUE), που αποτυπώνει πόσο αποδοτικά αξιοποιείται η ηλεκτρική ενέργεια μιας εγκατάστασης, η εταιρεία εμφανίζει τιμή 1,15, έναντι 1,36 που είναι ο μέσος όρος στην Ευρωπαϊκή Ένωση. Όσο πιο κοντά βρίσκεται η τιμή στο 1, τόσο μεγαλύτερη είναι η ενεργειακή αποδοτικότητα. Η πρόκληση της ψύξης των πανίσχυρων υπολογιστών Ο Τζον Βέρνβικ στις εγκαταστάσεις της EcoDataCenter στη Φάλουν της Σουηδίας. Φωτογραφία: Josefine Stenersen / The Guardian Το μεγαλύτερο μέρος της ενέργειας καταναλώνεται από τις μονάδες επεξεργασίας γραφικών (GPU), τα πανίσχυρα και ακριβά μικροτσίπ που χρησιμοποιούνται για υπολογιστικές εργασίες, κυρίως στην τεχνητή νοημοσύνη. Περίπου το 70% της υπολογιστικής ισχύος της εγκατάστασης εξυπηρετεί εφαρμογές τεχνητής νοημοσύνης, ωστόσο τα data centers υποστηρίζουν και πλήθος καθημερινών ψηφιακών υπηρεσιών, από τις τραπεζικές συναλλαγές μέχρι το streaming. Η συνεχής παροχή ηλεκτρικής ενέργειας είναι απολύτως απαραίτητη, καθώς ακόμα και μια διακοπή διάρκειας λίγων χιλιοστών του δευτερολέπτου μπορεί να προκαλέσει προβλήματα. Για τον λόγο αυτό υπάρχουν εφεδρικές γεννήτριες, οι οποίες όμως λειτουργούν με υδρογονοκατεργασμένο φυτικό έλαιο (HVO), ένα βιοκαύσιμο που παράγεται από χρησιμοποιημένα φυτικά έλαια και ζωικά λίπη. Εξίσου σημαντική είναι η ψύξη, καθώς οι επεξεργαστές παράγουν τεράστιες ποσότητες θερμότητας. Το ψυχρό κλίμα της Σουηδίας περιορίζει τις ανάγκες, ενώ η εγκατάσταση αντλεί το μεγαλύτερο μέρος του νερού της από κοντινή λίμνη, η οποία στο παρελθόν χρησιμοποιούνταν για την ύδρευση. Όταν η εξωτερική θερμοκρασία είναι χαμηλή, το νερό μπορεί να κυκλοφορεί στους χώρους χωρίς να απαιτείται πρόσθετη ψύξη. Σε θερμότερες ημέρες χρησιμοποιούνται ηλεκτρικά συστήματα ψύξης στις οροφές, τα οποία αξιοποιούν λεπτό ψεκασμό νερού. Η επόμενη γενιά τεχνολογίας, ωστόσο, στρέφεται προς την υγρή ψύξη. Σε αυτήν την περίπτωση, η θερμότητα μεταφέρεται απευθείας σε υγρό και όχι μέσω του αέρα. Το σύστημα που παρουσιάζει η εταιρεία λειτουργεί σε κλειστό κύκλωμα και δεν απαιτεί εξωτερική παροχή νερού. «Κάθε ικρίωμα εδώ είναι ουσιαστικά 25 σάουνες που πρέπει να ψύξουμε και να διατηρήσουμε περίπου στους 27 βαθμούς Κελσίου, ώστε να μην υπερθερμανθούν», εξηγεί ο Βέρνβικ, περιγράφοντας την τεχνική πρόκληση. Στους συγκεκριμένους χώρους λειτουργούν μικροτσίπ Blackwell, τα οποία χρησιμοποιούνται από την DeepL, τη γερμανική πλατφόρμα τεχνητής νοημοσύνης για μεταφράσεις. Μεταξύ των γνωστών πελατών της EcoDataCenter βρίσκονται επίσης η αμερικανική εταιρεία υπολογιστικού νέφους CoreWeave και η γαλλική εταιρεία τεχνητής νοημοσύνης Mistral, καθώς και ερευνητικά ιδρύματα και πανεπιστήμια. Διαβάστε ακόμα Η θερμότητα δεν πάει χαμένη Οι δεξαμενές νερού που χρησιμοποιούνται για την ψύξη των υπολογιστών στο data center της Φάλουν. Φωτογραφία: Josefine Stenersen / The Guardian Ένα από τα πιο ενδιαφέροντα στοιχεία του σχεδιασμού είναι η αξιοποίηση της θερμότητας που παράγεται από τους υπολογιστές. Μέρος της χρησιμοποιείται για την ξήρανση ξύλινων πέλετ, τα οποία αποτελούν παραπροϊόν της βιομηχανίας ξυλείας. Στη συνέχεια, τα πέλετ χρησιμοποιούνται ως καύσιμο σε μονάδες θέρμανσης σε κατοικημένες περιοχές. Μία τέτοια μονάδα βρίσκεται ακριβώς δίπλα στις εγκαταστάσεις της EcoDataCenter. Η υπόλοιπη θερμότητα, μεταξύ άλλων από τα συστήματα υγρής ψύξης, διοχετεύεται απευθείας στο δίκτυο τηλεθέρμανσης της Φάλουν. Η τηλεθέρμανση αποτελεί διαδεδομένη πρακτική στη Σουηδία εδώ και δεκαετίες. Το νερό θερμαίνεται σε κεντρικές εγκαταστάσεις και μεταφέρεται μέσω υπόγειων σωληνώσεων σε κατοικίες και επιχειρήσεις, περιορίζοντας την ανάγκη για μεμονωμένα συστήματα θέρμανσης. Με αυτόν τον τρόπο, η θερμότητα που διαφορετικά θα χανόταν αξιοποιείται για την κάλυψη πραγματικών αναγκών της πόλης. Ένα data center που ξεκίνησε από την τοπική κοινωνία Στο εσωτερικό των εγκαταστάσεων στη Φάλουν. Φωτογραφία: Josefine Stenersen / The Guardian Ίσως η σημαντικότερη διαφορά του συγκεκριμένου έργου να βρίσκεται στον τρόπο με τον οποίο ξεκίνησε. Σε πολλές περιοχές του κόσμου, οι κάτοικοι μαθαίνουν για την κατασκευή ενός data center όταν τα έργα έχουν ήδη δρομολογηθεί. Στη Φάλουν, αντίθετα, η πρωτοβουλία προήλθε από την ίδια τη δημοτική αρχή. Η ιδέα εμφανίστηκε το 2010, αρκετά χρόνια πριν από την έκρηξη της τεχνητής νοημοσύνης. Ο δήμος εξέτασε πώς θα μπορούσε να ενταχθεί μια τέτοια εγκατάσταση στην τοπική οικονομία και τις υποδομές, προτού αποφασίσει ότι η διαχείριση του εγχειρήματος θα έπρεπε να ανατεθεί σε ιδιωτική εταιρεία. Έτσι δημιουργήθηκε η EcoDataCenter το 2014, ενώ το πρώτο τμήμα της εγκατάστασης στη Φάλουν ξεκίνησε να λειτουργεί το 2019. Η εταιρεία υποστηρίζει ότι το 90% των προμηθευτών της προέρχεται από την τοπική αγορά και ότι το 60% των κεφαλαιουχικών δαπανών της κατευθύνεται στην περιοχή. Παράλληλα, χρηματοδοτεί εκπαιδευτικές και επιμορφωτικές δράσεις, αθλητικές ομάδες και δραστηριότητες για νέους. Η λογική αυτή συνεχίζεται και στη δεύτερη εγκατάσταση της εταιρείας, στο Μπορλένγκε, μια βιομηχανική πόλη περίπου 20 λεπτά μακριά από τη Φάλουν. Το νέο data center κατασκευάζεται σε έκταση 200.000 τετραγωνικών μέτρων, σε χώρο όπου λειτουργούσε παλαιότερα χαρτοποιία, η οποία έκλεισε το 2021. Η επιλογή της συγκεκριμένης τοποθεσίας επιτρέπει την αξιοποίηση υφιστάμενων υποδομών, όπως το ηλεκτρικό δίκτυο, η υδροδότηση και το σύστημα τηλεθέρμανσης. Η πρώτη φάση της εγκατάστασης αναμένεται να λειτουργήσει το 2027 και, όταν ολοκληρωθεί, θα διαθέτει ισχύ 240 MW, δηλαδή τριπλάσια από εκείνη της μονάδας στη Φάλουν. Εκτιμάται ότι θα απασχολεί 200 έως 300 εργαζομένους, αριθμός αντίστοιχος με εκείνον που εργαζόταν στην παλαιά χαρτοποιία. Το σουηδικό μοντέλο επεκτείνεται και σε άλλες χώρες Οι εργασίες κατασκευής του EcoDataCenter 2 στο Μπορλένγκε της Σουηδίας. Φωτογραφία: Byggpartner Η προσπάθεια αξιοποίησης των data centers ως μέρος μιας ευρύτερης ενεργειακής και οικονομικής στρατηγικής δεν περιορίζεται στη Φάλουν. Στη Στοκχόλμη, η πρωτοβουλία Stockholm Data Parks, που δημιουργήθηκε το 2014 από τον δήμο και εταιρείες ενέργειας, ηλεκτρικών δικτύων και οπτικών ινών, έχει στόχο να διευκολύνει την εγκατάσταση επιχειρήσεων του κλάδου, δίνοντας έμφαση στην καθαρή ενέργεια και την ανάκτηση θερμότητας. Η πόλη διαθέτει ένα από τα μεγαλύτερα δίκτυα τηλεθέρμανσης στον κόσμο, με περισσότερα από 3.000 χιλιόμετρα σωληνώσεων, το οποίο εξυπηρετεί σχεδόν το 90% της πρωτεύουσας. Περίπου 20 από τα 50 μικρότερα data centers της ευρύτερης περιοχής είναι συνδεδεμένα με το δίκτυο και συνεισφέρουν περίπου το 1,5% των ετήσιων αναγκών της πόλης σε θέρμανση. Ανάλογες πρωτοβουλίες αναπτύσσονται και σε άλλες σκανδιναβικές χώρες. Στη Δανία, η εταιρεία atNorth σχεδιάζει να αξιοποιήσει την πλεονάζουσα θερμότητα από ένα μεγάλο data center στο Βάρντε για τη λειτουργία θερμοκηπίων έκτασης 20 εκταρίων, με στόχο την παραγωγή ντομάτας κατά τους έξι χειμερινούς μήνες. Στη Νορβηγία, αντίστοιχα, η Green Mountain διοχετεύει θερμότητα από τις εγκαταστάσεις της σε γειτονική ιχθυοκαλλιέργεια. Οι προκλήσεις και τα όρια του μοντέλου Μακέτα των εγκαταστάσεων στο Μπορλένγκε της Σουηδίας. Φωτογραφία: Josefine Stenersen / The Guardian Παρά τα πλεονεκτήματα, η αναπαραγωγή του σουηδικού μοντέλου σε άλλες χώρες δεν είναι εύκολη υπόθεση. Η Σουηδία διαθέτει εδώ και δεκαετίες ανεπτυγμένες υποδομές ανανεώσιμης ενέργειας, ψυχρό κλίμα, αξιόπιστα δίκτυα και αυστηρότερο πλαίσιο περιβαλλοντικών και πολεοδομικών κανόνων. Η δημιουργία αντίστοιχων συνθηκών σε χώρες όπως οι ΗΠΑ θα απαιτούσε σημαντικό χρόνο και επενδύσεις. Την ίδια στιγμή, η ζήτηση από τους τεχνολογικούς κολοσσούς είναι τεράστια. Η συνολική δυναμικότητα των data centers στην Ευρώπη εκτιμάται ότι αντιστοιχεί μόλις στο 15% έως 25% εκείνης των ΗΠΑ. Μεγάλες εταιρείες επεκτείνονται ήδη στις σκανδιναβικές χώρες. Η Meta κατασκευάζει εγκατάσταση ισχύος 723 MW στη Λουλέο της Σουηδίας, η Brookfield σχεδιάζει ένα data center 750 MW στο Στρέγκνες, ενώ η Google ξεκίνησε την κατασκευή μονάδας 150 MW στο Χόρνταλ. Ωστόσο, η παρουσία των μεγάλων τεχνολογικών εταιρειών δεν συνοδεύεται πάντα από την ίδια αποδοχή. Η Google έχει δεχθεί επικρίσεις για την αποψίλωση δασικής έκτασης στη Φινλανδία, ενώ εργολάβοι που κατασκευάζουν εγκαταστάσεις της Microsoft στη Σουηδία έχουν κατηγορηθεί για κακές συνθήκες διαμονής και εργασίας των εργαζομένων τους. Οι εταιρείες έχουν απαντήσει ότι διαθέτουν κανόνες και διαδικασίες για την προστασία του περιβάλλοντος και των εργασιακών δικαιωμάτων. Ακόμη και στις σκανδιναβικές χώρες, πάντως, η αντίθεση στην κατασκευή νέων data centers αρχίζει να ενισχύεται, καθώς αυξάνεται η ανησυχία για την κατανάλωση φυσικών πόρων και την αλλαγή του τοπίου. Το ερώτημα, επομένως, δεν είναι μόνο πόσα data centers χρειάζεται ο κόσμος, αλλά και με ποιους όρους θα κατασκευάζονται. Η εμπειρία της Σουηδίας δείχνει ότι η ενεργειακή αποδοτικότητα, η αξιοποίηση της πλεονάζουσας θερμότητας και η συμμετοχή των τοπικών κοινωνιών μπορούν να αποτελέσουν βασικά στοιχεία ενός διαφορετικού μοντέλου ψηφιακής ανάπτυξης. Το αν η εγκατάσταση της Φάλουν είναι πράγματι το «πιο πράσινο data center στον κόσμο» παραμένει ένας χαρακτηρισμός που χρειάζεται συγκριτική αξιολόγηση. Ωστόσο, αποτελεί ένα χαρακτηριστικό παράδειγμα του πώς οι τεχνολογικές υποδομές μπορούν να σχεδιάζονται με μεγαλύτερη έμφαση στο περιβάλλον και στις ανάγκες των ανθρώπων που ζουν γύρω τους. items.title: 30% πτώση στα επίπεδα των Forever Chemicals στα ποτάμια της Αγγλίας, 49% στα ψάρια - "Brilliant to See"
items.titleOriginal: 30% Drop in Levels of Forever Chemicals in England’s Rivers, 49% in Fish – ‘Brilliant to See’
items.description: 2 εξέχουσες χημικές ενώσεις που απαγορεύονται βάσει του διεθνούς δικαίου λόγω ανησυχιών για την υγεία βρίσκονται σε σημαντικά χαμηλότερες συγκεντρώσεις στα ποτάμια της Αγγλίας. Οι συγκεντρώσεις αυτών των λεγόμενων «για πάντα χημικών ουσιών» που πέφτουν 30% στο νερό και 49% στα ψάρια ήταν «εξαιρετικές», είπε ένας ερευνητής στο BBC, λέγοντας ότι ήταν ένας δείκτης για το «πόσο μακριά έχουμε…
items.descriptionOriginal: 2 prominent chemical compounds prohibited under international law over health concerns are being found at substantially lower concentrations in England’s rivers. items.descriptionOriginal: Imagine receiving your monthly bank statement, opening the PDF on your phone and trying to find out how much money is in your account. But no matter how many times you try, the information remains out of reach. For a person with visual impairments, this can be an everyday experience. While a screen reader can read aloud the text on a phone or computer, it cannot always make sense of a PDF. The figures, tables and other information can remain inaccessible, leaving people dependent on someone else to read something as personal as their bank statement. The same problem extends to school textbooks, government forms and even company reports. When 17-year-old Yash Bhatnagar learnt about this gap, he began wondering if technology could help fix it. A self-taught coder who had already built a couple of digital tools, he decided to take on a problem that many people had overlooked. Visionably helps organisations convert inaccessible PDFs into documents that screen readers can navigate. Today, he is developing an AI-powered solution that helps convert inaccessible PDFs into documents that people with visual impairments can navigate using screen readers. But his idea goes beyond making a few documents readable. He wants organisations to rethink how they create and share information in the first place. From classroom tools to accessible PDFs Yash's interest in building things began early. Introduced to programming by his parents, he took a basic coding course on Khan Academy and continued learning independently, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic. His parents recall how he took to programming almost immediately. "Even as a very young kid, he was demonstrating a penchant for building new technology," they share. Yash developed Visionably after discovering how difficult it can be for visually impaired people to access everyday digital documents. Rather than treating coding as an experimental hobby, Yash wanted to create products that solved problems for actual users. His first major project was LitGrades, an AI-powered flashcard generation platform launched in early 2023. After piloting it at his school, the platform grew to reach around 720 students, including learners from Ukraine. He then developed Silenttype, a real-time transcription tool that converted classroom lectures into notes that students could save in their digital libraries. In October 2025, while pitching the idea at IIM Ahmedabad, he began exploring how the tool could also help deaf users by transcribing spoken conversations and lectures. However, a conversation with the team there introduced him to a different challenge. "They told me that while they thought it was a good tool, there were more blind people who needed technology for OCR and converting PDFs into an accessible format," Yash recalls. The suggestion stayed with him. He was introduced to a few sample documents and began experimenting with ways to make them accessible. As he explored the problem, he realised that the challenge went beyond converting text into speech. Most PDFs are created without the underlying structure that screen readers need to interpret their contents. A document may look perfectly readable to a sighted person, with headings, paragraphs, tables and images arranged on a page. But without proper accessibility tags, a screen reader may not understand the reading order, distinguish between sections or describe visual elements. For someone relying on assistive technology, the result can be a document that is difficult, if not impossible, to navigate. Yash began working on a solution , initially with guidance from people in the accessibility community. One was Rashi, who works with V-Shesh, an organisation that supports people with disabilities and promotes accessibility. "The fact that persons with vision impairment have to struggle in educational institutions because a document was not accessible is something I have seen closely," Rashi says. She recalls students having to request assistance just to have documents read aloud to them. That experience made the problem particularly meaningful to her. As conversations between Yash and accessibility professionals continued, the initial prototype gradually evolved into Visionably. What makes a PDF readable to a screen reader? Visionably works primarily with businesses and organisations rather than asking individual users to fix documents themselves. Yash's approach is simple: make information accessible at the source. "It would make sense to make a news article accessible for every reader, but the newspaper should make it accessible themselves," he explains. Organisations share their PDFs with Visionably, which processes them through its AI-powered remediation engine. In simple terms, the tool helps add the information that screen readers need to understand how a document is organised. The technology identifies and adds details such as accessibility tags, reading order and descriptions for images. These changes help documents meet internationally recognised accessibility standards, including the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2 and PDF/UA, which outline requirements for accessible PDF documents. Once processed, the accessible files are sent back to the organisation. Yash says the turnaround can be around 48 hours, depending on the engagement. Building this technology, however, was not as straightforward as developing a tool that could extract text from a PDF. The AI-powered tool adds accessibility tags, reading order and image descriptions to PDF documents. Documents come in countless formats, with different layouts, tables, images and formatting styles. A system that works for a simple text document may struggle with a complex financial statement or a textbook containing several visual elements. "Because the number of PDFs on the internet is so large and the formats are so vast, it's very hard to account for every possible use case," Yash says. He worked through more than 1,000 test cases and iterations, regularly sharing documents with accessibility professionals and visually impaired users for feedback. He also received technical guidance from SaralX AI, a company working in the same space. According to Yash, the engine now succeeds on around 95% of the PDFs it is tested on. Crucially, the development process involves people who actually use screen readers. Yash says he has worked with a recurring visually impaired tester who reviews the documents and helps identify gaps that he might otherwise miss. Rashi recalls one instance when a visually impaired person tested an early prototype and pointed out several areas that needed improvement. "Yash said he wanted to meet again after a week. He sat through the night and by morning he had fixed everything," she says. For her, that willingness to act on feedback is what sets his work apart. Making websites easier to navigate for everyone Document remediation is only one part of Visionably's work. The venture also conducts automated accessibility audits of websites. These audits help organisations identify issues such as images without alternative text, missing accessibility features and elements that do not meet WCAG requirements. The system uses open-source technology alongside AI-based adjustments to examine websites and generate reports highlighting areas that need attention. For instance, simply checking whether an image has alternative text is not enough. The description itself must communicate what the image contains. An image labelled only as 'image' may technically have text attached to it, but it does little to help someone using a screen reader understand its purpose. Visionably's AI layer helps assess whether such descriptions are meaningful. Yash's Digital Banking Accessibility Index 2026 identified 2,221 accessibility barriers across 30 major Indian bank websites. Yash also released Outloud, a free, open-source tool that allows people to test whether their PDFs meet accessibility requirements. Unlike some existing tools that are limited to particular operating systems or workflows, Outloud works across Windows, Mac and Linux. Users can run accessibility checks, examine the results and even incorporate the tool into their own development processes. The idea is to make accessibility testing more widely available, including to developers and organisations that may not have the resources for expensive assessments. From children's books to banking websites One of Visionably's first paying clients is V-Shesh, which works with organisations on disability inclusion and accessibility. Through this engagement, Visionably has begun remediating documents on a per-page basis. The venture is also working with Pratham Books to make 10 children's books on its StoryWeaver platform accessible, pro bono. Six books had been completed at the time of the interview, with the remaining four nearing completion. For Yash, making these books accessible is particularly important because their stories should be available to children with visual impairments too. Rather than creating separate versions that readers have to search for, the plan is to make the accessible versions available directly on StoryWeaver. Alongside this work, Yash has been examining how accessible some of India's major banking websites are. His banking accessibility audit is another attempt to bring attention to gaps that often go unnoticed. The Digital Banking Accessibility Index 2026 assessed 30 major Indian bank websites, identifying 2,221 accessibility barriers. Yash selected banks based on factors such as their popularity, size and publicly available website traffic data. The automated audit examined multiple accessibility criteria, including whether images had appropriate alternative text and whether website elements met established standards. Through a collaboration with Pratham Books, Visionably is making children's stories accessible to young readers with visual impairments. The findings were shared with the respective banks, along with reports outlining the issues that needed attention. Yash says Kotak Mahindra Bank and Punjab National Bank responded, indicating that the concerns had been forwarded to the relevant teams. He plans to reassess the websites in December 2026 and publish a comparative report to track whether improvements have been made. For Rashi, this kind of accountability is important because accessibility cannot remain an afterthought. "I have interacted with so many children who volunteer with organisations working with persons with disabilities, but Yash is someone who is doing it genuinely, because he truly believes in it and not because it looks good on an application," she says. His next goal: Make accessibility part of the design Running a technology venture while studying in Class 12 is not without its demands. Yash spends around two hours on weekdays managing emails, reaching out to organisations, developing the product and planning new projects. Weekends are often reserved for longer work sessions and meetings. His parents, who are the company's directors because he is a minor, support him with business discussions and outreach. However, they say he makes the decisions for the startup, seeking their advice when needed. Yash hopes to make accessibility an integral part of how organisations design and share digital information, rather than an afterthought. Yash, meanwhile, sees plenty of room to expand. Over the next two years, he hopes to remediate at least 5,000 files and conduct 200 to 300 website accessibility audits. He is also exploring an assessment of shareholder and investor reports published by India's top 100 listed companies. His larger ambition, however, goes beyond fixing documents after they have been created. One conversation with a visually impaired professional who had previously worked in Microsoft Accessibility left a lasting impression on him. The person pointed out that accessibility is often treated as an afterthought rather than being built into the development process. That is a distinction Yash wants Visionably to address. "Our eventual goal is to become an accessibility design firm, where we don't look at accessibility as something that happens after files are created, but as part of the process when all of this actually begins," he says. All images courtesy of Yash Bhatnagar

items.descriptionOriginal: On 12 November, a pregnant woman lay on an operating table at the All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS) in New Delhi while surgeons performed something no Indian hospital had done before. Over six hours, they repaired a gap in her unborn baby's spine at 25 weeks of pregnancy , then closed the womb so that the pregnancy could continue. The institute announced on 14 November that this was India's first open foetal repair of a lumbosacral myelomeningocele, the most severe form of spina bifida. Professor Deepak Gupta, who led the neurosurgical component and is president of the Indian Society for Pediatric Neurosurgery, says, "It establishes an important new capability for foetal care and paediatric neurosurgery in India." Why doctors operate before birth In myelomeningocele, part of the spinal cord and its protective coverings pushes out through an opening in the spine. Doctors usually close it after the baby is born, but the institute said that exposure to amniotic fluid during pregnancy can cause progressive neurological injury. Surgeons used microsurgical techniques and ultrasound guidance to repair an unborn baby's spinal defect inside the womb. Photograph: ( TNIE ) "Affected children can develop paralysis or hydrocephalus, a build-up of fluid in the brain," the team says. In open foetal surgery , the surgeons open the mother's uterus to reach the defect, then carefully repair and cover the exposed spinal tissue in layers using microsurgical techniques before closing the uterus and abdomen, which lets the pregnancy continue under close supervision. Five weeks of rehearsal for one operation The operation followed more than five weeks of preparation that included detailed foetal imaging, counselling of the parents, anaesthetic planning and surgical simulations. "More than 30 doctors, specialists and nurses then took part, drawn from obstetrics, maternal-foetal medicine, neurosurgery, anaesthesia, plastic surgery, radiodiagnosis and neonatology, working with high-end microscopy and continuous ultrasound guidance at the Neurosciences Centre," the team says. More than five weeks of preparation and surgical simulations preceded the six-hour operation at AIIMS Delhi. Photograph: ( Newsonair ) AIIMS Director Professor Nikhil Tandon says the operation's complexity made teamwork decisive. "It is a matter of both pleasure and huge pride that such a complicated surgery could be done in this institution," he says. "It is a testimony to multiple very highly skilled people. Individually skilled and skilled as a team who could come together, sit, plan, collaborate, coordinate, and implement." He adds that the surgery is difficult even on a small child , and here the baby was operated on inside the womb. "Imagine the size. It is such delicate surgery," he says. "At least 36-37 doctors" were in the operating theatre, he says, including obstetricians, anaesthetists, radiologists, geneticists, neurosurgeons and plastic surgeons, along with the nursing staff and other OT staff. "It is very hard work, and it needed a lot of coordination. I think that teamwork was extremely important for us." Professor Neena Malhotra and Professor K Aparna Sharma headed the maternal-foetal medicine and obstetric teams. Sharma says the decision to intervene came from a careful assessment of the benefits and risks to both mother and baby, adding that safety depends on "detailed counselling, high-quality anaesthesia, and coordinated surveillance" before and after surgery. Professors Vimi Rewari and Mihir Pandia, with Drs Rashmi Ramachandran and Gyanendra Pal Singh, handled anaesthesia; Dr Shashank Chauhan led plastic surgery, and Drs Ramesh Agarwal and Deepika Kainth supported neonatology. Dr Anubhuti Rana, Dr Deepali Garg and Dr Saloni Kamboj helped screen and counsel the patient. From an idea in 2012 to an operating table Prenatal repair of myelomeningocele in humans was first performed in 1997, and more than 200 foetuses had undergone it before the trial began in 2003, so AIIMS joins a technique refined over nearly three decades. The evidence comes from the Management of Myelomeningocele Study, a randomised trial of 183 women published in 2011. By 12 months, 40% of children who had prenatal surgery needed a shunt to drain brain fluid, against 82% after postnatal repair, though the trial also recorded more preterm deliveries and uterine scar complications. Gupta recalled where it began. "Fourteen years ago, we spoke of the possibility of foetal spinal surgery at AIIMS," he said, and the institute now says it has the integrated expertise to assess and offer the repair to appropriately selected families. What the surgery cannot promise The doctors were careful not to oversell the spina bifida repair. Gupta described prenatal repair as a way to limit ongoing injury to exposed nerve tissue and to reduce the later need for a shunt, yet he stressed that it is not a cure and that long-term care from several specialities remains essential. The risks include premature delivery and complications from the uterine scar, which can affect later pregnancies, so the institute recommends it only for carefully selected pregnancies at specialised centres. The mother and baby remain under close observation until birth and through the newborn period, so the outcome of the repair is not yet known. The institute's statement does not name the family, but it confirms that the procedure was provided free of cost under the Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram, the government scheme offering free care to pregnant women and sick newborns who use public health facilities. Tandon says this was central. "We are immensely grateful that in this hospital, which is a publicly funded hospital, this entire work was done supported through a government scheme, at no cost to the patient," he says. "That, I think, is another very important point which needs to be communicated." Prevention matters as much, the team added. The neural tube closes about 28 days after conception, often before a woman knows she is pregnant, so doctors urged folic acid counselling before conception, food fortification with folates and stronger national surveillance of neural tube defects. The team's next goal, in its own words, is to make the surgery "safe and accessible" to the Indian families who may benefit from it. Sources: ' AIIMS Delhi Performs First Foetal Spinal Surgery In India ': by Archana Jyoti for Outlook India, Published on 14 November, 2026 ' AIIMS-Delhi Performs India's First Open Foetal Surgery To Repair Severe Spinal Defect ': by PTI for ETV Bharat, Published on 14 November, 2026 ' AIIMS Delhi completes India's first open fetal repair for spina bifida ': for The News Mill, Published in November, 2026 ' A Randomized Trial of Prenatal versus Postnatal Repair of Myelomeningocele ': by N. items.descriptionOriginal: A revolutionary new wearable patch could help people get more restorative sleep without medication or surgery. Developed by University of Texas researchers, the device uses gentle ultrasound to stimulate deep brain regions, helping participants enter REM sleep 43 minutes faster and remain there 16 minutes longer on average. The technology also showed promising effects on stress regulation and brain circuits involved in emotion.
