items.titleOriginal: In This Assam Village, a Forest Spider Is Fried in Mustard Oil & Served as a Seasonal Delicacy. Here’s Why
items.description: Για τον Bhupen Rabha, έναν πρεσβύτερο του χωριού στο Assam, το να τρώει αράχνες είναι μια διατροφική παράδοση με την οποία μεγάλωσε. Θυμάται πώς οι γονείς και οι παππούδες του μάζευαν μεγάλες, τριχωτές αράχνες από τα κοντινά δάση, τις έφερναν στο σπίτι και τις ετοίμαζαν ως εποχική λιχουδιά. Η αράχνη, τοπικά γνωστή ως Bhaluk Makara, είναι η Ινδική Αράχνη Τίγρης της Μαύρης Γης (Lyrogn…
items.descriptionOriginal: For Bhupen Rabha, a village elder in Assam, eating spiders is a food tradition he grew up with. He remembers how his parents and grandparents collected large, hairy spiders from the nearby forests, brought them home and prepared them as a seasonal delicacy. The spider, locally known as Bhaluk Makara , is the Indian Black Earth Tiger Spider ( Lyrognathus crotalus ), a species of tarantula native to Northeast India. Every year, between April and June, members of the Indigenous Rabha community in Assam's Kamrup (Rural) district collect these spiders from underground burrows along the edges of sal forests. Back home, they wash the spiders, soak them in hot water and fry them in mustard oil with salt and garlic powder. The dish is traditionally enjoyed with locally prepared rice beer. But why do they eat spiders? For the Rabha families who follow this practice, the answer lies in generations of food knowledge, the seasonal availability of the spiders and their close relationship with the surrounding forests. In August 2026, a study published in the Proceedings of the Zoological Society documented the community's consumption of this particular spider species for the first time in scientific literature. The research offers a closer look at how this food tradition has survived across generations, while raising important questions about the conservation of the species. How are these forest spiders collected and cooked? Around 65 kilometres southeast of Guwahati lies Mouman village, where members of the Rabha community live close to forests dominated by sal trees. Here, Bhaluk Makara lives in underground burrows. Its local name comes from its appearance. Bhaluk means bear, referring to the spider's large, black body covered in dense hair, while Makara means spider. To understand the community's relationship with the species, researchers Jyotiprakash Boro, Kuldeep Bora, Chandramita Boro and Samir Terdalkar conducted fieldwork between April and June 2025. They interviewed 34 Rabha community members, including village elders and experienced collectors, to understand when the spiders are gathered, how they are prepared and how the practice has been passed down. According to the villagers, the spiders are particularly abundant during April and May, making these the preferred months for collection. Collectors typically venture into the forests for three or four days a month during the peak season. Depending on availability, a single outing can yield around 20 to 30 spiders. Finding them requires familiarity with the forest. Collectors identify burrows along the forest fringes and either carefully dig into the ground or insert a wooden stick to encourage the spider to emerge. Once collected, the spiders are brought home, washed and repeatedly soaked in hot water for several minutes. They are then fried in mustard oil for approximately seven to 10 minutes until browned, with salt and garlic powder added for flavour. For families who have followed this practice for generations, collecting Bhaluk Makara involves knowledge of the spider's habitat, seasonal availability and preparation methods learnt from their elders. Between April and June, members of the indigenous Rabha community venture into areas adjoining sal forests to collect a large, dark, hairy spider from its burrow. Photograph: (Jyotiprakash Bora; iStock) Why has the Rabha community been eating spiders for generations? For the Rabha community, Bhaluk Makara is part of a wider food culture closely connected to the surrounding forests. Agriculture is an important livelihood, while fishing, livestock rearing, weaving and gathering forest resources are also part of community life. Rice is a staple food, accompanied by fish, meat, vegetables and locally collected edible plants. Bhaluk Makara belongs to this tradition of preparing foods available in the local environment. The practice has been passed down through generations, with older family members teaching younger ones where to find the spiders and how to prepare them. Bhupen Rabha told Mongabay India that the tradition had been passed down orally within the community. "The spider was regularly collected and eaten by our parents and grandparents as a seasonal delicacy," he recalled. And the tradition continues among younger community members. Ashok Rabha, a spider collector in his early 20s, described gathering spiders as an enjoyable shared experience and "a kind of rite of passage". For him, searching for burrows, collecting the spiders and eating them together is also a way of participating in a practice learnt from earlier generations. Rohini Kumar Nongbag, another experienced collector, told Mongabay India that younger people continue to collect the spiders during the pre-monsoon months. These accounts show that the practice remains part of community life, rather than something remembered only by older generations. However, researchers point out that the tradition may be limited to particular Rabha villages and households, rather than being followed by the entire community. Similar food practices have also been documented elsewhere in Northeast India. In March 2026, a study published in Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems recorded the consumption of two species of orb-weaver spiders among Indigenous communities in Nagaland. Known locally as siyanky in the Lotha Naga language, these spiders are prepared using ingredients such as ginger, chillies and bamboo shoots. Researchers interviewed 33 people and found that knowledge of collecting and cooking the spiders was similarly passed down through generations. Although the species and recipes differ, both studies show how traditional food practices are connected to local biodiversity and the knowledge communities have developed over time. Its local name, Bhaluk Makara, refers to its bear-like appearance, with its relatively large, black body covered in dense hair. Photograph: (EastMojo) Can this food tradition continue while protecting the spiders? While the August 2026 study has documented an established food tradition, it has also highlighted how much remains unknown about the species. Within the Rabha community, Bhaluk Makara is regarded as a nutritious seasonal food. However, its nutritional composition has yet to be established through laboratory testing. The researchers also found no reported medicinal use of the spider among the community members interviewed. Another important question concerns the spider's population. Some collectors believe the species remains as abundant as it was years ago. Manoj Rabha, who has been collecting spiders for around 12 years, told Mongabay India that he has observed no noticeable decline. According to him, experienced collectors can still gather as many as 30 spiders during an outing. But these observations have yet to be supported by scientific population surveys. Jyotiprakash Boro, a wildlife biologist and research scholar at Fergusson College, Pune, explained to Mongabay India that the researchers had not independently assessed the spider's population or abundance. Scientists still need to understand how many spiders inhabit these forests, how quickly they reproduce and whether repeated collection affects their numbers. This is particularly relevant because some tarantula species grow slowly and take years to reach maturity, potentially making them vulnerable to excessive collection. Importantly, the study does not establish that the Rabha community's existing harvesting practices are harming the spider population. Instead, the researchers have called for further studies into the species' ecology, population dynamics, nutritional composition and conservation status before drawing conclusions about sustainability. For Bhupen and other members of the Rabha community, Bhaluk Makara remains a familiar seasonal food, connected to the forests around their villages and the knowledge they have inherited. The new research brings that knowledge into the scientific record, while opening up opportunities to better understand the spider and its habitat. It also highlights the importance of documenting Indigenous food traditions through the experiences of the people who practise them, so that both their cultural knowledge and the biodiversity connected to it can be better understood and protected. Sources: 'First Record on the Traditional Consumption of the Indian Black Earth Tiger Spider (Lyrognathus crotalus Pocock, 1895) Among the Rabha Tribe from Northeast India' : By Jyotiprakash Boro, Kuldeep Bora, Chandramita Boro and Samir Terdalkar, Published on 18 August 2026 'Edible spiders: an unconventional source of nutrition and therapeutic agents' : By Lobeno Mozhui, Kekhesino Sale, L. N. Kakati, Published on 9 March 2026 'For the Rabhas of Assam, this giant spider is a seasonal delicacy' : By Roopak Goswami, Published on 24 August 2026

Τα φέρετρα με μανιτάρια και οι πράσινες επιλογές ταφής δίνουν στις οικογένειες έναν νέο τρόπο φροντίδας για τον πλανήτη. Η Loop Biotech, μια εταιρεία στο Ντελφτ της Ολλανδίας, τα αναπτύσσει…
items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Mushroom Coffins and Green Burial Give Families a Soil-Enriching Choice Reading Time: 3 minutes Mushroom coffins and green burial options let families return nutrients to the soil. Mushroom coffins and green burial options give families a new way to care for the planet. Loop Biotech , a company in Delft, the Netherlands, grows these products from living mushroom roots. The company says traditional funerals can harm the environment. It points to cutting old trees, releasing carbon dioxide, and adding toxic chemicals to soil. Loop Biotech wants to offer a gentler choice. Interest in greener funerals is growing. A 2023 report from the National Funeral Directors Association found that 60% of consumers would explore green funeral options. That is about six in every ten people, so mushroom coffins and green burials meet a real demand. The idea began at Delft University of Technology. Founders Bob and Lonneke Hendrikx were graduating there when they asked a simple question: Could a final act help the earth instead of harming it? They found an answer in mycelium, the root network of mushrooms. It grows underground and breaks down dead plant matter. As it does, it releases nutrients that feed new life. Mycelium is known as one of nature’s biggest recyclers. Researchers have only recently given it close attention. For years, many of them focused on plants and animals above ground. Loop Biotech grows its products from local mushrooms and upcycled hemp fibers. Upcycled means the fibers are reused instead of thrown away. Hemp is a tough plant often used for rope and cloth. The growing process takes just seven days. Trees used for traditional coffins can take many decades to grow. That difference shows how quickly this material can be made. Once the coffin is buried, it begins to break down. The company says it biodegrades in about 45 days. Mushroom coffins and green burial materials like these return to the soil faster than most wood and metal. The coffin is also strong. Hendrikx says it can carry about 440 pounds (200 kilograms). He adds that people are often surprised by how soft and sturdy it feels. The company invented the world’s first mushroom coffin, called the Loop Living Cocoon. It also makes the Loop EarthRise and the Loop ForestBed. The company describes its products as patented and award-winning. Mushroom coffins and green burial options now include the Loop EarthRise, the world’s first urn made from mushrooms, grown in seven days from local mushrooms and upcycled hemp fibers to nourish the earth and grow a tree in your memory. Photo courtesy of Loop Biotech . Each product is 100% natural and biodegradable. Biodegradable means it breaks down naturally over time. The company also says its products enrich the soil. Soil-enriching is a bold claim, so families should look at the details. Asking a funeral provider about materials, local rules, and cemetery policies is a smart first step. Green burial is a broader movement. It generally avoids embalming chemicals and uses naturally biodegradable materials. Mushroom coffins and green burial fit together because both aim to leave the ground healthier. Why does this matter to families? Many people want a funeral that matches how they lived. For someone who loved gardens or forests, a soil-enriching option may feel personal. Loop Biotech describes its approach as working with nature rather than against it. The founders chose living organisms over dead materials. That idea shapes every product the company grows. The founders describe their mission as turning endings into new beginnings. This view invites people to think about death differently. It treats a funeral as part of a natural cycle. The company grows its products at a facility in Delft, close to where the founders studied. Local mushrooms keep the process tied to the region. That choice also supports the company’s goal of a positive footprint. A footprint is the mark people leave on the environment. The company wants that mark to be positive. It aims to return nutrients to the soil. Demand is spreading beyond Europe. Hendrikx estimates it has sold more than 2,000 coffins in Europe and has started selling in North America. Mushroom coffins and green burial alternatives are now reaching families on both continents. The company shares a brand video. It tells the story behind the products and the people who make them. For more detail, people can watch a TEDx talk by Bob Hendrikx. TEDx is an independently organized event that follows the TED talk format. He explains how mycelium works, how the products grow in seven days, and his vision of a regenerative world that restores natural systems. Mushroom coffins are one of several ideas for gentler goodbyes. Families are also finding new ways to honor loved ones while protecting the planet. Choosing a funeral involves many feelings and practical questions. Families who want an earth-friendly path now have more to consider. Mushroom coffins and green burial may help more people leave a positive mark. The post Mushroom Coffins and Green Burial Give Families a Soil-Enriching Choice appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.titleOriginal: Can Barbershops Turn Trust Into Better Health for Black Men?
items.description: Είμαι Τρίτη πρωί στο Against Da Grain, ένα κουρείο σε έναν ήσυχο δρόμο στη North Shore του Staten Island. Ο ιδιοκτήτης Σον Γουάιτ ολοκληρώνει την περικοπή για έναν μεσήλικα μαύρο ενώ ένας άλλος πελάτης περιμένει εκεί κοντά. Γύρω τους, οι κομμωτές εργάζονται μέσω μιας ροής πελατών. οι συζητήσεις κινούνται μεταξύ αστείων, κοινωνικών ζητημάτων και συνηθισμένων προβλημάτων — α…
items.descriptionOriginal: I t is a Tuesday morning at Against Da Grain, a barbershop on a quiet street on Staten Island’s North Shore. Owner Sean White is rounding off a cut for a middle-aged Black man while another customer waits nearby. Around them, hairstylists work through a stream of clients; conversations move between jokes, social issues and the ordinary problems — and pleasures — of life. “It’s always usually like a community conversation inside of a barbershop,” White says. The shop hosts back-to-school giveaways, free haircut events and Christmas toy distributions, and partners with local organizations to connect residents with resources. White describes the shop as “like a third party to the community.” Against Da Grain was one of 22 Staten Island barbershops that participated in a hypertension screening program. Credit: Tolu Olasoji That intermediary role also creates an opening for health care: a way to reach Black men through a place and relationships already woven into their everyday lives. Dr. Joseph Ravenell is the principal investigator of the Community-to-Clinic Linkage Implementation Program , or CLIP, which brought hypertension screenings into barbershops as part of an American Heart Association study. He remembers going with his father to Mr. Mike’s shop every other Saturday, where the same men returned over months and years. That repetition, he says, builds “a level of trust, a level of camaraderie” that can be difficult to reproduce in health care. Men talked there about sports, politics and relationships, but also about health, and Ravenell was struck by how comfortable they were discussing intimate concerns — and how closely they listened to their barber. “It’s been said to me many times that many Black men trust their barber more than they trust their doctor,” he says. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] CLIP sought to build on that familiarity as a way to reach people with undiagnosed hypertension. The condition is both common and easy to miss. About six in 10 non-Hispanic Black men in the United States have hypertension, according to federal data. Yet high blood pressure often produces no symptoms. Among men ages 18 to 39 who have hypertension, the federal data found, fewer than one in four know they have it . Routine access to health care can make early detection more likely, but access is only part of the problem. A 2019 study linked medical mistrust and perceived racism in health care with delayed checkups and blood-pressure screening among Black men. “It’s always usually like a community conversation inside of a barbershop,” says Sean White. Credit: Tolu Olasoji Led by NYU Langone in partnership with Community Health Action of Staten Island (CHASI), CLIP brought blood-pressure screening and health support into 22 Black-owned barbershops from Staten Island zip codes with high hypertension prevalence . Against Da Grain was one of them. W hite’s appointments that Tuesday often stretched beyond 30 minutes. “The barber chair is perfectly set up for measuring blood pressure,” Ravenell says. Some patients experience what’s known as “white coat syndrome,” meaning the stress of a clinical setting causes their blood pressure to rise temporarily. By contrast, getting a haircut gives someone time to sit and grow comfortable before being screened, so with proper technique, a reading taken at the barber shop may better reflect their usual levels. The challenge, Ravenell adds, was to “leverage what’s special about the barbershop without ruining what’s special about the barbershop.” Unlike in a clinical setting, getting a haircut gives someone time to sit and grow comfortable before being screened. Credit: Tolu Olasoji During CLIP, local Black male community health workers measured patrons’ blood pressure, counseled them, and connected them with medical and social services. Barbers encouraged customers to participate, but screenings were offered without pressure. “I allowed the men to decide whether they wanted to engage with me,” says a community health worker. Importantly, the community health workers were often themselves customers at the participating barbershops and knew the barbers and customers. Ravenell says that familiarity meant “their presence is not an intrusion, as it might be for someone with a white coat.” Across the program, 636 men were screened. Four hundred sixty-one were found to have elevated blood pressure or untreated stage one hypertension, 430 of whom enrolled in the study. Participants were 38 years old on average; only 24 percent reported having a primary care provider, and about half had health insurance. The study followed up with enrolled men at six-month intervals through 18 months, even after recruitment at individual shops had ended. At 18 months, community health workers obtained a repeat blood-pressure reading from 96 percent of participants. That level of follow-up, Ravenell says, is unusual and difficult to achieve in a long-running study. Dr. Chidinma Ibe, a community health workers researcher at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Equity, calls the figures “extremely, extremely impressive,” adding that they reinforce the value of meeting people where they are. D espite these successes, however, CLIP did not produce the primary result researchers had hoped for . At 12 months, participants’ systolic blood pressure had changed little. Fewer men met the study’s definition of incident stage two hypertension at 12 months, but the difference was no longer statistically significant at 18 months. Dr. Ibe says that given that the intervention was among men with elevated blood pressure or untreated stage one hypertension rather than severely uncontrolled disease, the limited movement in its main blood-pressure outcome was “not terribly surprising.” The challenge for CLIP, notes Dr. Joseph Ravenell, was to “leverage what’s special about the barbershop without ruining what’s special about the barbershop.” Credit: Tolu Olasoji For Derek Griffith, a University of Pennsylvania professor who studies Black men’s health, success in simply reaching men is separate from controlling their blood pressure. He says the major determinants of blood-pressure control remain in what men experience outside both barbershops and clinical care. Dr. Idris Robinson, research project manager for Penn’s Program for Research on Men’s Health, likewise cautions against treating the barbershop itself as the intervention. “The blood pressure outcomes weren’t rooted in some magical equation where barbers plus Black men equals guaranteed improvements in Black men’s health,” he says. Sustained engagement, he argues, also depends on collaboration among academic and community partners, barbers’ relationships with clients, and a wider support network. “That infrastructure is critical.” That becomes crucial after an elevated reading. When this occurred with CLIP participants, community health workers explained what the number could mean and encouraged medical follow-up. When it came to a referral, notes Joseph Ebron, CHASI’s director of health equity, “We would let them know what we offer, but it was up to them to take it.” Credit: Tolu Olasoji Even when people wanted help, navigating existing services could complicate the handoff. Workers sometimes met people who thought they lacked coverage, only to discover they were already enrolled elsewhere but were not getting the help they needed. And because they were already attached to another provider or organization, CHASI could not always simply move them into a different service. “We can’t just, like, snatch them,” says Ebron. Ibe points to a structural problem behind that handoff: the fragmented American health care system. Insurance issues, the absence of an established primary care relationship, and weak connections between community organizations and clinical teams can all interrupt the route to care. “If the [community health worker] isn’t employed by that clinic, there’s only so much they can do,” she says. Sustaining even the community side required labor. Active recruitment through Against Da Grain lasted about two months. “We did it for some time without receiving any type of payments,” says White, adding that the program brought “a lot of extra work.” CHASI adapted around the business in real-time: For instance, Ebron says to work around Against Da Grain’s preferences, they screened outside, where workers could pull up a small mobile health unit and barbers could direct interested customers to it. Workers learned to take up less space, getting rid of tables and flyers in favor of a simpler setup: a blood-pressure monitor and materials carried in a bag. Though CLIP is now over, there are larger screening events every two to three months and health workers can return to shops when requested. Credit: Tolu Olasoji Ravenell sees funding — and therefore sustainability — as the broader limitation. When CLIP ended in September 2025, he says Staten Island screening partners continued some services “essentially pro bono” during a funding gap. His team has since received two new NIH grants to build on CLIP’s infrastructure and train community health workers to screen in barbershops for diabetes and diabetic eye disease. For now, CLIP itself is over, though Ebron says CHASI conducts larger screening events every two to three months and can return to shops when requested. Whether the model can travel is another question. Ravenell says Staten Island had an advantage before CLIP began: CHASI had already spent more than 30 years working in the borough through community health workers. “Replicated, yes, easily, no,” Ebron says, because success depends on what already exists locally. CLIP reinforced White’s sense of responsibility to the community he has served for more than 35 years, while sharpening his awareness of the health concerns moving through it. “It helped me realize how many people have elevated levels,” he says. Join Cancel anytime Around noon at Against Da Grain, White’s final appointment brings in a young couple and their son, there for the boy’s first haircut. His mother livestreams the occasion to relatives. When the boy climbs down, his father takes his place in the chair. One generation giving way to another, if only for a haircut. items.titleOriginal: The Cozy Emergence of Repair Cafés
items.description: Στα υπόγεια των εκκλησιών και στις κοινοτικές αίθουσες, οι Αμερικανοί συγκεντρώνονται όχι μόνο για να επισκευάσουν σπασμένες λάμπες και ραγισμένες καρέκλες, αλλά για να απωθήσουν μια οικονομία που επωφελείται από τη μοναξιά και τη σπατάλη. Όταν η Lilly Pettus έφερε μια καρέκλα τραπεζαρίας -- μετακόμισε σε έξι πολιτείες για τριάντα χρόνια, κρατώντας στο ξύλο της το βάρος του οικογενειακού γέλιου και της σκληρής συνέλευσης…
items.descriptionOriginal: Across church basements and community halls, Americans are gathering not just to fix broken lamps and cracked chairs, but to push back against an economy that profits from loneliness and waste. When Lilly Pettus brought a dining room chair -- moved across six states over thirty years, holding in its wood the weight of family laughter and hard conversations -- to a repair caf in Decatur, Georgia, she left with something more than a mended joint: strangers' hands had pressed her family's history back together. "When a product breaks and you have to throw it away, it's very lonely," says Martine Postma, who founded Repair Caf International in 2010, and the repair caf s she helped seed around the world are a quiet argument against that loneliness. In neighborhoods where the need is economic as much as environmental, and in ones where it is sentimental, the impulse turns out to be the same: a refusal to let things, and the connections they carry, be so easily discarded. What these gatherings reveal, almost incidentally, is that the skills of care have never really disappeared; they've just been waiting for a place to gather.

items.descriptionOriginal: At 48, after 19 years in the classroom, Ruksana Begum found herself preparing for a different kind of working day. In November 2019, she started Ghar Batti Food Service with a modest aim: to turn the food she loved making into a livelihood. The first customers were buying familiar meals, not a grand new concept. Begum, now 55, had spent 19 years teaching before resigning in 2019. Her children encouraged her to take her cooking beyond the family kitchen, repeatedly telling her that people would enjoy what she made. She was not certain the venture would work. A new beginning after 19 years of teaching Cooking was not an unfamiliar skill that she had to acquire for the business. Begum credits her mother-in-law with teaching her recipes and techniques that continue to shape her food. "My mother-in-law taught me a lot about cooking. I learned all these dishes and techniques from her, and I still carry those things with me in my cooking today," she told Startup Pedia. She chose the name Ghar Batti to keep that domestic connection visible. 'Ghar' means home, while 'Batti' is the Kashmiri word for rice. The name reflected what she wanted customers to receive. Cooking was not an unfamiliar skill that she had to acquire for the business. Begum credits her mother-in-law with teaching her recipes and techniques that continue to shape her food. Photograph: ( startuppedia ) The business began with little financial outlay. Begum bought a tiffin box and used the gas, spices, ingredients and kitchen equipment already available at home. She described the initial investment as almost zero, but was clear that the work itself demanded time and effort. She initially handled the work largely alone, with her husband's support; other family members joined as orders grew. The first model was a tiffin service. It brought in customers, but the routine of preparing and delivering meals every morning and evening was demanding. Individual orders ranged in value from less than ₹100 to ₹2,000, depending on what customers wanted. After running the service for about a year, Begum began looking for a way to make the work more flexible without giving up the business she had started. From a small tiffin service to catering for 200 people The shift came through customers who had already tasted her food. They began asking her to prepare meals for special occasions and larger gatherings. Instead of relying only on daily tiffin deliveries, Begum started accepting catering orders for events. Ghar Batti now caters to events and supplies food to hospitals, schools, banks and offices, according to Begum. She sometimes handles 10 to 12 events in a month, although the number varies. The business can cater for up to 200 people at a single even t, giving the home-based operation a reach far beyond its first tiffin customers. She chose the name Ghar Batti to keep that domestic connection visible. 'Ghar' means home, while 'Batti' is the Kashmiri word for rice. Photograph: ( NDTV ) The menu carries both familiar Indian preparations and dishes associated with Kashmir. Customers can order rogan josh, yakhni, dum olav and mirchi korma, alongside palak paneer, chicken 65, chilli chicken and butter chicken. In winter, the menu includes harissa, a traditional Kashmiri meat dish, as well as pickles, smoked fish and other local preparations. The challenges of building a business at 48 Despite the expansion, Begum says she wants the food to remain home-cooked. Ghar Batti takes advance bookings through phone calls, WhatsApp and social media, preparing quantities to match each order rather than operating as a dine-in restaurant. She also says the kitchen does not use preservatives or artificial colours. The venture has grown beyond a one-person operation , too. Begum now works with a team of four: three women who help prepare food for bulk orders and one delivery worker. She says the business also brings work to people in its supply chain, including butchers, fish vendors and vegetable sellers. Repeat customers and word-of-mouth referrals have brought in orders. Her next ambition is to grow without losing the way Ghar Batti works. Begum hopes to take on as many as 20 catering events a month while continuing to operate from home. She remains cautious about borrowing money and is assessing how much the business can expand with the resources she has. The tiffin box that helped her test the idea has given way to larger orders, a small team and institutional clients. Begum's advice to others considering a late start is simple: "There is no age limit." Sources: ' She Quit Teaching at 48 to Start a Tiffin Service, Today Her Srinagar-Based Small Business Handles 10–12 Events a Month ': by Tauseef Ahmad for Startup Pedia, published on 25 October 2026 ' At 48, This Kashmiri Teacher Started A Food Business From Home. Today, It Serves Hospitals And Banks ': by NDTV Food Desk for NDTV Food, published on 27 October 2026 ' Kashmiri Woman Left Teaching To Start Tiffin Service, Now She Is Catering 10-12 Events Every Month | The Ghar Batti Story ': by Swati Kumar for The Daily Jagran, published on 28 October 2026 ' Cloud Kitchen Entrepreneurship ': Centre for Career-Counselling, Coaching and Placement, University of Kashmir. items.descriptionOriginal: Ever bought a packet labelled 1 kg, only to wonder if it actually contained that much? Maharashtra wants to make sure consumers get what they pay for. The state government has proposed raising the maximum fine for violations of weights and measures rules from ₹3,000 to ₹75,000. Under the draft rules, manufacturers, packers and marketers of packaged goods, along with e-commerce platforms, could face a ₹25,000 fine for a first offence and ₹75,000 for a second. Repeated violations could also lead to their business registrations being suspended or cancelled. Petrol pumps and CNG/LPG retailers could face the same ₹25,000 and ₹75,000 penalties for tampering with weighing and measuring instruments. The proposal also provides for fines of up to ₹2 lakh for repeated violations involving non-standard weighing and measuring instruments. The draft notification was issued on 2 November 2026, and the government has invited public suggestions and objections before finalising the rules. These penalties are not in force yet. Would higher fines make businesses more accountable and protect consumers from being short-changed? Tell us in the comments! #ConsumerRights #ConsumerProtection #Maharashtra #ConsumerAwareness

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Extended Producer Responsibility Laws Worldwide Now Cover More Than 70 Countries Reading Time: 3 minutes Extended Producer Responsibility laws worldwide have expanded from a single German packaging rule in 1991 into a global compliance landscape spanning more than 70 countries today. Extended Producer Responsibility laws worldwide shift the financial and physical burden of waste management from governments and taxpayers to the companies that manufacture and sell products. Under these laws, producers must collect, recycle, and properly dispose of the packaging and products they put on the market, fundamentally changing the economics of how goods are designed and sold. The concept traces back to Germany’s Packaging Ordinance of 1991, the world’s first EPR regulation. At the time, packaging waste accounted for roughly half of landfill volume and a third of total waste in Germany, pushing national landfill capacity toward its limits and forcing policymakers to act. More than three decades later, extended producer responsibility laws worldwide have evolved from that single national response into one of the most significant regulatory trends reshaping global manufacturing and retail. Europe remains the most mature region for these frameworks, with approximately 40 to 45 countries now operating established EPR schemes. The European Union’s Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation, which entered into force in February 2025 and applies fully from August 2026, replaced the previous directive with uniform, directly applicable requirements across all member states. The regulation requires packaging to meet EU recyclability performance criteria, sets recycled-content targets for plastic packaging starting in 2030, and restricts PFAS in food-contact packaging starting in August 2026. Extended producer responsibility laws worldwide increasingly extend beyond packaging alone. France’s framework, codified in its Environmental Code in 1992, now covers packaging, paper, textiles, electrical and electronic equipment, and batteries, with industrial and commercial packaging added to the scope in January 2025. This expansion reflects a broader pattern: once EPR infrastructure exists for one product category, governments frequently extend similar accountability to additional waste streams. In Asia, Japan’s Container and Packaging Recycling Law dates to 1997, obligating producers to fund recycling for designated packaging materials, while recent circular economy obligations have supplemented rather than replaced that core framework. South Korea operates what is widely considered one of the strictest EPR systems globally under its Resource Circulation Act, requiring companies to reduce packaging weight, improve recyclability, and submit to public disclosure of violators as a reputational enforcement mechanism alongside heavy fines. Extended Producer Responsibility laws worldwide increasingly rely on eco-modulated fees that reward recyclable, reusable, or sustainably designed packaging, creating market pressure for companies across Europe, Asia, and the Americas to redesign products proactively rather than simply absorbing compliance costs. Photo by Mikhail Nilov on Pexels. China’s approach folds extended producer responsibility obligations into its broader Law on Prevention and Control of Environmental Pollution by Solid Waste, expanding registration and recycling reporting requirements for both electronics and packaging sectors. India’s Plastic Waste Rules, first introduced in 2016 and amended in 2022, require producers, importers, and brand owners to register and take direct responsibility for collecting, recycling, or disposing of plastic packaging waste they introduce into the market. Extended producer responsibility laws worldwide show particularly rapid momentum across the Americas. In Canada, most provinces are fully transitioning to EPR models for packaging and printed paper, requiring registration with provincial programs, annual reporting by material type and weight, and payment of eco-modulated fees that vary by packaging performance and recyclability. Brazil’s National Policy on Solid Waste requires manufacturers, importers, distributors, and sellers to implement reverse-logistics systems that ensure packaging is reused or recycled rather than discarded. Chile’s Law 20.920 similarly requires producers of priority products to establish their own collection, recovery, and recycling schemes to meet government-set targets. In the United States, more than half a dozen states have already implemented EPR legislation, with additional states expected to follow as the model gains bipartisan traction. This state-by-state approach creates a patchwork of overlapping requirements that producers selling nationally must navigate simultaneously. Beyond mandatory frameworks, some nations have pursued voluntary or co-regulatory pathways as stepping stones toward fuller accountability. Australia’s National Packaging Targets, administered by the Australian Packaging Covenant Organization, aim for 100% of packaging to be recyclable, reusable, or compostable and operate through industry-led stewardship rather than direct government mandate. New Zealand has introduced voluntary EPR initiatives for packaging, with mandatory requirements expected as the voluntary phase matures. A common thread across extended producer responsibility laws worldwide is eco-modulated fee structures, financial penalties or incentives tied directly to how recyclable, reusable, or sustainably designed a product’s packaging is. This design creates market pressure encouraging companies to redesign packaging proactively rather than simply paying compliance costs passively, since better-designed packaging typically carries lower fees under most EPR schemes. For companies operating or distributing products internationally, this patchwork of national and regional requirements creates genuine compliance complexity. Registration requirements, reporting formats, fee structures, and penalty regimes vary significantly by country, even as the underlying principle that producers bear responsibility for their products’ end-of-life impact remains consistent across jurisdictions. As extended producer responsibility laws worldwide continue expanding into new product categories and new countries, the regulatory trajectory points firmly in one direction: toward holding manufacturers accountable not just for what they sell, but for what eventually becomes of it, transforming waste management from a public cost into a cost of doing business built directly into product design and corporate strategy. The post Extended Producer Responsibility Laws Worldwide Now Cover More Than 70 Countries appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.description: Όταν ο Gautam Ram Chandra άρχισε να δέχεται κλήσεις από queer και τρανς άτομα που αναζητούσαν συναισθηματική υποστήριξη, μερικές από τις εμπειρίες που άκουσαν ήταν οδυνηρά οικείες. Ως διανδρικό άτομο, είχαν επίσης αντιμετωπίσει διακρίσεις ενώ…
items.descriptionOriginal: When Gautam Ram Chandra began taking calls from queer and transgender people seeking emotional support, some of the experiences they heard felt painfully familiar. Years earlier, living in Lucknow, Gautam had struggled to find other queer and trans people they could connect with. As a transmasculine person, they had also faced discrimination while seeking healthcare. "I had no hope back then, and I thought I couldn't survive," they recall. Today, Gautam helps create the kind of space they once needed. Listening to people who were going through similar experiences gave their work a deeply personal meaning. "I was helping myself… I was helping my inner teenager when I was talking to those people," they share. Gautam joined Safe Access in 2019 and later helped develop its Community Wellbeing Project. Gautam is part of Safe Access, a non-profit organisation working to make healthcare and emotional support more accessible to LGBTQ+ people across India. Through its Community Wellbeing Project (CWP), trained queer and transgender peer supporters offer a listening ear to people who may have nowhere else to turn. The programme receives an average of more than 750 support calls every month, according to its founder, Shubham Choudhary. For Gautam, however, the journey began with a simple desire to find people who understood what they were going through. Finding a place where they could belong In 2019, Gautam came across an advertisement for a fellowship with Safe Access. At the time, they were living in Lucknow and felt isolated from the queer and transgender community. Their own experiences of discrimination had also made accessing healthcare difficult. They applied for the fellowship and began helping the organisation identify queer-affirmative healthcare professionals in Lucknow. Gautam's initial work at Safe Access involved identifying queer-affirmative doctors in Lucknow. The experience introduced Gautam to people who understood their struggles. It also helped them recognise that the discrimination they had experienced was something they could speak up against. "I realised what happened to me was not normal and that I should raise my voice," they say. What began as a fellowship eventually became a longer commitment. "I joined them as a permanent employee after the fellowship because I liked the work. I wanted to do more, specifically around health, as a trans person," Gautam explains. They would go on to help develop the Community Wellbeing Project, a programme that brought together people from the LGBTQ+ community to offer emotional support to one another. Why finding the right mental health support was so difficult Safe Access was founded in 2019 by Shubham Choudhary, now 33, who grew up in Delhi. The idea took shape when Shubham was filling out an application for an incubator programme. One question made him think seriously about the work he wanted to do. "What do you want to do for your own community?" The 2019 Safe Access fellowship linked participants to work on improving queer-affirmative care. "This is when everything came together, and I knew that I wanted to work for queer and trans healthcare because it is a very neglected topic," he tells The Better India. Although the 2018 Supreme Court judgement decriminalising consensual same-sex relationships between adults was an important milestone, Shubham says many LGBTQ+ people continued to struggle with accessing healthcare. Finding a doctor who understood their identity could involve travelling long distances, worrying about discrimination or deciding whether it was safe to disclose personal information. Safe Access was founded in 2019 to improve access to affirming healthcare for LGBTQ+ people. "There was a shared struggle with me and people from the community in seeking healthcare. Travelling long hours, fearing discrimination, feeling a constant push and pull about disclosing identities to doctors," he recalls. Safe Access initially focused on building a directory of queer and trans-affirmative doctors and mental health professionals. But conversations with community members and a survey conducted by the organisation revealed another pressing need: accessible mental health support. The challenge became more apparent during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. As people faced isolation and emotional distress, demand for mental health services increased. Several affirmative mental health professionals listed in the directory were booked for six to 12 months and asked to have their names removed. Safe Access works on LGBTQ+ healthcare access, including links to affirming medical professionals. Shubham and his team began exploring another possibility. What if people within the LGBTQ+ community could be trained to offer emotional support to others who shared similar experiences? "Peer support has existed within the community for a very long time. People have been turning to each other for support for years," Shubham says. "We may not have called it peer support, but we have always been doing it. I have received it, and I have provided it." The Community Wellbeing Project trains LGBTQ+ peers to provide emotional support to others. The team wanted to build on this existing practice by providing structured training, supervision and clear boundaries. That idea became the Community Wellbeing Project. How the programme helps people find someone to talk to In early 2021, Safe Access brought together its first group of 30 peer supporters. They were queer and transgender students and working professionals from different regions, languages, religions and backgrounds. Over approximately three weeks, the group completed 32 hours of online training. The sessions covered active listening, basic counselling skills, ethical boundaries, preventing burnout, suicide prevention, and identifying resources for people seeking support. They also practised through mock calls and supervised sessions. Peer-support training covers active listening, ethical boundaries and preventing burnout. After training, the peer supporters began a six-month period of supervised practice. If they encountered a situation they were unsure how to handle, they could seek guidance from queer mental health professionals associated with the programme. For someone looking for support, the process is designed to be accessible. A person can visit the Safe Access website, browse the available peer supporters and choose someone based on factors such as language, identity or location. They can then connect through a common helpline number for a free, confidential, one-on-one conversation. Participants practise listening and other skills before beginning supervised peer-support calls. If they feel comfortable, they can arrange another call with the same peer supporter. They can also choose someone else if they prefer. The programme provides a space for emotional support and listening, with trained peers and professional supervision forming part of its model. Since its beginning, CWP has grown to four cohorts, with 120 peer supporters trained or involved across them. Some have continued their involvement for four to five years, something Shubham considers particularly meaningful. Trained peer supporters can consult mental health professionals when they need further guidance. For him, another encouraging sign is when someone who initially reaches out for support eventually decides to become a peer supporter themselves. One such person is Rohan (name changed), a medical student who first discovered Safe Access in 2024. 'I felt like I was being heard without being judged' In his medical college, Rohan did not know a single openly queer person. He found it difficult to speak about his identity or share what he was experiencing. "I don't even know any other queer person in my college, and I cannot talk to anyone about my feelings… because of this, I feel like my identity gets pushed back," he says. During his first year, an experience involving someone he trusted left him feeling anxious and emotionally overwhelmed. But speaking about what had happened also meant potentially revealing his queer identity to people around him. "I couldn't tell anyone what I was going through without revealing my identity. I felt like I was in a bubble that I couldn't burst," he recalls. Safe Access held a documentary screening at an LGBT centre in Delhi as part of its community work. In 2024, he came across Safe Access on Instagram and began using its peer-support service. For the first time in a difficult period of his life, he felt that he could speak openly about his emotions. "I felt like I was being heard without being judged, and that my emotions had a place in society. It was very helpful for me during that time in my life," Rohan shares. What stayed with him was the way his peer supporter listened. "The concept of active listening and reflecting emotions was very helpful when my peer supporter did that for me," he explains. Alongside community events, Safe Access offers free peer-support calls to LGBTQ+ people in India. The experience made Rohan think about other queer people who might be going through similar situations without anyone to talk to. "I was in a place where I couldn't even talk about my problems with my mother or my brother. I wanted to join Safe Access because I want to provide a much better space to other community members. A non-judgmental space where their voices could be heard." He eventually joined the programme as a peer supporter himself. Safe Access's wider work seeks to improve LGBTQ+ healthcare access, beyond its peer-support project. At the time of the interview, he had been offering support through CWP for a little over two months. His experience reflects something Shubham has seen within the programme: people who once needed someone to listen are now choosing to become that person for others. Finding purpose in helping someone else feel less alone For Gautam, becoming a peer supporter also changed how they understood the challenges faced by other members of the community. They had initially expected to offer support and connect people with useful resources. But as the calls began, they heard about experiences that went far beyond their own. "Once I started working under CWP, I thought that I could provide help or resources to people, but after I completed my training and started doing calls, the stories and the people were a major awakening for me," Gautam shares. They encountered transmasculine and non-binary people facing restrictions at home, forced marriage, violence, interrupted education and financial barriers to seeking mental healthcare. Gautam's work with CWP has brought them into contact with queer and trans people across India. Gautam was particularly concerned about those living in smaller cities and rural areas, where accessing affirming counselling could be difficult. "They can't even go for counselling because they don't have money, and this was the only way they were able to talk to someone," they say of some people seeking support. These conversations made Gautam more aware of how differently people experience discrimination and isolation, even within the same community. The work also gave them a sense of connection they had struggled to find earlier in life. They built relationships with other peer supporters who understood the importance of listening, respecting boundaries and making space for difficult conversations. "We were trained to listen to people, but we were also practising that with each other. I got that kind of space for the first time in my life," Gautam recalls. Safe Access has also conducted sessions at the Center for Justice at Jindal Global Law School. For someone who had once felt alone in Lucknow, being able to offer that same understanding to others has become an important part of their life. And for Rohan, who has only recently begun his journey as a peer supporter, the purpose is similar. There is a message he often returns to, especially when he begins doubting himself. "I heard this line, 'You Are Enough'. Sometimes I think, am I enough? I have to keep reassuring myself of this, because I am enough," he says. "Now, my mission is to also tell others that they are enough, too." If you or someone you know is looking for queer-affirmative emotional support, Safe Access's Community Wellbeing Project offers free, confidential peer-support calls across India. You can contact its helpline at +91 01141219911 or email contact@safeaccess.co.in. Editor's note: The contact details and current availability of the service should be reconfirmed before publication.

items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗΝ ΚΑΘΗΜΕΡΙΝΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ OPTIMIST Σε μια κλινική δοκιμή του 2023 σε 121 άτομα στο Ηνωμένο Βασίλειο, η χρήση μιας πρωτότυπης συσκευής καρπού μείωσε τη συχνότητα τικ κατά μέσο όρο 25 τοις εκατό. Η συσκευή καρπού του Tourette, που ονομάζεται Neupulse, προέκυψε από έρευνα στο Πανεπιστήμιο του Νότιγχαμ και τρία χρόνια μετά, οι άνθρωποι που τη χρησιμοποιούν περιγράφουν την επίδρασή της πολύ πιο ισχυρά.…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM In a 2023 clinical trial of 121 people in the UK, wearing a prototype wrist device reduced tic frequency by an average of 25 percent. The Tourette’s wrist device, called Neupulse , came out of research at the University of Nottingham, and three years on, the people using it describe its effect in far stronger terms than a one-in-four reduction would suggest. How a Tourette’s wrist device targets tics Rhythmic pulses to the median nerve Neupulse sends rhythmic electrical pulses into the median nerve, which runs through the wrist and into the hand. Trials have shown that this stimulation changes activity in the brain regions responsible for movement control, and that the rhythm of the pulses can lower both the frequency and the intensity of tics. The device was developed by the university and its spin-out company, Neurotherapeutics Ltd, which secured £1 million (about $1.3 million) in additional funding to bring it to market. Stephen Jackson, the Nottingham professor who has led the research, described the response from users as “a dream come true.” Some of the feedback he has received is very concrete. “We’ve had people saying they managed to get through their wedding vows without ticking,” he said. Others told the team they could move through an airport and board a flight without tics. Tourette’s syndrome in the UK Tourette’s syndrome is a neurodevelopmental condition, usually beginning in childhood, that causes involuntary sounds and movements known as tics. More than 300,000 people in the UK have it, according to the charity Tourettes Action , and there is no cure. The condition reached a wider audience in 2023 when singer Lewis Capaldi, who has Tourette’s, tried the device before a concert in Nottingham, and again through the film I Swear , a drama based on the life of Tourette’s campaigner John Davidson. Three users, three measurable changes Katie, 15: years of constant vocal tics Katie, from Hertfordshire, started having tics at age seven. Her snorting tic ran almost nonstop, to the point of leaving her with a sore throat that kept her in bed for two weeks, and it disrupted her sleep, her eating, and her school attendance. “It was constantly moving, constantly making sounds and then I was kind of getting looked at like, ‘why are you doing that?'” she said. Her mom, Julia, called it “heartbreaking” to watch. “You feel helpless. You feel you don’t know where to turn really,” she said. After reading about the Nottingham research, Julia brought Katie to try the device in December, before it went on sale. The effect was immediate, Katie said, and she became “really calm.” “It was absolutely life-changing. It was like the best day of my life,” she said. On the drive back to Hertfordshire, she “just cried the whole way home.” Ollie, 15: a different diagnosis, a similar response Ollie’s case extends the picture, because he does not have Tourette’s. Nearly two years ago he cracked his neck, and about 48 hours later the movement had become involuntary and constant. “It was incredibly sudden,” he said. He was later diagnosed with functional neurological disorder (FND), a condition that affects how the brain sends and receives signals. His father, Alex, said sleeping, eating and drinking all became “incredibly difficult.” Ollie stayed inside for about a month at one stage and missed six to seven months of school ahead of his GCSEs, the exams British students sit around age 16. He came close to telling his parents not to bother with the device. A few months ago, when he switched it on for the first time, he phoned home. “You could hear that he was crying on the telephone because it had worked and his neck movement had stopped,” Alex said. Ollie put it this way: “It’s like a light switch. I remember my hands were quite shaky when I was calling my parents because it’s like getting part of your life back.” Mylo, 17: from trial participant to owner Mylo, from Buckinghamshire, was 13 when he joined the 2023 trial. He recently received his own device as a gift and said the urge to suppress his facial tics went away “instantaneously.” “As soon as it comes on, I can feel it,” he said. “I feel different… I feel new almost, which is strange.” Why Neupulse is not yet an NHS treatment Wellness product versus medical device The device comes in two versions. Neupulse-C is sold as a consumer wellness product, and the university says “thousands” have been purchased. Neupulse-M is the version intended for marketing as a medical treatment for tics and Tourette’s syndrome, and it is still working through regulatory approval. That distinction determines whether the National Health Service can offer it. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) has identified the technology as “promising” but asked for more evidence of long-term benefit. In 2025, it said its committee would meet again to assess the device’s clinical and cost-effectiveness. “They were unable to recommend it for use in the NHS until we have the regulatory approval,” Jackson said. “That’s something we’re working towards.” He hopes to see the Tourette’s wrist device available through the NHS “in the next year or so.” Early reports from the Tourette’s community Emma McNally, CEO of Tourettes Action , said the users she has spoken with have given the device “nothing but praise.” “Some people have said it’s helped them to go to places that they’ve not been for a long time, such as the cinema or a library,” she said. Others told her it helped them come out of a tic attack and feel more relaxed. Wrist stimulation beyond Tourette’s syndrome The Nottingham team is now testing the same approach on other conditions. Early trials have examined whether the pulses can reduce tremors in people with Parkinson’s , and Jackson said the university plans a UK-wide clinical trial covering anxiety and obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). The next milestone is regulatory, since medical approval for Neupulse-M would open the door to NICE guidance and NHS prescriptions, and the trials that follow will show whether a signal sent through the wrist can shape movement and mood in conditions well beyond tics. items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM You know that feeling when it’s two in the afternoon, and you can’t quite account for where the morning went? Not because you weren’t doing things, but because the busyness didn’t add up to anything you can point to. It’s demoralizing in a specific way, and it has surprisingly little to do with how early your alarm went off. Time management experts Melinda Rathkopf, M.D., M.B.A. , and Julie Morgenstern , the author of multiple bestselling books on productivity, say most of what shapes your morning was set in motion the night before, and the solution is usually far simpler than the elaborate routines you’ve seen floating around online. Start the night before Where do both experts begin? The evening before. When you make decisions about tomorrow before you go to sleep, you take some of the friction out of the morning itself. “Preplanning the day ahead and making decisions ahead of time makes the rest of your day potentially calmer and less stressful,” says Rathkopf. “Set yourself up by knowing what’s coming.” Transition time is one of the things that tends to get left out when people plan their days. It’s easy to schedule back-to-back tasks and forget that moving between them really does take time. Build that in the night before and the morning feels a lot less like you’re already behind before you’ve started. This extends to sleep, too. Rathkopf recommends starting with how much sleep you genuinely need to feel refreshed, then working backward from your wake time to set a consistent bedtime. “ Sleep is so vital to daily functioning and brain health,” she says. Most people schedule everything else first and try to fit sleep in around it. She suggests reversing that. Put the phone away before bed and after waking up If there’s one habit both experts come back to, it’s keeping your phone out of your first and last hour of each day. Morgenstern is direct about it. “The number one thing that can boost morning productivity has to do with screen time ,” she says. “We should not be on our devices an hour before bed, and we should not be on our devices for our first hour of the morning.” Checking your phone first thing does more than eat up time. It pulls you into a reactive state before you’ve had a chance to figure out your own priorities for the day. “The phone can be a useful tool, but it’s designed to keep us on there,” Morgenstern says. “Think of it like sugar — you have to really manage your consumption, and take charge. It’s the key to morning productivity, engagement, your relationships, everything.” She recommends replacing that screen time with something restorative: reading, getting outside, or having a conversation with someone. The goal isn’t deprivation; it’s starting the day on your own terms instead of somebody else’s notifications. Keep your routine simple One persistent myth about productive mornings is that they require an elaborate ritual. If you’ve ever felt vaguely inadequate watching someone describe their two-hour routine involving cold plunges , journaling, and a complicated smoothie, you’re not alone. Those routines often backfire. “It can make you stressed out — ‘Oh god, I didn’t meditate long enough!'” Morgenstern says. “Add three to four elements maximum for a morning routine. Otherwise, you’re habituating to something that’s unsustainable.” Find the small handful of things that reliably start your morning feeling calm and grounded, and stick with those. If you’re getting ready alongside young children, Morgenstern suggests completing your own routine before they’re up, then putting some thought into making their mornings smoother too. Laying out clothes or choosing breakfast the night before can take a surprising amount of stress out of a weekday morning. Train your brain with predictability Your brain is a creature of habit in the most useful sense. “Our brains love predictability,” says Rathkopf. “When you have a predictable routine, you’re reducing your stress and cognitive load.” When your morning follows a consistent pattern, you spend less mental energy on logistics and more on the work itself, which sounds obvious until you notice how rarely most mornings feel that way in practice. Morgenstern describes building a regular block for deep thinking as a kind of training for your brain: “If you have a predictable head-down time, your brain gets acclimated to it — it’s 10:30, that’s when we do our deep thinking. I’ve never seen anyone build proactive work with an erratic schedule.” For creative work especially, consistency turns out to matter more than inspiration. Start with the work that matters most A lot of mornings get swallowed by emails, messages, and reactive tasks before you ever reach work that needs your purest attention. “The number one difficulty people have is that the day starts off all reactive, and they can’t get to proactive work,” Morgenstern says. Her suggestion is to start with the most important thing on your list, the one that needs your freshest thinking. Even if everything else gets away from you after that, you’ve done something that mattered. “Even if you only get that one thing done, you’ll feel the greatest sense of relief that you’ve done your job,” she says. If your workplace opens with a morning meeting, Morgenstern recommends blocking off a half hour to an hour right after it for focused work, to address anything that came out of the meeting before settling into your main task. Better yet, see if you can get your whole team to protect the first hour of the day. Build in small moments of recovery Self-care doesn’t need to be a whole thing. What Morgenstern recommends is more modest: short pauses woven throughout the day, especially during your busiest stretches. “Add microbursts of self-care in your day — five to 20-minute activities that recharge you,” she says. A short walk, some music on your commute, ten minutes with a book. Small enough to fit into almost any day, and consistent enough to keep you from burning out by three in the afternoon. “The harder you’re working, the harder you have to recover,” she says. Stopping feels like the last thing you can afford when you’re slammed, but that’s usually when it matters most. Give yourself room to change, and to have off days Both experts caution against treating your morning routine as something fixed. Life changes, seasons change, your circumstances shift, and what works at one stage may not work at another. “You may need to change it based on other obligations, at different stages of your life, or even in different seasons,” says Rathkopf. And when a morning doesn’t come together the way you hoped, she has one more piece of advice: don’t be hard on yourself about it. “Everybody’s different, and what you’re seeing in posts is someone else’s best versions and best days,” Rathkopf says. “They have those not-so-perfect days, too.” A morning routine isn’t something you get right once. It’s something you keep adjusting until it fits. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . items.descriptionOriginal: Recommendations are independently selected by our team but may result in a commission to Nice News which helps keep our content free. We likely all have a person in our lives who’s impossibly hard to shop for. Maybe they’re the family member who says they “don’t want anything” or the friend who seems to already have it all. You can go two routes for recipients like these: Get them something practical (items that make life a little easier) or not so practical (gifts intended simply to delight). To help with your search this holiday season, we rounded up a mix of both. And if you’re still on the hunt for the right present after perusing this guide, check out the Nice News team’s favorite products of the year for more ideas. Aura Digital Picture Frame For the sentimentalist who always asks for more photos Courtesy of Aura A sweet gift for loved ones near and far, Aura’s digital frames let people share photos from multiple phones and then display them like a slideshow. My sister and I each have one, and it’s a thrill to see new pics of my niece and nephew pop up on mine. For those who prefer tangible photos, consider pairing a fun frame with this compact printer that makes 4-by-6-inch prints directly from a smartphone. Shop Aura Shop Amazon Soligt Wooden Cookbook and Tablet Stand For the one who uses their iPad to pull up recipes in the kitchen Courtesy of Amazon This nifty stand is ideal for holding medium-sized cookbooks as well as iPads, Kindles, and other tablets. It features a kickstand you can position at multiple angles, and its elegant cutting board-esque design helps it blend in with other kitchen accoutrements. Your recipient can use it to watch tutorials or read recipes — or to FaceTime you while they’re cooking. Shop AMAZON La Lune Upcycled Leather Crossbody Bag For the stylish friend who’s always on the go Courtesy of La Lune Everyone needs a purse — and this one from La Lune couldn’t be more practical. The vivid Electric Blue Crossbody fits a phone, wallet, keys, sunglasses, and lip balm, making it an easy pick for errands, sightseeing, or a dinner out. Handcrafted by Los Angeles artisans from upcycled Italian leather, each vintage-inspired bag from La Lune comes from a limited supply of leftover leather with its own color and grain that softens with wear. It’s a gift as distinctive as the person who will carry it, and it will last for years to come.* Shop La Lune *Indicates a Nice News brand partnership or affiliate Bee Cups Watering Stations For the gardener who wants to attract more wildlife to their yard Courtesy of Bee Cups Bee Cups are patented watering stations, and they happen to be both practical and whimsical. Each cup holds about a teaspoon of water — just enough to hydrate a visiting bee or butterfly while preventing them from getting submerged. They’re handmade from 100% porcelain, so they’ll hold up in changing weather conditions, and painted with a special UV-reactive glaze to mimic flowers, so they’re extra enticing to pollinators. Shop Bee Cups SHOP AMAZON Fitbit Air For the person who wants to track their steps without getting distracted by notifications Courtesy of Google Think of this as a yoga-class-friendly fitness tracker. It delivers the benefits of typical trackers — like monitoring steps, sleep, and heart rate — but it’s screen-free, with no buttons or notifications (the data is accessible via a companion app). It’s also water-resistant, and a single five-minute charge can last up to a week. Tip: Include a few replacement straps with the gift so your recipient can select the best color for their outfit on any given day. Shop GOogle SHOP AMAZON Ban.do Quilted Blanket For the one who loves a cozy night in Courtesy of Ban.do This quilt is as cozy as it is cheerful. It’s soft, machine washable, and a sweet way to help someone stay snug. Check out the brand’s other four designs, which are equally as delightful to look at. Shop Ban.do Terrain Forget-Me-Not Flower Press For the crafty soul Courtesy of Terrain Hobby gifts can be hit-or-miss, but this one’s sure to go over well with gardeners and flower lovers. It comes with everything needed to start preserving blooms (sans the blooms themselves) in one very pretty package. They can then use the pressed flowers to make things like coasters, jewelry, and boho decor . If you think your loved one would rather skip over the DIY component, consider this lovely preserved flowers keepsake box or picture frame . Shop Terrain Loop Earplugs For the concertgoer who’s concerned about their hearing Courtesy of Loop Know someone with misophonia — or a pal who simply wants to protect their hearing? Loop earplugs lower the decibel level of noise (to varying degrees based on the different models), and work wonders for focusing, calming an overstimulated nervous system, enjoying concerts without damaging your eardrums, and sleeping. Each pair comes with a handy case and four sets of washable, silicone ear tips. Shop Loop Shop AMAZon Cabin Nine 20-Minute Candles For the analog enthusiast Courtesy of Cabin Nine Who knew a timer could be so lovely? This set includes 12 small beeswax candles that each burn for approximately 20 minutes, as well as a reusable candle holder, matches, and a charming blue tin to keep everything in. It’s ideal for anyone who wants to carve out more time for journaling, reading, meditating, or yoga without relying on a digital timer. Shop Cabin nine Algae Cooking Club Nara’s Roasted Garlic Oil For the home chef who doesn’t like the smell of garlic on their fingers Courtesy of Algae Cooking Club For the foodies, this oil gives dishes all the flavor of garlic without them having to actually chop any garlic. It’s made primarily from algae, which has an extremely high smoke-point (higher than avocado oil) and is infused with garlic, yuzu, miso, and scallions. In other words, it’s delicious and can be used for sautéing, roasting, drizzling, you name it. Shop algae cooking club Shop AMAZON Audible Membership For the bookworm who loves to listen to their literature Courtesy of Audible Got a friend with a never-ending TBR list? An Audible gift membership lets them download an audiobook each month from a catalog of over 1 million titles. If they already have a login, that’s no problem — they’ll just receive more credits to use. You can give three months for $45, six months for $90, or a full year of reading for $150 (with no automatic auto-renew). It comes quite in handy when they’re 135th in line for a library book in the Libby app. Optional: Pair the membership with this silly mug . shop Audible SHOP AMAZON America the Beautiful Parks Pass For the nature lover Courtesy of Recreation.Gov Another blend of practical and delightful, the America the Beautiful Pass covers entrance fees and standard amenity fees (aka day-use fees) at more than 2,000 national parks and federal recreational sites for one year. The digital version is convenient, but you can add in a physical card at checkout for people who might prefer to keep the pass in their car’s glove compartment. Shop Recreation.gov Baggu Packing Cubes For the frequent traveler Courtesy of Baggu A packing cube goes a long way, particularly for overpackers who could use a little help squeezing just one more thing into their bag. Baggu’s cubes are a favorite of Staff Editor Ally Mauch, who says “you’d be amazed at how much you can fit in these.” The cherry on top? They come in such fun, punchy patterns and colors. Shop Baggu Shop Amazon Board For the avid game night host Courtesy of Board Where to start with this snazzy gift? It’s a “face-to-face game console” that’s designed to be a happy medium between digital games and board games. The touchscreen device lays flat on a table and comes with physical pieces that interact with the screen, so players can gather around for a classic yet modern game night experience. It includes a built-in starter pack of seven games, and tons more can be purchased with no subscription required. Oh, and it made Time magazine’s Best Inventions of 2026 list. Shop Board Q uokka Hotel Wildeluxe 1,000-Piece Puzzle For the one who loves a good challenge Courtesy of Amazon This is no ordinary puzzle. It doubles as a mystery game with 321 “secrets” that are unlocked by putting together the 1,000 pieces, opening the riddle envelopes, and listening to an accompanying audio story. It’s gotten rave reviews, and it’s under $25. Shop AMAZON Related: 19 Gifts for Readers Who Always Have Their Nose in a Book
