items.descriptionOriginal: There’s been a lot of discourse on the state of modern dating and a lot of theories on why it seems harder than ever for people to find connection with romantic partners. Could it be that the achievement and education gaps between men and women are altering the dynamics? Have social media and dating apps broken our brains and hearts? Do we all have unrealistic expectations and unlimited options, leading to never feeling satisfied with anything or anyone? Those are all intriguing options, but an alternate theory has been gaining steam: Maybe being single isn’t as lonely as we think. Maybe being single is actually freaking awesome. A guy on TikTok who goes by @gettothepointbro shared a hilarious monologue on why women who have been single for a long time “don’t want to date anymore.” Women say he absolutely nailed it. Woman enjoying some self-care time. Photo credit: Canva Why it hits so close to home At first, it might seem like he’s poking fun, either at single women or at the men who can’t seem to win them over. But not so! What he’s done is perfectly captured the joy many people find in being single and, frankly, able to do whatever the hell they want. “Some women have been single for so long they don’t date anymore, they grant you access to their peaceful little empire like a reluctant queen handing you a visitor’s badge,” he says. “You text her good morning and she’s already annoyed, like ‘Why are you disturbing the sacred silence of my personal growth journey?'” He goes on, “Bro she’s been sleeping diagonally in her bed for three years, she’s not giving up that territory because you opened the door and paid for coffee.” “You plan a cute date, she’s thinking ‘That sounds nice but also I could stay home, deep clean my apartment, do a 12-step skincare routine, order sushi and not have to listen to a man breathe.'” “You try to check in emotionally, ‘How are you feeling?’ She’s feeling fantastic because you’re not here.” “You’re not competing with other guys. There are no other guys. You’re competing with her weighted blanket, her peace, her cat named Chairman Meow, and the simple joy of not having to share her fries.” @erosbrousson DATING A GIRL WHO IS USED TO BE ALONE CAN BE VERY HARD . ♬ original sound – Éros Brousson Women say he got it exactly right The best thing about the video is the discussion in the comments. Women want to know how this man got access to this top-secret information. The rant is so eerily, frighteningly accurate that women are convinced this guy is living in their heads. That, or someone’s secretly leaking intel. “Dammit. Somebody call a meeting of the council. He knows too much.” “I dont often offer this compliment to the male species but you explained it better than I ever could.” “Alright, who’s told him this info??? So exposed right now” “The joy of sleeping diagonally across my bed cannot be fully explained.” “This is the most accurate profiling I’ve ever heard. You absolutely nailed it.” Clearly, we’ve tapped into a real phenomenon here, with users lovingly calling him The Croissant King. @erosbrousson CAN YOU RELATE LADIES ? THAT’S WHY WE LOVE YOU ♬ original sound – Éros Brousson This reflects a much bigger shift The truth is that many people, both men and women, are disillusioned with the sad state of the dating scene these days. App burnout is a real thing, and meeting new people in real life is a ton of work. So, it’s no surprise that more and more people are just choosing to stay single and enjoy all the perks that come along with it. This is a stark change, especially for women. According to FiveThirtyEight, “Women were also more likely than men to say that they weren’t dating because they have other priorities right now.” Priorities like travel, career, friendship, and even just self-care , all things that wind up taking a backseat when people get involved in relationships. It wasn’t too long ago that women of a certain age who were still single were called “ spinsters ,” but that word has lost a significant amount of power. This new generation of women isn’t embarrassed or ashamed to be single; they’re loving it for exactly all the reasons this video describes. Is having a boyfriend embarrassing now? And to make matters even more interesting, British Vogue published an opinion piece in late 2025 from writer and podcaster Chanté Joseph simply titled, “Is Having a Boyfriend Embarrassing Now?” In the mega-viral piece, Joseph interviewed lots of women and, based on their answers, explores a budding new era of women finding their boyfriends or even the simple idea and prospect of a boyfriend “embarrassing.” @chantayyjayy So many thoughts! This is my 2AM summary please go and read ♬ original sound – Chanté Joseph Some say it’s because of too much “boyfriend content” on social media. Others note the issue seems to be that once a woman gets a boyfriend, her entire personality (and social media) revolves around him. Other women cite being embarrassed by men’s behavior and the oft-experienced paradox of losing the relationship the moment it’s made public (i.e. the “hard launch” to breakup pipeline). That said, women would rather keep their boyfriends on the down low for privacy and to avoid the “ evil eye ” as Joseph reveals, or else do the next best thing and stay happily single. A lot of people have a lot of thoughts about Joseph’s piece, its virality, and what that means for the current state of dating and relationships worldwide. CNN even caught up with Joseph in November 2025 to understand more about her piece and the polarizing response to it. Watch: We may not yet have a final answer on where this shift in women’s attitudes toward dating will land, but one thing’s for sure: whether you’re single or partnered, embarrassed or proud, Croissant King’s take is resonating with the masses. items.title: Πριν από εκατό χρόνια, όλοι φορούσαν καπέλα. Το 1960 σταμάτησαν ξαφνικά. Να γιατί.
items.titleOriginal: A hundred years ago, everyone wore hats. In 1960, they suddenly stopped. Here’s why.
items.description: Ήταν παντού. Άντρες, γυναίκες, ακόμη και παιδιά το έκαναν κάθε φορά που έφευγαν από το σπίτι. Αν δείτε παλιά πλάνα ειδήσεων με άνδρες στο γραφείο ή στα τρένα του προαστιακού από την εμφάνιση της κινηματογραφικής κάμερας μέχρι τις αρχές της δεκαετίας του '60, σχεδόν όλοι φορούν καπέλο. Τα καπέλα ήταν εξίσου συνηθισμένα για τις γυναίκες εκείνη την εποχή. Για να βγει μια γυναίκα χωρίς καπέλο στο τ…
items.descriptionOriginal: It was everywhere. Men, women, and even children did it every time they left the house. If you see old newsreel footage of men in the office or on commuter trains from the advent of the motion picture camera to the early ’60s, nearly everyone is wearing a hat . Hats were just as common for women in that era. For a woman to go out without a hat in the first half of the 20th century was akin to going out without clothes. The funny thing is that everyone’s headgear is so similar in the old-timey footage that it makes previous generations look like big-time conformists. Then, in the early ’60s, everything changed, and men and women started to go out in public with their hair exposed. Why did such a big aspect of fashion seem to change overnight? Warmbru Curiosity investigated the question in a popular YouTube video. Warmbru’s channel is a lighthearted look at some of the more unusual people and events from our history and how they have influenced the world in which we live. Why did people stop wearing hats? Warmbru says fashion changed dramatically after World War II, when people in developed countries began to care less about expressing their social status. “This was especially true among the younger generation. The rise of youth culture in the 1950s and 1960s emphasized rebellion against traditional norms, including formal dress codes,” the YouTuber says. Another big reason for the change in fashion was technology. Cars became the preferred mode of transportation for many after World War II, and indoor environments became more hospitable. “People spent far less time exposed to the elements as people increasingly moved to urban areas and started using cars,” Warmbru says. “The practicality of wearing hats diminishes. Hats can be cumbersome in cars and on public transport, improvements in heating and air conditioning reduce the need for hats to provide warmth.” How JFK and The Beatles played a role Warmbru adds that President John F. Kennedy, elected in 1960, rarely wore a hat, and the widely circulated idea that he single-handedly killed the hat industry has stuck in the public imagination. In reality, Kennedy did wear a top hat to his 1961 inauguration, removing it only for his speech, and hat sales had already been declining for years before that. Further, in 1963, the mop-topped Beatles proudly flaunted their hatless heads as they shook them while singing, “Wooooo.” Hat-wearing among women began to decline around the same time as the restrictive and complex headgear clashed with the burgeoning women’s liberation movement. John F. Kennedy with his family. Photo credit: Wikimedia Commons The decline in hat purchases meant that manufacturers closed and the headgear became harder to come by. This reduced availability further contributed to the decline in hat-wearing. As fewer people wore hats, there was a greater demand for high-quality hair products and services. “Why spend a fortune at the hairdressers or the barbers just to cover the end result with a hat?” Warmbru asks. Could hats be due for a comeback? Ultimately, there were many reasons why people stopped wearing hats. It appears that it was a combination of technology, influential people such as Kennedy and The Beatles, and the overwhelming mood of change that swept most of the Western world in the 1960s. But if one thing is true about fashion, it goes in cycles. So, it seems that hats may be ready for their big comeback. This article originally appeared two years ago. It has been updated. The post A hundred years ago, everyone wore hats. In 1960, they suddenly stopped. Here’s why. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.description: Ανεξάρτητα από το πόσο αγαπούν οι ιδιοκτήτες γατών τα γούνινα αιλουροειδών τους, όλοι έχουν ένα κοινό παράπονο: το κουτί της γάτας. Κανείς δεν αγαπά τη διαχείριση ενός κουτιού απορριμμάτων. Εκτός κι αν μείνετε ακριβώς πάνω τους, γίνονται ακατάστατα και μυρίζουν, τα σκουπίδια ή/και η σκόνη από τα σκουπίδια πέφτουν παντού, και γενικά είναι ένα σκληρό πράγμα που πρέπει να αντιμετωπίσετε για να απολαύσετε το όφελος…
items.descriptionOriginal: No matter how much cat owners love their furry felines, they all have one complaint in common: the cat box. No one loves managing a litter box . Unless you stay right on top of them, they get messy and smelly, the litter and/or dust from litter gets everywhere, and it’s just generally a gross thing you have to deal with in order to enjoy the benefits of having a cat. Companies have tried making litter boxes better, of course. Now we have extra deep boxes for the “flingers,” covered litter boxes (which are great if your cat doesn’t refuse to use them), and fancy self-cleaning litter boxes (which are also great if your cat doesn’t refuse to use them). And regardless of the kind you use, there’s still the problem of where to keep the unsightly poop receptacle in your home. Finding a suitable place for the cat box can be tricky. Photo credit: Canva So a couple in Japan built a solution That’s where an innovative design from a couple living in Japan comes in. Rachel and Jun have three cats and a knack for designing cool things, and their custom “Japanese Poop House” is a next-level litter box solution. “Litter boxes inevitably come with problems — cats kicking out litter, smells, where do you even put them in your home, and the list goes on and on,” Rachel wrote on YouTube. “I have been working on designing the ultimate litter box that solves every one of these problems for the past two years. I spent six months building it. AND IT WORKED. Behold: the Poop Abode.” Rachel and Jun are fortunate to have a small space in their home that they can dedicate to cats (they call it “the cat room”) where they can keep their litter boxes. Rachel said they’ve tried various litter box configurations and litters and that the wood pellet litter works best for them. However, it does result in a lot of sawdust, which gets all over everything. That was one of the problems they wanted to solve. The six rules the design had to meet In coming up with the perfect custom litter box, Rachel said they had six criteria that needed to be met: 1) It needed to be big enough for their large Maine Coon cat, Haku. 2) It needed tall walls because their cat Nagi “likes to pee horizontally.” 3) It needed to be easy and comfortable for the cats to use. 4) It needed to trap litter and dust from escaping. 5) It needed to be easy to clean. And 6) It needed to look good. Rachel came up with a bunch of designs, and the winner ended up looking too much like a dumpster, so she made the design a little bit more complicated so that it would look more like a house. Mission accomplished. Watch to see how she did it and the final result: So how did the poop house turn out? The “Japanese Poop House” really does look like a beautifully designed house, and even with the clear walls, it doesn’t really look like a litter box. The lid that opens and closes for ease of scooping is great, and the cats seem to enjoy going through their little custom “hallway” to get to their litter box. People in the comments are loving it: “Rachel, you could seriously market this design professionally!!! This is absolutely genius.” “Nothing says ‘I love my cats’ more than Rachel building them a poop house that actually looks like a modern home. It is so extra! Amazing work Rachel x.” “I can’t believe I watched 25 minutes of designing a Japanese-Modernistic ‘poop house’ with better architecture than any apartment I’ve ever lived in.” “The magnet disassembly of the whole frame is so smart!!! I love seeing people go the extra mile for their pets like this.” “Rachel, you don’t just deserve a high five, you deserve a patent! This is amazing!” Can you actually buy one of these? Many people wanted to know if the cat box would be available to purchase. “Thank you to everyone who has shown interest!” wrote Jun . “We’re in the process of gaining design rights for this litter house and other cat projects my wife made such as her cat food station. We’re trying to figure out how to make these available for those who’re interested in buying.” Not everyone can or is interested in making this kind of litter box “poop home” themselves, but Rachel did provide the step-by-step example of how to do so right there in the video. Might be worth a shot. You can follow Rachel and Jun on YouTube . This article originally appeared in July. It has been updated. The post Couple in Japan invents a nearly perfect cat litter box that solves many common problems appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: 22 «περίεργα συγκεκριμένα» life hacks που θα μπορούσαν να σας εξοικονομήσουν χρόνο, χρήματα, ενέργεια ή λογική
items.titleOriginal: 22 ‘oddly specific’ life hacks that could save you time, money, energy, or sanity
items.description: Οι συμβουλές για το life hack αφθονούν στην εποχή της βελτιστοποίησης και των επιρροών, αλλά η επιθυμία να ζήσετε τη ζωή λίγο καλύτερα δεν είναι κάτι καινούργιο. Ακόμη και οι αρχαίοι φιλόσοφοι αναλογίστηκαν τις πιο σοφές χρήσεις του χρόνου, της ενέργειας και των πόρων μας. Αλλά στον σημερινό πιο περίπλοκο κόσμο, οι απαντήσεις σε τέτοιες ερωτήσεις μπορεί να είναι πολύ πιο συγκεκριμένες. Οι νέοι ενήλικες έχουν ζητήσει «ο…
items.descriptionOriginal: Life hack advice abounds in the era of optimization and influencers, but the desire to live life a little better is nothing new. Even ancient philosophers pondered the wisest uses of our time , energy, and resources. But in today’s more complicated world, the answers to such questions can be a lot more specific. Young adults have been asking for “oddly specific” life tips, and people are delivering their favorite hacks. These aren’t the “surround yourself with positive people” kind of tips we typically see, but rather random, specific bits of advice. I’m 25. Give me oddly specific life tips. No general ”surround yourself with positive people” tips. I want the most random, specific advice possible. — Tokyo (@otokyo__) March 2, 2026 Here are some of the most universally applicable ones shared on X: Food Thinking about what to eat, preparing what to eat, and actually eating it takes up a decent amount of our daily lives. It makes sense to give it a little extra thought, both for efficiency and enjoyment’s sake. “When in an unknown small town, pick your restaurant based on the number of pickup trucks in the parking lot. Nobody goes on vacation in the pickup. Those are locals, who know where to eat.” – @KeelowSierra “Learn to cook 3 meals extremely well. It will save money, impress people, and make rough weeks easier.” – @Alacritic_Super Learn to cook three things well. Photo credit: Canva “Make a weekly rotating menu so you never have to agonize over what to make for dinner. Like Taco Tuesday. Vary the specific item each week to keep it fresh but man it saves time, energy, and money.” – @RuralUrbie Health There’s a lot of health advice out there, and a lot of it is conflicting. But here are a few tips that seem solid no matter what your approach to health might be: “Always wash your hands standing on one leg. We lose our balance with age and this simple habit forces you to consistently practice it without interfering with your life.” – @catpoopburglar “Drink a full glass of water before you touch your phone in the morning.” – @EarthOriginHQ “Speaking as someone who *didn’t* do this enough: Literally touch grass as often as you can. Go outside, get some sun, go camping, disconnect from your phone and social media and go explore the world without a filter. It’ll do wonders for your mental health, it’ll force you to spend some time alone with your thoughts, and you’ll gain some perspective about yourself and life in general.” – @CitizenAmedia Money Getting money advice from strangers can be dodgy, to say the least. But a few folks offered some pretty universal bits of wisdom: “Before any purchase over $100, wait 48 hours. If you still want it after two days, buy it. You’ll be surprised how often the urge disappears. This one habit will save you thousands over the next decade without any willpower required.” – @BellaBaddie__ “I wish I had practiced minimalism. I’m spending the second half of my life getting rid of expensive junk for free that I thought I needed. I wish I had invested that money for my future instead. That’s solid advice.” – @starjaxranch “Roth IRA and regular investment brokerage accounts. Contribute every month, even if it’s only $20. Just keep doing it and don’t stop. When people panic about the market crashing just keep contributing. It isn’t a loss if you don’t sell and it always bounces back higher, crashes are nothing but buying opportunities to increase your returns down the road. Just keep investing in funds. Learn how to get a shopping high from investing.” – @AnteEcho Work Most adults spend much of their day working, so advice in this area is particularly valuable. Here are some nuggets of wisdom that apply no matter what kind of work you do: “Keep a ‘brag document’ – a running list of every win, project, compliment, or achievement at work. Update it weekly. When it’s performance review time or you’re updating your resume, you won’t be sitting there trying to remember what you did six months ago.” – @PursuDr Keep a running list of your wins at work. Photo credit: Canva “At work no matter what your job is or how much you are currently being paid, if someone offers to teach you a new skill… Get out a notebook and a pencil and say ‘Thank you, I want to learn how to do that!’ This is how you increase your value.” – @TimothyMcGuire “Always keep one skill you’re quietly improving that nobody knows about yet.” – @Alacritic_Super “For all the jobs you have, don’t burn bridges when you leave a place. Keep your colleagues contact info from each job. Leave on good terms. These things help in networking for a new job in the future.” – @daoc151 General Outside of those big life categories, people offered all sorts of great tips born from experience. Keep these in your pocket when you need them: “After you spend ages looking for something store it in the first place you looked.” – @floboflo “Buy your concert t-shirts one or two sizes larger. You’ll likely be larger yourself for the reunion tour.” – @TeamToad Buy your concert t-shirts one or two sizes larger. You'll likely be larger yourself for the reunion tour. pic.twitter.com/teJoxj8lpS — Michael Mauldin (@TeamToad) March 9, 2026 “When you find a pair of shoes or sandals or a bra that fits you comfortably and perfectly, buy three more just like it immediately and save them in your closet. Everything good gets discontinued.” – @Suzanne08053 “The mental energy associated with procrastination is costing you the same (if not more) as the energy required to take action. Pick action over mental suffering.” – @ConMcGovy “Check the toilet paper holder in the gas station bathrooms BEFORE you sit down….” – @scdavem “Treat every microphone like it’s on.” – @RobOps_xyz “Never make a major life or business decision after 10 PM. You aren’t yourself when you’re tired; you’re just a high-stress version of yourself. Sleep on it. The solution is almost always waiting for you at 7 AM.” – @ria_rustagi “When you drop something. Especially something small like a screw. Don’t grab wildly at it to keep it from falling. Concentrate on watching it fall with absolute focus.” – @GeorgiasGiant “If you find a toilet in your dream, don’t use it.” – @Sandy166059 (If you know, you know.) The best advice is the kind you use There’s a lot we need to learn on our own, of course. No thread, no matter how oddly specific, can replace lived experience. But we can also learn from the lessons others have shared, taking what works and leaving what doesn’t. That’s really the beauty of crowdsourced wisdom like this: nobody expects you to adopt all of it. Pick the two or three that actually fit your life, try them for a week, and see what sticks. Sometimes the smallest, weirdest tip is the one that ends up saving you the most time, money, or sanity. This article originally appeared in March. It has been updated. The post 22 ‘oddly specific’ life hacks that could save you time, money, energy, or sanity appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Οι άνθρωποι μοιράζονται τις «αποφάσεις 10 δευτερολέπτων» που βελτίωσαν ουσιαστικά τη ζωή τους για πάντα
items.titleOriginal: People share the ’10 second decisions’ that meaningfully improved their lives forever
items.description: Ο μέσος ενήλικας παίρνει πάνω από 35.000 αποφάσεις την ημέρα. Αυτά μπορεί να περιλαμβάνουν τα μεγαλύτερα, πιο υπαρξιακά ερωτήματα που απαιτούν προβληματισμό για να σταθμιστούν τα υπέρ και τα κατά. Όμως η συντριπτική πλειονότητα των αποφάσεων φαίνεται ασήμαντη: Τι θα φορέσω σήμερα; Να παραγγείλετε φαγητό σε πακέτο ή να φτιάξετε φαγητό στο σπίτι; Podcast ή playlist; Ωστόσο, αυτές οι φευγαλέες επιλογές παρόρμησης μπορούν να παίξουν…
items.descriptionOriginal: The average adult makes upwards of 35,000 decisions a day. These can include the bigger, more existential questions that require reflection to weigh the pros and cons. But the vast majority of decisions seem insignificant: What will I wear today? Order takeout or make food at home? Podcast or playlist? Still, these fleeting impulse choices can play just as big a role in our lives as the more thought-out ones. Prime examples of this were shared on Reddit earlier this year, when people were asked to share a “ decision you made in under 10 seconds that changed your life forever.” These seemingly insignificant choices changed fates in profound ways. When love found them by accident “Decided to go to Subway instead of Dairy Queen. They were across the street from each other and I was passing through town during lunchtime. Ended up hitting it off with the woman making my sandwich. Next week is our 11 year anniversary.” “My best friend said she wanted to move 2000+ miles across the country back to her home state and asked me if I wanted to come. I didn’t think, said ‘Yup, I’ll go.’ We moved, less than a year afterwards I met my now wife. Couldn’t be happier.” A van travels down the road. Photo credit: Canva “Said yes to adopting a stray dog that followed me home. 10-second ‘sure why not’ moment, now he’s my best buddy for 8 years.” A coin flip led to new passions Others were able to uncover new passions they never imagined. “I flipped a coin to decide if I was going to quit my job. Heads. I quit. A friend saw my lights on that night and stopped by to see what I was doing. I told him what happened, and he told me it was great timing. They let someone go at his job that day. He set me up with an interview for the next day, and I was hired. There were only three people who worked there. I eventually became the plant manager and have been working in management ever since!” “Saw a random advert advertising scuba diving certification. I signed up thinking ‘why not?’ I’m now an aspiring diving instructor!” “Early 20s and my sister asked me to drive her to the music shop to buy a guitar. I point one out and say ‘that black and gold one is gorgeous. Get that one.’ She tries it out and says ‘ehhh, I dunno if I really feel this one.’ I tell her that if she doesn’t buy it, I will, and she says ‘you don’t even play guitar! What are you gonna do with it?’ Walked out of the store with it on a complete whim, spent 3 months learning before I started doing open mics, making friends at the music shop, joining a band, and having the time of my life throughout my 20s.” A man playing guitar. Photo credit: Canva When luck came out of nowhere For some, a 10-second decision ended up with an unexpected windfall. “Decided not to get into an elevator with my ex and her new boyfriend, so I took the stairs instead. On the third flight, I found a discarded scratch-off ticket that ended up being worth $50,000. It’s the only time in my life where being socially awkward actually paid off my mortgage.” “A family in my marina announced that they are moving away the following week. They were going to turn their sailboat over to a broker to sell it for them. I mentioned that I was contemplating a larger boat with a smaller engine and would be interested in theirs. I asked what price would they consider? He said, $10k. I said, okay, and we shook on it. The boat was worth over $24k. I got a wheelbarrow from the marina corral and removed stuff from my smaller boat, walked it over to their dock, and loaded it onboard. That was ten years ago, and I still live on it six months out of the year. Sweet.” Sometimes, these kinds of life-altering changes are simply fresh new outlooks on life. “I was going through old text messages with my then girlfriend and realized I had become a very negative person. I decided right there to always look for the bright side of things. It takes some effort but that was 12 years ago and I’m much happier. It becomes second nature after a while.” When a split second saved a life In many instances, a 10-second decision prevented tragedy for themselves or others. “Most of these answers are super happy and mine really isn’t but fits the question. Mine would be double checking on my wife before bed. She suffers from PTSD, depression and anxiety and had just been ‘off’ all day. I checked with her a couple times and she said everything was alright each time. It might sound weird but she was too happy and calm but kind of sad at the same time. It just didn’t sit right with me. She said she was going to bed and we kissed and I asked again she chuckled and said to stop worrying. She went upstairs and I waited a few seconds and went up to say I think something is wrong. I stopped her from committing suicide that night. Normally I would take her for her word but that decision was 12 years ago and we are having the best version of our lives because I listened to my gut and went and checked.” “One night I drove home from working evening shift (like 2 miles) and when I glanced in the rear view I had chills when I saw the headlights behind me at a red light. I got to my house and was about to park but then heard a voice in my head tell me to keep driving, so I did… and they continued to follow me. Called my dad to stay on the phone as I drove to a police station. Car stopped following when a cop car pulled up behind us (coincidentally). Next morning read about an armed carjacking in the area about an hour later.” “In middle school my best friend invited me to Knott’s Berry Farm with another group of kids he was friends with… I got to my friend’s house after running some errands with my mom. There were 5 kids aged 14-15 there. I asked my friend how we were getting [to Knott’s Berry] and he said he was driving his dad’s car (he was underage and had no license). I was nervous but I wanted to look cool so, I said ok. Right before we got into the car, I had the worst feeling come over me. In approximately 5 seconds, I felt a drop in my stomach to a bottomless pit, a hot flash followed by chills, and intense nausea. I literally left without making a sound, running to a nearby Starbucks and using a stranger’s phone and asking my mother to pick me up. I felt so embarrassed. I knew I was going to get shit all month from my friend… A few hours later, they were on their way home on the freeway and lost control of the vehicle. All 5 died.” What’s a decision you made in under 10 seconds that changed your life forever? by u/nathannnate01 in AskReddit What about when you can’t decide? And yet, for some (make that many) of us, knowing that every decision is uniquely important can be a major source of anxiety, causing us to freeze via “analysis paralysis” and not choose at all, which, in itself, is a choice (they’re inescapable!). In fact, research suggests our brains can struggle more with low-stakes decisions . Interestingly, experts seem to suggest combating this ambivalence with tools that force a quick deadline . You can either toss a coin or set a time limit , which would arguably incite one of these potentially life-changing 10-second decisions. In one well-known study, people who let a coin toss decide a major life choice and made the change were happier six months later. Life will inevitably call on us to make both long, thought-out decisions and to go with our gut. But hopefully, this reminds us that even our whims can lead to something truly pivotal without making us lose our minds. This article originally appeared in February. It has been updated. The post People share the ’10 second decisions’ that meaningfully improved their lives forever appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: “Hijda! Half-man!” These were some of the insults Bani J faced simply for having muscles. But she refused to change herself to fit society's idea of femininity. 💪 At just 18, Bani entered MTV Roadies. Soon, she became a VJ and began working on one project after another. With 12–13-hour workdays, the gym became her personal space. But weightlifting gave her more than physical strength. It changed how she saw herself. People mocked her muscles, called her manly and questioned her femininity. Bani refused to apologise for being strong or taking up space. Her story goes beyond fitness and appearance. Growing up in an abusive home, she witnessed her mother being physically abused by her father. Those experiences shaped her understanding of how women's pain is often silenced. Today, she uses her platform to speak up for survivors. From her muscles and tattoos to walking away from work for a year to reclaim her happiness, Bani has made her choices on her own terms. Because being a woman doesn't come with a prescribed look, body type or set of rules. You are allowed to define femininity for yourself. ❤️ #BaniJ #VJ BaniJ #MTVRoadies #WomenWhoInspire #BreakingStereotypes #WomenEmpowerment #BodyPositivity #StrongWomen #FitnessJourney #Femininity #BeautyStandards #MentalStrength #WomenSupportingWomen #thebetterindia Subscribe Us Now : https://www.youtube.com/thebetterindia Follow us for more: Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/thebetterindia Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/thebetterindia/ Twitter: https://twitter.com/thebetterindia LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/company/thebetterindia/ Website: https://www.thebetterindia.com/

items.descriptionOriginal: You wake up and your nose is the first thing to tell you what the air is like. One side is blocked, then the other. There is a dull pressure behind your cheeks, your eyes itch, and the sky outside is the colour of dishwater. You open the AQI app and it says "severe" . Then the questions begin. Is this my sinusitis flaring up? An allergy? Or is it just the smog? Should I reach for that decongestant spray in the drawer? Do I need a doctor, or will this pass when the air clears? If you live in Delhi NCR with chronic sinusitis or allergic rhinitis, you may know this morning well. Your nose was inflamed long before the first particle of smog arrived, and now you're left guessing, often with whatever is nearest to hand. Dr M. Shantanu, an ENT specialist in Delhi, says that guesswork is where people go wrong. "Not every blocked nose is sinusitis," he says, and treating it as if it were can backfire. Here are his answers to the questions people ask most on bad air days, as a field guide for when the sky turns grey. It does not replace a consultation with your own doctor. Why smog hits sinus and allergy patients harder Why does a high AQI make a blocked nose worse? "Think of the nose as a security checkpoint. Mucus and tiny hair-like structures called cilia catch dust, allergens, and microorganisms, while the sinuses rely on that same system to drain," he explains. People living with chronic sinusitis may experience increased congestion, facial pressure and reduced smell during periods of severe air pollution. Photograph: (TNIE) When fine particles slip in, they irritate the lining and set off inflammation. The swelling narrows the small passages linking the sinuses to the nose. Drainage slows, and an old problem feels brand new. Dr Shantanu points to research linking particulate exposure with chronic rhinosinusitis and with greater severity. If your congestion, sneezing, facial pressure, postnasal drip, headaches or dulled sense of smell keep flaring when the air is bad, he says, take it as a cue to identify your triggers. Which pollutants are the troublemakers? PM2.5 and PM10, particles measuring 2.5 and 10 micrometres or less, top his list. They arrive via vehicle exhaust, construction dust, industrial emissions and smoke. Traffic-related nitrogen dioxide, a gas produced mainly by burning fuel, adds to the irritation. "If you live or work near a building site, expect more sneezing and a runnier nose, especially if you have allergies," he says. Is it sinusitis, allergy, or just pollution irritation? The three overlap, so Dr Shantanu reads the pattern. Pollution irritation burns, blocks, and makes you sneeze during or after exposure, usually without fever. Allergic rhinitis brings sneezing, an itchy nose, watery eyes and a runny nose after contact with pollen, dust mites or pet dander. Sinusitis means congestion, facial pressure, reduced smell and nasal discharge, sometimes with fever. Chronic rhinosinusitis generally means symptoms lasting at least 12 weeks. Pollution and allergy can also feed each other, so your symptoms may refuse to sit in one box. Can a smoggy day give me a sinus infection? Not automatically, he says. " Pollution can make symptoms harder to control in people who already have a nasal or sinus condition." Allergic rhinitis can cause repeated sneezing, itchy eyes, nasal irritation and a runny nose when pollution levels rise. Photograph: ( TNIE ) Viral infections, especially colds, are the most common cause of acute sinus infections. Mucus colour alone cannot confirm a bacterial infection. Your cause, the duration of symptoms, and a clinical examination should decide treatment, because not every blocked nose needs antibiotics. What does it do to daily life? Persistent congestion, sleep broken by difficulty breathing through the nose, a foggy head, repeated flare-ups and allergies that are harder to manage. Dr Shantanu adds that not everyone who breathes dirty air develops chronic sinusitis . Genetics, allergies, nasal anatomy, infections, and smoking all shape individual risk. His survival guide for a high-AQI day Where do I start? Check the AQI before you plan anything outdoors. When it is poor, cut both the length and the intensity of outdoor exercise, especially near busy roads and construction sites. Saline nasal sprays and rinses can help clear mucus and trapped irritants, provided sterile, distilled or boiled-and-cooled water is used. Photograph: ( Dreamstime ) Keep a note of whether your symptoms worsen on high-pollution days. That record helps an ENT specialist pin down your triggers. Reduce smoke and chemical fumes at home too, and follow workplace safety measures if your job is dusty. Does a mask really help? A well-fitting N95 worn outdoors can cut inhalation of many airborne particles. It is not a force field, though. It does not remove every harmful gas, so he treats it as one layer of protection and not the whole answer. Ordinary cloth or surgical masks do far less against fine particles. How do I keep my home air cleaner? Keep windows and doors shut when the air outside is bad, and run a correctly sized HEPA purifier if you have one. HEPA air purifiers can help reduce indoor particulate pollution, while limiting incense, cigarette smoke and other indoor pollutants. Photograph: ( India Today ) Skip cigarettes, incense, and other indoor smoke. Open up the house only when the air outside is cleaner than the air inside. How do I rinse my nose safely? Saline sprays or rinses clear mucus and irritants, so they suit the end of a day spent outside. The water is what makes it safe: distilled, sterile, or boiled and cooled. Never untreated tap water. Clean the device as its instructions say. Can I reach for a decongestant spray? Dr Shantanu advises against self-medicating with them, because some cause rebound congestion when used longer than recommended. If symptoms are frequent, get them assessed instead of treating them again and again with over-the-counter medicines. Do fluids and sleep help? They support general wellbeing, and he recommends both. But they do not prevent pollution-related sinus inflammation on their own, so they belong beside the steps above, not instead of them. Delhi NCR's air pollution, driven by vehicle emissions, construction dust and smoke, can make breathing uncomfortable and aggravate existing nasal and sinus conditions. Photograph: ( Conway Airmen ) The goal of the whole routine is to reduce irritation and keep symptoms manageable, not to promise they will never appear. And home remedies? Warm compresses, rest, and saline rinses can ease a viral infection but cannot reliably clear a bacterial one. If symptoms continue, see a doctor. When to see an ENT specialist How do I know it has gone beyond a bad air day? Occasional sneezing often settles once you leave the trigger behind. Persistent or recurring symptoms deserve attention. Book a consultation if you have: congestion or facial pressure that will not improve repeated episodes of suspected sinusitis a persistent loss or reduction of smell blockage mainly on one side symptoms that disturb sleep or daily activities persistent or recurrent headache or ear heaviness What will the specialist do? An ENT specialist can tell pollution irritation apart from allergic rhinitis, recurrent sinusitis, nasal polyps or structural problems like a deviated septum. Saline nasal sprays and rinses can help clear mucus and trapped irritants, provided sterile, distilled or boiled-and-cooled water is used. Photograph: ( AI-Generated image ) That can mean reviewing your symptoms, exposure history and past treatments, examining your nasal passages, identifying allergy triggers, and advising on tests or imaging when clinically indicated. Treatment follows the cause, from saline irrigation to nasal medication or allergy management. Antibiotics are not routine for every episode, and surgery is for selected cases only. Which symptoms are urgent? Swelling or redness around the eyes, vision changes, a severe or unusual headache, confusion, or any rapidly worsening symptoms. Go to a doctor straight away. The one-breath version Check the AQI before you step out. Wear a snug N95 if you must. Keep indoor air clean. Rinse with safe water. Note whether your symptoms follow the smog. "None of this guarantees your sinuses will stay quiet. But if symptoms linger, recur or worsen, take that record to an ENT specialist. But most importantly, know that help is always available and self-medication is not a solution," Dr Shantanu says.

items.descriptionOriginal: On a Saturday morning in October 2026, seven Pune residents gathered at Madhavrao Scindia Garden beside the Mula River. Across the water, two fishers steered their boat past a thick patch of trees. The residents had brought smartphones and measuring tapes. They were there to document trees that people might pass every day without giving them much thought. They photographed individual trees, noted their species, measured the circumference of their trunks and recorded their locations on a phone app. Each entry added another piece to a growing map of Pune's riverbank greenery. It may seem like a small weekend exercise. But for these volunteers, knowing exactly which trees grow where could make a difference when the city decides what to build next. Why are Pune residents counting trees? The volunteers belong to Pune River Revival (PRR), a citizen group that began mapping trees more systematically in 2024, amid concerns about the ₹4,727-crore Pune Riverfront Development Project. The plan includes promenades, recreational spaces and other construction along the Mula-Mutha riverbanks. The group wanted a clearer record of the trees and other living things already thriving there. That meant going beyond counting trunks. "We started organizing the tree mapping exercise systematically in 2024," volunteer Raghunandan Patil told Mongabay. Earlier, he explained, the group had mapped trees by hand but lacked the technical knowledge to document them properly. Today, volunteers use iNaturalist, an app on which people can upload photographs and locations of plants and animals. It helps them identify species and build a record that others can consult. During mapping walks, volunteers spread out across stretches of the riverbank, taking photographs and measurements as they go. Every entry helps answer an important question: if a patch of greenery disappears tomorrow, will anyone know what was there? More than 500 trees faced removal. Residents got to work. That question became urgent on Ganeshkhind Road, where plans to widen a busy stretch threatened 529 trees , including mature trees believed to be decades old. When residents approached PRR, volunteers documented over 500 trees within a month. The records helped put names, numbers and locations to trees that people feared losing. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Pune Tree Mappers PRR (@punetreemapping.rivers) The concern spread beyond the mapping group. On 18 and 19 April 2026, residents, artists and environmentalists came together for tree mapping, live painting and music, drawing attention to the proposed widening of the road between Sancheti Hospital and Savitribai Phule Pune University. Under an earlier proposal, 469 trees were to be transplanted and 60 cut down. Environmentalists questioned whether older trees could survive being moved. "I grew up with these trees and they are part of every Punekar's heritage," artist Janaki Gandhi told Pune Mirror. "Through art, we want people to see each tree as a living identity, not just an obstacle in a road plan." Citizens also raised objections and pushed for changes to the road design. By September 2026, the Pune Municipal Corporation had revised its proposal, reducing the number of trees marked for removal from 529 to 33. That meant 496 trees could be spared under the revised plan. The change came through wider citizen action and efforts by environmental groups. Mapping helped document what was at stake and gave residents another way to make their case. What can a sacred grove teach a growing city? Along the rivers, PRR has also drawn attention to Ram-Mula Devrai, a sacred grove where the Ram and Mula rivers meet. A devrai is a forest patch traditionally protected by local communities because it is believed to be the dwelling place of a village deity. In a busy city, it can also offer shelter to plants, birds and other wildlife. Reports cited by Mongabay record around 1,000 heritage trees and at least 450 species of plants and animals in the grove. Among them are 160 bird species, as well as the Bengal monitor lizard and checkered keelback snake. During a mapping exercise, volunteers divide themselves across assigned stretches of the riverbank. Each person records observations directly on the platform. Photograph: (Pune River Revival-Via-Free Press Journal) To help more people discover this place, volunteers organised butterfly and insect walks, tree-painting competitions and other activities. They also suggested ways visitors could enjoy the space while protecting its trees. Their efforts showed how people could explore and appreciate a natural space while keeping its greenery intact. From riverbanks to hilltops, more people are joining in Elsewhere in Pune, citizens are building similar records. On Chatushrungi, Taljai and ARAI hills, the Green Hills Group uses an app called TrackMyTree to record saplings, their locations, species and caretakers. Revisiting those records can tell volunteers which trees are surviving and where they need attention. Along the Mula, PRR and JeevitNadi volunteers have also used ConnecTree, a tool developed by the Pune Knowledge Cluster, to document riverbank trees and saplings . View this post on Instagram A post shared by Civic Sense Task Force (CSTF) PCMC Pune (@civicsensetaskforce) Pune Municipal Corporation says it conducts a tree census every five years. But citizen groups believe accessible, regularly updated records are important too, especially when residents want to understand how a proposed project may affect their neighbourhood. Back at the river, the work still comes down to a photograph, a measurement and a location saved on a phone. The same simple steps the seven volunteers took that October morning could one day give residents a record to point to when an old tree is marked for removal. And as Pune continues to grow, these records give its residents something valuable: a clearer picture of the trees around them and a stronger voice in deciding how to protect them. Sources: 'How citizen scientists are mapping Pune's trees, with hopes of a greener future' : By Stephin Thomas, Published on 30 October 2026 'Pune Citizens Take Geotagging Of Green Cover Into Their Own Hands' : By Urban Acres, Published on 21 July 2025 'Citizens Launch Weekend Art and Music Protest to Save Ganeshkhind Road Trees' : By Chaitraly Deshmukh, Published on 18 April 2026

Ο προβληματισμός της δεν φτάνει ως συμβουλή αλλά ως άδεια: να νιώθει ημιτελής και ολοκληρωμένη ταυτόχρονα, να σταματήσει να περιμένει…
items.descriptionOriginal: At twenty-two, Haile Thomas sat with a question most of us quietly carry for decades: what do I do with all of this existence? Rather than answer it, she did something braver -- she wrote her way into the uncertainty itself. Her reflection arrives not as advice but as permission: to feel incomplete and whole at the same time, to stop waiting for the map that will never come. She offers a quietly radical image of identity -- that growing up is less about finding yourself than noticing "the entity that gets dressed," the spaciousness beneath every costume we try on and discard. There is no finish line in her telling, only transformations meeting us in the moments we least expect. "Growing up is a never ending journey," she writes -- and somehow that lands not as defeat but as relief. What she offers, finally, is not wisdom so much as weather: a loosening, a liquefying of the hard certainties we grip when life refuses to hold still.

items.descriptionOriginal: An Indian Village with ZERO Electricity Bill, FREE Cooking Gas & Women Own Every Home? Sounds like a fairytale? Meet Shelkewadi, Maharashtra! For 20+ years, Shelkewadi has solved problems that Indian cities still struggle with: LPG dependency, power cuts, water crisis, pollution, and waste, all without crores in budget. In this episode of Solved In India, we visit this tiny village in Karvir Taluka, Kolhapur, where barely 80 families live. They’ve built a real-life zero-waste, self-sufficient, sustainable village model that every Indian village can copy. With 60% of India’s LPG imported and a big part of it passing through the Strait of Hormuz, Shelkewadi shows what energy independence looks like at the village level. Imagine if every village in India followed this model. Would you move to a village like this? items.descriptionOriginal: A stick figure family, a googly-eyed monster, a happy rainbow. Children’s artwork represents how they see the world at any given age — a sweet, fleeting perspective that the adults in their lives yearn to preserve. But kids are prolific creators, so what’s to be done with all these construction paper canvases as more continuously flood in? Artist Shana Blakley came up with a creative way to save her kids’ drawings while breaking out of a rut she’d been in with her own work: She turned them into a big, colorful collage to hang in her family’s home. When she shared the result on Instagram, her comment section exploded. The idea clearly resonated with other moms, dads, and grandparents. Heirloom Collage Shana Blakley’s first kids’ artwork collage “We want to honor what our kids make,” Blakley told Nice News, adding: “Nearly every parent around the world has a growing pile of kid art, and it’s in our nature to save it. We feel guilty throwing it away, but storing it also begins to feel unsettling. There comes a time when you realize how much of it you have and you ask yourself: ‘What am I keeping this for?’” Heirloom Collage Molly Revers with her grandkids and the collages made from their artwork Shortly after posting the piece last year, she launched Heirloom Collage and started taking commissions. Now, she offers an online course that guides participants in producing their own artist-quality collages out of kiddos’ creations. The course consists of six video modules totaling one hour, and Blakley provides feedback in a private Facebook group where students can post their in-progress and completed work. Molly Revers enjoys dabbling in different artistic endeavors, so she signed up for the $99 e-course. “The most meaningful aspect was the joy it brought me when creating the collages and the joy it brought my little grandsons when they saw their work displayed in such a cool way,” she shared. “They love picking their favorite creations and memories associated with them.” Heirloom Collage Another parent’s completed collage For Blakley, who lives in Richmond, Virginia, and began her career as a fine artist over a decade ago, the project reconnected her to a sense of spontaneity after a period of creative stagnation. “Halfway through it, I recall thinking, ‘[My kids] didn’t second-guess their creativity in these pieces, so I shouldn’t either,’” she said. “That was a big breakthrough for me.” It’s something many adults, artists or not, can relate to. “A lot of my students haven’t made art since they were kids, and this brings them back to it,” Blakley added. Overall, though, the memorable shared experience of making that first collage with her two children — the youngsters helped select the included drawings and “were buzzing with pride” — is what she wishes for her clients. “That connection is what lasts, and they end up with something their family really treasures,” she said. Heirloom Collage Jeanine Long-Tuohy with her granddaughter Ava and the collage they made Jeanine Long-Tuohy, who loves her granddaughter Ava’s artwork, created her first piece with Ava’s help and has since started a new one with another grandchild. “Working on this made me feel like there’s a lot more we can do together,” Long-Tuohy said. “It’s a memory they will always have of me.”

Όπως και στη νέα σειρά AKKA, για αιώνες, πολλές οικογένειες Nair ακολούθησαν ένα μοναδικό μητρογραμμικό σύστημα που ονομάζεται Marumakkathayam, όπου η οικογενειακή ταυτότητα και η κληρονομιά περνούσαν από την πλευρά της μητέρας. items.descriptionOriginal: In Kerala, your father’s property could belong to your aunt’s children! Just like in the new series AKKA, for centuries, many Nair families followed a unique matrilineal system called Marumakkathayam, where family identity and inheritance passed through the mother’s side. Even a king’s son could not inherit the throne. It went to his sister’s son! But here’s the twist: women passed down the family name, while men, especially the eldest maternal uncle, held the power. The system was abolished in 1975, but matrilineal traditions continue in parts of India. items.descriptionOriginal: In Bajaura, in Himachal Pradesh's Kullu district, farmers have had to rethink their orchards twice. As changing weather made apple cultivation harder, they turned to pomegranates. Then plant viruses began affecting those orchards too. Now, persimmons are offering another possibility. For anyone who associates Himachal with bags of apples brought home after a holiday, that change may be surprising. For the people tending these orchards, it comes down to a pressing question: what can they grow to keep earning from their land? Rising temperatures, declining snowfall and unpredictable rainfall are making familiar crops harder to rely on. Farmers are responding by trying different fruits, growing crops together and changing how they care for their soil. Their efforts feature in a study by the Council on Energy, Environment and Water (CEEW), supported by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD). Released on 31 October 2026, it draws on experiences across 12 gram panchayats in Mandi, Kullu, Sirmaur and Shimla . The study identifies 25 ways communities can prepare for climate risks. Among them are practices villagers have already begun putting to work, shaped by what they see happening in their fields and around their homes. What do you plant when the familiar crop struggles? Bajaura's move towards persimmons shows how much adjustment farming now demands. Replacing apples with pomegranates did not end the uncertainty. Farmers had to look for another option when disease affected the replacement crop. Growing a mix of crops can help spread the risk of a poor harvest, though poor transport and limited cold storage still constrain farmers' earnings. Photograph: (Himachal Watcher) And choosing a fruit is only part of making an orchard viable. Farmers need water to grow it and roads to get the harvest to buyers. In Bajaura, dwindling irrigation water and roads damaged during disasters continue to make both difficult. In Parara, Sirmaur, growers face a related problem. Residents report that changing rainfall and rising temperatures have altered planting schedules and increased diseases affecting tomatoes and garlic. Some farmers are combining garlic cultivation with specialised apple varieties . The village's efforts also include natural farming and rainwater harvesting. Growing a mix of crops can help spread the risk of a poor harvest, though poor transport and limited cold storage still constrain farmers' earnings. For a farming household, finding something that grows is the beginning. Being able to sell it is what helps pay the bills. In Sandhu, change begins with the soil In Sandhu, Shimla, farmers are reconsidering how they grow their crops. Community members report that prolonged chemical fertiliser use has affected soil quality and fertility. Local women have responded by taking up natural farming, which avoids synthetic fertilisers and pesticides and uses resources available on the farm. The aim is to nurture the soil while reducing reliance on purchased chemical inputs . According to community accounts documented in the study, the practice has spread to more than 20 families after residents found it profitable and better able to withstand extreme weather. That experience gives neighbours something practical to consider: a different way of farming already being tried close to home. Yet even healthier soil and a different crop need water. In nearby Sirmaur district, that has brought women's groups back to the traditional sources their villages once relied on. Bringing water back to village life Thana Kashoga once had 35 perennial baoris, traditional spring-fed water structures that supplied households throughout the year. According to the study, only 10 remain. Residents report declining rainfall and rising temperatures , putting increasing pressure on these sources. The shortage reaches into everyday life, affecting drinking water, irrigation and livestock. Fodder scarcity and forest fires have also made pastoral livelihoods harder to sustain. Local women have responded by taking up natural farming, which avoids synthetic fertilisers and pesticides and uses resources available on the farm. The aim is to nurture the soil while reducing reliance on purchased chemical inputs. Photograph: (Triya Gulati via The Print) Women's groups have taken on the work of maintaining and restoring the baoris. Their efforts connect directly to what farmers are trying to do: keep village life possible as the conditions supporting it change. These communities still need dependable irrigation, transport and support to carry their work forward. A new crop cannot fix a damaged road, and a restored water source needs continued care. But in Thana Kashoga, there is a tangible reason to keep going. Women's groups clean the baoris monthly. Five springs have been revived, with work on another five or six under way. Sources: 'Villages in Himachal adapting climate change with new crops, revived springs' : By Shailee Dogra, Published on 1 November 2026 'How can Himalayan communities anticipate risks and adapt to a changing climate? Evidence from 12 Gram Panchayats of Himachal Pradesh' : By Ahana Chatterjee, Meet Kumar, Srishti Mandal, Taveri Rajkhowa, and Shreya Wadhawan, Published on 31 October, 2026

Μέσω πραγματικών γονέων, προπονητών γονέων, επιρροών και ειδικών, η σειρά φέρνει ειλικρινείς, διαφορετικές και σχετικές προοπτικές για το q…
items.descriptionOriginal: This story is part of "Parenting: What Google Won't Tell You" — The Better India's people-led parenting series that goes beyond conventional advice to document how real families are actually raising their children. Through real parents, parenting coaches, influencers and experts, the series brings honest, diverse and relatable perspectives on the questions, choices, challenges and solutions that shape everyday parenting — the things Google can't always answer. For a five-year-old, changing schools can mean more than walking into a new classroom or learning a different routine. It can also mean leaving behind familiar faces, favourite teachers and friends who have been part of their everyday lives. Four months after her daughter moved to a new school, Shivani Tyagi decided to revisit the experience with a simple question: "When we changed your school, how did you feel?" Her daughter's answer caught her attention. "It was very upsetting," she said, explaining that the hardest part was leaving her friends behind. She hadn't wanted to do that. Even after settling into a new school, children may need time and space to process the emotions of leaving old friends behind. Rather than brushing aside the response or reassuring her that everything was fine, Shivani chose to listen and ask her daughter more about how she had managed the change. Making room for difficult feelings Shivani, a certified nutritionist, parent coach and NLP coach, believes that children do not always express what they are feeling immediately. Sometimes, they need time, reassurance and a comfortable space to put their emotions into words. Her daughter had settled into the new school, made friends and appeared to be adjusting well. But Shivani wanted to understand what the transition had felt like from her daughter's perspective. When she asked how she had managed the move despite finding it upsetting, her daughter explained that she was willing to try. Having the space to express what she was feeling made it easier for her to navigate the change. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Shivani Tyagi - Parent coach, Nutritionist, NLP practitioner (@parenting_with_shivani) For Shivani, that was a moment of pride. She was happy to see her daughter acknowledge that something had been difficult while still finding the courage to give a new environment a chance. She also understood that making new friends did not mean forgetting the old ones. They could still stay in touch with their previous classmates while gradually building new friendships. Keep asking, even after they seem settled School transitions can bring a mix of emotions for young children. Excitement about a new classroom may exist alongside sadness about leaving familiar surroundings. And just because a child appears comfortable after a few weeks does not necessarily mean they have processed everything. This is why Shivani makes it a habit to have open conversations with her daughter about everyday experiences, whether big or small. For parents navigating a similar transition, the approach need not be complicated. A simple conversation over dinner, during a bedtime routine or on the way back from school can create an opportunity for children to share what is on their minds. Simple everyday conversations can help children feel safe expressing emotions they may otherwise struggle to put into words. Instead of immediately offering solutions, parents can begin by asking what they miss, what they enjoy about the new school or whether anything has been difficult. The idea is not to have all the answers but to let children know that their feelings are welcome. Sometimes, a child does not need to be told that everything will be fine. They simply need to know that they can talk about what isn't. All images courtesy of Shivani Tyagi Source: 'Helping Kids Handle Change at School' by PBS Kids, Published on 11 January 2022.

items.descriptionOriginal: In South Sudan in 2024, just out of high school, Nyakangba Nelson Luka Poyo asked himself what kind of life a kid born in 2021 in Tambura would have apart from killing, hatred, bloodshed, and living in a camp. Amid tears, that question gave him his life’s purpose. He thought if young people had opportunities to learn and communicate, and the space in which to express themselves, they could realize alternatives to violence. He called it a “Peace Voice.” Young people make up an estimated 70% of South Sudan’s population, yet they have no voice. They are swept up into conflict at a shockingly young age. In a Peace Journey program, Nyakangba learned about Laddership, and how to become a “ladder” for others lifting them up through support and opportunities. Now, through Peace Voices to Vision, he helps young people “develop a common understanding of how to live together peacefully. Everyone deserves peace.”

items.descriptionOriginal: This article is published in partnership with Museum of Solutions For a child who has never used a computer independently, the first lesson in artificial intelligence isn't about algorithms. It's about a cursor. For one Grade 6 student from a government school in Maharashtra's Raigad district, that lesson began inside a 10-storey children's museum in Mumbai's Lower Parel, tucked into the old Kamala Mills compound: the Museum of Solutions (MuSo). When the student joined an immersive artificial intelligence (AI) learning programme there, computers were still unfamiliar territory. Even using a laptop touchpad and typing basic commands were challenges. But over the next few sessions, that began to change. By the end of the programme, the student had created an email account, learnt to use Microsoft Word and OneDrive, and taken part in coding challenges through Minecraft Education. What started with the basics of operating a computer had opened a door to exploring artificial intelligence, experimenting with technology and understanding how it works. "From day one, it was pretty interesting. The AI workshop at the Museum of Solutions brought teachers and students together to learn about technology, explore AI and understand how it can be used to find solutions to different problems, from those in our classrooms to challenges at a global level," says Meera, a student, who attended the workshop at MuSo. For thousands of children from underserved communities across Maharashtra, such opportunities are becoming a first introduction to the technology that is increasingly shaping the world around them. Students experiment with machine learning by training models to recognise objects and understanding how the information they receive shapes their results. Through AI Explorers, an initiative at MuSo, children are learning about AI through interactive games, experiments, creative exercises and coding activities. The programme, supported by Microsoft Philanthropies India and implemented by JSW Foundation, aims to make AI education more accessible to children who may have limited opportunities to engage with digital learning. Between July 2025 and June 2026, the initiative reached 9,087 children through foundational AI workshops, while another 313 students took part in a more intensive 10-hour learning pilot. It also trained 80 teachers and worked with 36 schools and 17 NGO and community partners across six districts of Maharashtra. But the numbers tell only part of the story. At its heart, the initiative is about making sure that a child's access to emerging technologies is not decided by the circumstances they grow up in. Bringing AI education beyond privileged classrooms AI is already influencing how children interact with the world, from the content they watch to the apps they use. But knowing how to use a digital device and understanding the technology behind it are two very different things. For children from underserved communities, opportunities to explore AI, experiment with coding or even use a computer independently can be limited. The data bears this out. According to the Ministry of Education's UDISE+ 2024-25 data, only 57.9% of schools in India have computers that work for teaching, and in government schools the figure falls to 52.7%. In Maharashtra, more than 25,000 of the state's 1.08 lakh schools, nearly one in four, had no functional computer. Children explore how AI works through interactive activities, learning to question its outputs rather than simply accept them. At home, the gap is wider still. The ASER 2023 'Beyond Basics' survey of rural youth aged 14 to 18 found that while about 90% of households had a smartphone, only 9% had a computer or laptop. Those with a computer at home were far more likely to know how to use one (85%) than those without (33.9%). Meanwhile, AI is arriving in classrooms. From the 2026-27 academic year, the Ministry of Education is introducing AI and computational thinking in schools from Class 3 onwards. This gap led MuSo to conceptualise AI Explorers. It's a natural fit for a museum whose very name is a mission statement. Opened in November 2023 by the JSW Group and founded by Tanvi Jindal Shete, a former Teach For India fellow, the not-for-profit museum aims to empower children to find solutions to India's most pressing problems. Within a year, it was named on TIME's list of the World's Greatest Places of 2024 and became the first Indian museum to win the international Hands On! Children in Museums Award, competing against 32 museums from 17 countries. "AI already shapes children's lives through the phones in their homes, the apps they use and the content they are shown. Yet children from underserved communities rarely get the chance to understand how it works, let alone question it," says Susan Vaidyan, Head of Education MuSo. The programme introduces students from Classes 5 to 10 to foundational AI concepts, machine learning, prompt engineering, digital literacy, coding and responsible technology use. Rather than beginning with technical explanations, the sessions use familiar examples and hands-on activities. In one activity, students use a teachable machine to train a machine-learning model to recognise different objects or images. They experiment with the data being fed into the system, and then do something unexpected: they deliberately train it incorrectly to see what happens. When the model begins producing inaccurate results, the children grasp an important truth about AI: its outputs depend on the information it learns from. The programme also introduces students to AI-generated creativity, prompt-based exercises and community problem-solving challenges, allowing them to explore how the technology can be applied to everyday situations. Microsoft's involvement brings technology platforms, learning resources and expertise in responsible AI to the programme. The programme introduces children to responsible AI use, including online privacy, misinformation, bias and cyber safety. "An inclusive AI economy cannot begin at college or the workplace; it has to begin in the classroom," says Kishore Kumar Thangavelu, CSR Lead, Microsoft Corporation India Private Limited. Through Microsoft 365, students learn to create email accounts, organise their work using OneDrive, write documents in Word and use Excel to organise information. They also explore Copilot to improve sentences, summarise information and help with everyday tasks. Minecraft Education and MakeCode introduce coding through play. Students programme a virtual agent to chop trees, build walls and construct structures using instructions, loops and conditional statements. The programme also uses Minecraft's CyberSafe world to introduce online safety through games and practical challenges. That matters: ASER 2023 found that nearly half of rural young people on social media didn't know basic safety features, such as blocking or reporting a profile. But the learning isn't limited to how these tools work. Children are also encouraged to question the technology, recognise its limits and consider when it should or shouldn't be used. AI Explorers began as a two-hour introductory workshop. But the team soon realised that children needed more time to move beyond demonstrations and engage with the concepts themselves. "It's important for children to not just use AI tools but to question their outputs and understand their limitations," says Susan. The 10-hour programme, spread across three days, gives children the time to do just that. They begin by exploring how AI and machine learning work, including the exercise where they deliberately train a model with incorrect information. On the second day, they explore agentic AI through block coding and a game that shows how AI agents observe their surroundings and make decisions. The final day focuses on responsible AI, covering privacy, transparency and bias, with examples such as deepfakes, phishing and voice assistants that struggle with different accents. Coding activities through Minecraft Education help students understand instructions, loops and conditional statements while learning through play. For Susan, the aim is to move children beyond watching demonstrations to experimenting, asking questions and recognising that a machine's answers are not always right. "They stopped watching and started doing: trying things, getting wrong results and working out why," she says. Their questions began changing too, from what AI could do to how it arrived at an answer, and when its outputs should be questioned. What changes when children get access? Over the course of a year, AI Explorers reached 9,087 children through its foundational workshops. Another 313 students spent more time with the subject through the 10-hour immersive pilot. The programme travelled across six Maharashtra districts (Mumbai, Mumbai Suburban, Thane, Raigad, Ahilyanagar and Pune), reaching children through 36 government and aided schools and 17 NGO and community partners. There was also an effort to ensure girls were part of this learning experience. Of the 7,398 student records collected, 54% were girls. That matters in a country where, ASER 2023 found, rural boys were more than twice as likely as girls to own a smartphone, and half the boys surveyed had an email ID, compared with under 30% of girls. But what did the children take away from these sessions? Between July 2025 and June 2026, AI Explorers reached 9,087 children through foundational workshops across six districts of Maharashtra. The assessments offer some clues. In the foundational workshops, 81% of the students assessed showed greater interest in AI, while 61% showed an improvement in AI literacy. Among the 126 students assessed in the immersive pilot, 80% demonstrated an understanding of AI and machine learning. Around 75% showed awareness of coding and cyber safety, while the same proportion had set up an email ID and accessed Microsoft 365, in some cases for the first time. For some children, the change was also visible in how they began to look at technology. At a Marathi-medium school in Mumbai, a group of girls initially felt that technology and AI were too difficult for them. But as they experimented with AI games and prompt engineering, they began creating AI-generated content, discussing ethical questions and using digital tools to explore sustainability challenges. What had once seemed out of reach had become something they could try, question and create with. From first steps to future dreams The Raigad student's journey offers a glimpse of what this access can make possible. At the start of the immersive programme, using a touchpad and typing basic commands were challenges. By the end, the student had independently navigated several digital tools, created an email account and taken part in coding activities. For Meera, it was a fun, experience-oriented way of learning, where she learnt about AI in depth through games and interactive activities. For children with limited access to computers, the programme offers an opportunity to explore technology, build digital skills and imagine new possibilities. "What I found interesting was that we were not just learning about technology, but also understanding how to use it safely and think about things like online privacy, fake information and bias," she adds. As Susan puts it, success is not simply about children learning to use AI tools. It is about seeing them experiment, doubt what a machine tells them and ask questions of their own. As AI becomes part of more aspects of everyday life, the ability to question it may prove just as important as knowing how to use it. And that is a lesson these children are beginning to learn early. items.descriptionOriginal: Every year, tonnes of paddy stubble are set on fire across Punjab, adding to the air pollution choking North India. But what if this farm waste could become something useful? For eight years, Gurdaspur-based innovator Parminder Singh experimented with paddy waste in his garage, even when people mocked his idea. His hard work led to an unusual innovation: drop-down ceiling tiles made using paddy stubble. Designed to provide heat and cold insulation, these tiles are also waterproof and fire-resistant. Through his startup, Agro Stubble Management, Parminder hopes to give farmers a reason to earn from crop residue instead of burning it. His vision is to establish production plants across Punjab, where discarded stubble can become a valuable raw material. It’s an idea that could turn agricultural waste into a resource, create livelihood opportunities and offer another way to tackle stubble burning. #StubbleBurning #Punjab #SustainableInnovation #ClimateAction #AgriTech
