items.descriptionOriginal: For 560 children at New Life School in Dharavi, Mumbai, the future of their education depends on one question: will their school continue to exist where it stands today? The preschool has been educating children in the neighbourhood for four decades. Yet, throughout its 40-year history, it has never owned the land on which it operates. Now, as Dharavi undergoes redevelopment, securing that land has become central to ensuring the school's future. An effort to help the institution do so has brought together an unlikely group: a 19-year-old college student, his friends and a community determined to preserve access to education for the neighbourhood's children. Taking on a fundraising campaign of this scale meant Daniel had to understand several areas beyond his college curriculum, including corporate social responsibility (CSR) funding, institutional philanthropy and campaign strategy. Daniel Gupta, a third-year advertising and media student at Mumbai University, is leading the effort through an initiative called Dharavi Rising. After raising Rs 22 lakh against an initial target of Rs 20 lakh for the school's expansion, the team has now set its sights on a much larger goal: Rs 1.5 crore to help the school secure its land and continue serving children in the neighbourhood. For Daniel, the initiative is about more than keeping a school open. It is also an attempt to change how people see Dharavi, a neighbourhood often discussed through the lens of overcrowding, poverty and redevelopment, rather than through the lives, aspirations and institutions of the people who call it home. And he is learning to take on this challenge while still attending college, without any prior fundraising experience or an established professional network. Building a movement around a school Daniel's connection with New Life School began through a friend whose parents run the institution. Learning about the school's four-decade-long journey also brought him face to face with a pressing question: how could an institution that had served generations of children secure a future for the next ones? "People are often surprised when they learn that this school has been running for 40 years without owning its land. We want more people to know that it exists and understand why securing its future matters," Daniel says. What began as an effort to support the school gradually took shape as Dharavi Rising, an initiative that brings together young people and the wider community to address the institution's long-standing challenges. For the teachers, the campaign offers an opportunity to draw attention to a school that has continued to serve children despite the uncertainty surrounding its future. "We wholeheartedly support Daniel's mission to secure the future of our school in Dharavi. We want to do everything we can to ensure that the children's education continues without disruption," say teachers Kelsi Rani Raja and D. Packia Hincy. For the teachers, the campaign offers an opportunity to draw attention to a school that has continued to serve children despite the uncertainty surrounding its future. Their support also reflects a practical concern for families who depend on accessible schooling. The team wants to preserve an institution that parents can afford, rather than see its future compromised by the changes taking place around it. From Rs 20 lakh to Rs 1.5 crore When Daniel and his college friends began working on Dharavi Rising in November 2025, the idea was to find creative ways for young people to contribute to a cause. Daniel was just 19 when he took on the responsibility of building the initiative. With no previous experience in fundraising or social-impact work , he had to learn how to approach potential donors, understand funding mechanisms and communicate the school's needs. The team's first fundraising effort set a target of Rs 20 lakh for the school's expansion. They eventually raised Rs 22 lakh, marking an important milestone for a student-led initiative. However, the initial achievement was only a starting point. The larger challenge of securing the land on which the school stands remained. The new campaign takes on a more ambitious, long-term challenge: ensuring that an institution that has educated generations of children can continue to do so. Learning to navigate an unfamiliar challenge Taking on a fundraising campaign of this scale meant Daniel had to understand several areas beyond his college curriculum, including corporate social responsibility (CSR) funding, institutional philanthropy and campaign strategy. "I had absolutely no prior experience in any of this, so I needed guidance. I realised there would genuinely be no better tool than ChatGPT," he says. Daniel had been using the AI tool even before starting Dharavi Rising. Like many students, he initially turned to it for help with college presentations and assignments. But as the initiative took shape, his questions became more specific. How does CSR funding work? What policies should he understand? How could he explain the initiative to potential supporters? What would a fundraising campaign need to communicate to people who knew little about the school? ChatGPT became one of the tools he used to work through these questions. "I used it to explore naming and branding ideas, work on campaign strategy , understand broad fundraising and CSR concepts, and develop outreach material. I also used it to identify website requirements and organise my thinking about how to present Dharavi Rising to prospective donors," he tells The Better India . The tool helped him break down an unfamiliar and complex task into smaller, more manageable steps. He also used AI-generated text in donor communications. View this post on Instagram A post shared by New Life School | Dharavi Rising (@new_life_school_dharavi) Daniel estimates that ChatGPT saves him two to three hours a day, helping him balance college with the demands of organising the campaign and communicating with potential donors. However, he recognises that AI cannot replace the judgement and effort required to run an initiative of this nature. He says he rejects suggestions that do not align with Dharavi Rising's objectives and is careful about the information he shares with the tool. He also acknowledges that he has not followed a systematic process to independently verify all the guidance generated by ChatGPT. Ultimately, the campaign continues to depend on people: the school staff who understand its needs, the families whose children attend it, the friends supporting the initiative and the donors willing to contribute. Keeping education within reach For New Life School's teachers, the central concern remains the children. The campaign is not simply about raising money for a building or an expansion. It is about helping secure the future of an educational institution that has remained accessible to families in the neighbourhood for four decades. The challenge now is to build on the team's initial achievement and reach enough people to support the school's longer-term needs. The challenge now is to build on that initial achievement and reach enough people to support the school's longer-term needs. For Daniel, the effort also carries a larger purpose: changing perceptions of Dharavi and highlighting the aspirations, initiatives and community institutions that exist within the neighbourhood. "My work with Dharavi Rising began with a desire to change perceptions of a neighbourhood. It has since developed into a concrete effort to help protect one of its educational institutions . Yes, AI has helped me navigate some of that unfamiliar territory, but the purpose of all our work remains rooted in the school and the children it serves," Daniel says, pointing at the colourful artwork-laden boards in the classroom where he was sitting during a conversation with The Better India . For the 560 children who attend New Life School, the goal is simple: to ensure that a school that has been part of their neighbourhood for decades can continue to be part of their future. This Children's Day, those who wish to support Daniel's efforts to secure the future of New Life School and its 560 children can contribute by visiting dharavirising.com and making a donation.

items.description: Η νόσος Lafora είναι μια σπάνια γενετική πάθηση που συνήθως επηρεάζει παιδιά και εφήβους, προκαλώντας συχνές κρίσεις και σταδιακή απώλεια της γνωστικής λειτουργίας. items.descriptionOriginal: Lafora disease is a rare genetic condition that typically affects kids and adolescents, causing frequent seizures and the gradual loss of cognitive function. There is no cure, so the focus for many parents inevitably turns to quality of life. That’s something Detroit mom Azeza Kasham was struggling to maintain for her 17-year-old son, Gigi Breadiy, earlier this year. He was diagnosed in 2019, just days after his older brother died of the disease. Kasham’s husband has his own health problems and isn’t able to work, and the couple has two younger boys as well, so she took on multiple jobs to pay off medical debt. Breadiy uses a wheelchair, and the family home wasn’t fully accessible, so caring for him was becoming increasingly difficult. She’d tried fundraising on social media, but still felt like she was drowning. A stranger she connected with online would be her rescue buoy. Josh Liljenquist is a Minnesota content creator with over 23 million followers. Many of his videos fall into the somewhat controversial random-acts-of-kindness genre, but the 28-year-old’s main focus is rallying tangible support for people in need. After learning about Breadiy, he posted footage of himself meeting mother and son in February. Less than two months later, a GoFundMe he launched for them had raised nearly $600,000. “It’s just completely changed my life, you know?” Kasham shared during a recent phone call with Nice News. “It’s enabled me to give Gigi everything he needs, but that’s not all [Josh] did. And that isn’t even the most important thing. He restored my faith in humanity.” In the nearly seven months since meeting, Liljenquist and Kasham have become extremely close. “She’s literally like my second mom,” he said, adding: “She keeps saying that I changed her life, but I think she changed my life more than I changed hers.” His own mother also speaks to her often, and even flew out to Michigan to spend time with the family. The women connected so strongly because they both know what it’s like to care for a sick child, and the financial toll it can take. For the first six years of Liljenquist’s life, he was in and out of the hospital. He has a genetic disorder called alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency as well as eosinophilic esophagitis, a chronic inflammatory disease of the esophagus. That background has led him to direct more energy into helping families experiencing similar situations. “I want other parents to not have to deal with the same thing that my parents dealt with,” he said. But his fundraising has benefited people in all sorts of circumstances: a man in need of a new roof, a couple facing homelessness, a woman hoping to open a permanent pay-what-you-can cafe. For Kasham, the support from Liljenquist’s felt like God had answered her prayers. He, too, felt a divine hand in their meeting. The fact that they belong to different religions was a moot point. “She kept asking me, ‘Well, you know, you’re a Christian person. I’m Muslim. Does that matter?’ And I’m like, ‘Oh my gosh, no, not at all,’” he recounted. “That’s the first thing she would ask me. And I said, ‘Why would that matter?’” Before the GoFundMe, Kasham had to bathe Breadiy in the garage because the shower wasn’t accessible. Now, the family has paid down debt and made upgrades to their home, including a roll-in shower, that allow him dignity and privacy. “He has his good days. He has his bad days,” she said, noting that his seizures have worsened in recent months. “But one thing he has that puts the biggest smile on his face is he has his own space.” You can donate to Lafora disease research through Chelsea’s Hope .

Highlighted projects include the Dove Valley Kitchen Remodel, Harris Kitchen & Bar, and Brown New Build Scottsdale. Reviews consistently mention responsive communication and a team that listens before making any recommendations. It’s a stronger fit for clients who want guidance through the whole process rather than buyers looking to pull from existing stock. 3. Hardware Resources Best for: Custom cabinet makers, OEMs, and dealers sourcing hardware and functional components at scale Location: Headquartered in Bossier City, Louisiana; distributes nationally Products: Decorative and functional hardware, dovetail drawer boxes, vanities, cabinet hinges, drawer slides, organizers, LED lighting, sinks, and linear moulding Standout: 140 patents filed; part of Dimora Brands, operating across cabinet hardware, door hardware, faucets, and accessories Hardware Resources has been in business since 1990 and employs around 201 people. It doesn’t sell finished cabinets. The company’s focus is the components and hardware that cabinet makers and dealers build around, so it fills a different need than full-cabinet suppliers. Trade buyers who fabricate their own boxes, or who need a consistent hardware supplier across multiple projects, will find the product catalog deep. Acquired by Harbour Group in 2010, it now operates under the Dimora Brands umbrella, which spans several related product categories. 4. Decore-ative Specialties Best for: Cabinetmakers and industry professionals sourcing custom doors, drawer fronts, and RTA components in volume Location: Monrovia, CA headquarters; manufacturing in Irwindale, CA; Elk Grove, CA; and Monroe, NC Products: RTA cabinets, doors, drawer fronts, drawer boxes, moldings, accessories, finishing, and hardware in wood, plywood, 3D laminate, and melamine Standout: Founded 1965; ranked 68th on the FDMC 300 list of top North American wood products producers; fast ordering software Decore-ative Specialties has manufactured cabinet components since 1965 and employs between 501 and 1,000 people across three production facilities. Their ordering platform lets cabinetmakers spec and order ready-to-assemble frameless components with a six-working-day ship window, faster than most made-to-order competitors. The company holds U.S. Green Building Council membership and won a WMIA Wooden Globe Award for Innovator of the Year in 2016 for a CNC sander shaper capable of producing 500 doors per day. Shipping from California adds lead time for Phoenix-area buyers, but the component depth and production scale make it worth considering for larger orders. 5. Premium Wholesale Cabinets of Arizona Best for: Phoenix metro homeowners and contractors who want custom cabinetry with financing options Location: Serves Phoenix metro including Chandler, Gilbert, Mesa, Scottsdale, Tempe, Glendale, Peoria, and Queen Creek Products: Custom kitchen and bath cabinets, closets, wet bars, outdoor kitchens, pantries, and offices; countertops and hardware included Standout: Featured in Phoenix Home & Garden and LUX Magazine; financing available; over 100 years of combined team design experience Premium Wholesale Cabinets of Arizona is locally owned and operated, with a decade-plus track record in the Phoenix market. The team – owner Eric Skinner, designers Michael and Brianna, and installation specialists Ralph and Billy – takes projects from design consultation through final install. Case studies on their site include the Mountain Residence and Harris Kitchen & Bar builds. The financing option sets this company apart from most wholesale suppliers, making it accessible to homeowners who aren’t paying fully out of pocket. Coverage across nine Phoenix-area cities means most metro projects fall within their service footprint. What separates cheap from quality in wholesale cabinet suppliers Price alone doesn’t tell the full story when comparing Phoenix wholesale cabinet suppliers by price and material quality. The construction matters more than the finish. All-wood boxes with dovetail joinery and soft-close hardware hold up through years of daily use; particleboard carcasses with stapled corners don’t, regardless of how good the door looks. Lead time is the second variable most buyers underweight. It matters. A supplier quoting an attractive per-unit price on a six-week lead can cost more in carrying costs and delayed closeouts than a slightly pricier source with stock already on the shelf. Phoenix’s build pace is fast, and inventory availability is a real differentiator. And the service model matters. Trade buyers running multiple projects benefit from dedicated account management and volume pricing, both of which reduce administrative overhead across the board. Full-service shops suit homeowners who need design help and one point of contact. Knowing which model fits the buyer’s workflow before committing to a supplier saves friction later. Sustainability and material choices in wholesale cabinets Sustainability is becoming an increasingly important consideration for contractors, builders, and homeowners comparing wholesale cabinet suppliers in Phoenix. Beyond appearance and price, buyers should consider where cabinet materials come from, how they are manufactured, and how long the finished products are expected to last. Cabinets made with durable materials can reduce the need for premature replacements, helping minimize material waste over time. Material selection plays a major role in a cabinet’s environmental impact. Solid wood, responsibly sourced plywood, and composite materials with low formaldehyde emissions are worth considering. Buyers can also ask suppliers whether their products meet recognized environmental standards, such as FSC certification for responsibly sourced wood or GREENGUARD certification for low chemical emissions. These credentials provide additional insight into material sourcing and indoor air quality. For trade buyers managing multiple renovation or construction projects , durability is another important part of sustainable sourcing. Features such as dovetail drawer construction, soft-close hardware, and sturdy cabinet boxes can extend product lifespan and reduce replacement needs. Choosing suppliers that maintain consistent inventory and offer reliable delivery can also help limit unnecessary transportation and project-related waste. When evaluating wholesale cabinet suppliers, contractors should look beyond claims of being eco-friendly and ask for specific information about material composition, manufacturing practices, certifications, and product durability. A supplier offering a combination of responsible material choices and long-lasting construction can provide better long-term value while supporting more sustainable building practices. Bottom Line The top Phoenix wholesale cabinet suppliers compared by price and material quality serve meaningfully different buyers. Volume-focused contractors benefit most from sources with real inventory, tiered pricing, and fast turnaround. Custom shops and full-service providers fit homeowners or smaller projects where design support and installation coordination matter more than unit cost. Hardware and component specialists like Hardware Resources and Decore-ative Specialties serve fabricators rather than end buyers. Match the supplier model to the project type, and pricing usually works itself out. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Algae Could Be Nature’s Secret to Energy Efficient Solar Panels Reading Time: 4 minutes How Algae Could Be Nature’s Secret to Energy Efficient Solar Panels With global temperatures hitting record highs, and energy demand continuing to increase, the need for cleaner, more renewable power generation has never been more urgent. Investment in solar was greater than all other power generation technologies combined. But despite this high level of investment, solar power still faces challenges in real world applications. The most notable are efficiency and stability issues, especially in low light conditions. While commercial silicon solar panels convert roughly 15-20% of the sunlight they are exposed to, and recent record-breaking perovskite research having led to energy efficiencies surpassing the 30%-mark, nature has spent billions of years perfecting a far superior alternative. Algae, Natures 95% Efficiency Secret When we think of solar power, we usually think of traditional silicon-based panels baking upon suburban rooftops, yet some of the most groundbreaking advancements are happening at an intersection between materials science and biology. Researchers are looking towards nature, specifically algae, to unlock the future of clean energy. Microalgae and cyanobacteria have evolved over billions of years to become the planet’s most efficient solar harvesters, these photosynthetic organisms can process 95% of the sunlight they absorb even in low-light, underwater, or filtered light environments. Researchers are now looking toward these organisms and asking, “Could they hold answers to how solar panels can be more efficient?” Photosynthesis is an important chemical reaction in which plants, algae, and certain bacteria convert solar energy into chemical energy, that is then used by the living cells. Researchers are using this framework to study bio-photovoltaics (BPVs), devices that harvest electrical currents directly from the photosynthetic activity of living microorganisms. Microalgae, namely cyanobacteria and red algae, use a unique geometric protein arrangement, their surface is made from a mass of light harvesting antenna called phycobilisomes in a way that mimics a funnel. This outward-facing geometry vastly increases the cell’s surface area for light absorption. A major cause of energy loss in standard solar photovoltaics is photon scattering, in algae’s case the geometric rods catch photons from multiple angles and funnel them inward toward a single, central reaction center. It is important to note that compared to the land environment, which typical solar panels would be located, light intensity decreases underwater and becomes unstable as it is refracted or absorbed by the water. Yet cyanobacteria and red algae can live in water as deep as 100m because they have evolved sophisticated light harvesting antennae allowing them to harvest a much more diverse range of wavelengths, most notably short-wave light (blue-green light). Additionally, some freshwater alga can absorb far-red light, typically out of the optimal range for chlorophyll to absorb, by rearranging chlorophyll molecules into larger clusters within its photosynthetic antenna. Decoding Nature with Spectroscopy Researchers use benchtop spectrofluorometers to run highly sensitive fluorescence extraction and emission measurements. Image Gemini Spectroscopy is an invaluable technique used to study the interaction between radiative energy and matter, or in this case how light of varying wavelengths interacts with algae. To translate the characteristics of algae into scalable technology, researchers must first precisely map how these organisms handle photons. This requires analyzing the organisms’ internal pigment-protein complexes for a range of metrics: Light Absorption – The process in which light is absorbed by matter and converted into energy. Energy Transfer – The process by which energy is passed between one ion to another ion, vital to the development of efficient luminescent materials. Fluorescence Emissions – The process where a substance absorbs light or other electromagnetic radiation and immediately re-emits it as light of a longer wavelength. To achieve this level of precision, modern research laboratories rely on advanced spectroscopic equipment. Researchers use benchtop spectrofluorometers to run highly sensitive fluorescence extraction and emission measurements. Fluorescence Emission Spectra: Researchers shine a fixed wavelength of light into the algal culture to capture the exact fingerprint of the re-emitted light. This reveals how energy is distributed across different pigment groups (i.e. Chlorophylls and Phycobiliproteins). Fluorescence Extraction Spectra: Researchers can pinpoint exactly which specific colors of light are most effective at driving energy transfer within the organism. This is achieved by sweeping across a broad spectrum of light wavelengths and measuring resulting emission at a target wavelength. How Can Algae Impact the Future of Solar? The long-term vision of this research stretches far beyond boosting power metrics. Algae are part of a paradigm shift in renewable energy by serving as the blueprint and living engines for next-generation “Bio-Solar Cells,” also known as biophotovoltaics (BPVs). Bio-solar cells leverage living, self-repairing photosynthetic microorganisms like microalgae and cyanobacteria to convert sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide directly into electrical current. Traditional silicon-based photovoltaic panels require resource-intensive, toxic manufacturing which relies heavily on rare earth metals, and when they reach the end of their lifespans, recycling them creates a large electronic waste challenge. In comparison, BPV solar units offer a circular alternative with potential future iterations that could function as disposable, compostable solar elements. BPV power output is currently low (around 0.345 mW/m², which is much lower than standard silicon panels), making them unviable for whole-home power, though suitable for low-voltage sensors or trickling light. Another avenue sees specialized algae being integrated into traditional solar panels, not as a living organism but by using diatom shells. Diatoms are a unicellular phytoplankton that naturally build porous, glass-like silica shells to aid in the capturing of light during photosynthesis, even in murky water. Researchers have found that when these shells are applied as an antireflective coating or integrated into the panel’s encapsulant layer, their nano structures trap and scatter visible light effectively, which has been found to boost silicon solar panel efficiency by at least 4%. The use of diatom shells has also led to reduced panel degradation and extended panel lifespans as the material naturally blocks UV light. UV exposure degrades materials and reduces performance over time, which is unfortunate for devices that, by design, are exposed to it consistently. While scalability and long-term performance remain as the biggest challenges for energy efficient solar panels. By using precision spectroscopic research to take a closer look at our natural world and using spectroscopy tools to uncover its “secrets”, researchers are proving that the greenest future for solar energy might come from the very planet we are trying to protect, in one of nature oldest organisms. The post How Algae Could Be Nature’s Secret to Energy Efficient Solar Panels appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News What to Look for in a Long-Term RV Campground: Examining Sustainability, Facilities and More Reading Time: 4 minutes What to Look for in a Long-Term RV Campground: Examining Sustainability, Facilities and More Choosing a long-term recreational vehicle (RV) campground brings everyday comfort and environmental care onto the same checklist. Over several weeks or months, you’ll want suitable hookups and a site that makes settling in straightforward. Recycling and water conservation deserve attention, too. The right base should suit your daily routine while giving you practical ways to camp responsibly at an affordable rate. Look for Flat Sites and Flexible RV Hookups Knowing what to look for in a long-term RV campground starts with your vehicle’s size and the room you’ll need to maneuver. Flat, wide sites should provide enough clearance to enter and leave comfortably. Ask about dimensions and whether a pull-through or back-in layout suits your setup. An RV-friendly description may still leave you with questions, so give the campground your vehicle’s measurements when discussing available site types. Full hookups provide water and sewer connections with electrical service. Confirm that the available electrical supply matches your RV, and clarify whether wastewater disposal is via a site connection or a shared dump station. You’ll also want to know where the bathrooms and laundry facilities sit relative to the RV camping area. Ask which holding-tank products the campground’s wastewater system accepts. The Environmental Protection Agency warns that some deodorizer chemicals can contaminate groundwater if dumped improperly , while formaldehyde-containing products can disrupt septic treatment. Its guidance identifies biodegradable enzyme- and citrus-based alternatives. Follow the product’s dosage instructions and the campground’s disposal procedures. Check the Campground’s Sustainability Efforts Recycling facilities and clear conservation guidance provide practical details for evaluation. Your own habits also shape how you use those shared resources. 1. Conservation and Site Upkeep Practices Clearly labeled recycling containers are a useful starting point, although you’ll want to ask what happens after collection. Find out which materials the campground accepts and where guests should take them. Recycling ranked as the most important sustainable practice to campers in the 2025 Camping and Outdoor Hospitality Report, with 53% of respondents selecting it. Water conservation and wildlife conservation each received 45%, while roughly one in five campers valued electric vehicle charging stations. Those findings can help you choose questions that match your plans. A campground should be able to explain how guests report leaking taps and follow its wildlife guidance. If you travel with an electric vehicle, confirm that a suitable charging station will be available during your visit. 2. Low-Impact Camping Habits Leave No Trace campground guidelines recommend using durable surfaces , including established trails and paved paths, to reach shared facilities. Leave No Trace also advises keeping trash out of fire rings and collecting overlooked belongings before departure. During your stay, keep equipment within your site boundaries so neighboring campers and shared paths have their own space. Leave bathrooms and other communal areas ready for the next person. Before you leave, make one final walk around your site to pick up any trash and forgotten tent stakes. Compare Long-Term Rates and Overall Value Monthly or seasonal pricing may offer better value than paying nightly. Request a quote for your specific dates, including any minimum-stay requirement, before comparing campgrounds. Your quote should show whether the rate covers water and sewer service, as well as electricity. Laundry or visitor charges may need a separate line in your comparison. Ask which facilities will operate during your visit, especially if you’re planning a winter stay. Confirm availability for the whole reservation, including any dates when services change. A useful comparison connects the price to your routine. If laundry access matters every week, establish its cost and availability while reviewing the rate. The same principle applies to optional activities. Give the facilities you expect to use more weight than extras you’re unlikely to try. RVing also has a substantial economic footprint. The Bureau of Economic Analysis puts its 2024 contribution at $27.5 billion , using current-dollar value added. RVing ranked second among conventional outdoor recreation activities nationally and first in nine states. That figure measures industry activity, while your campground quote gives you the information to assess your own costs. Consider Top Long-Term RV Campground Providers These providers offer starting points for an extended stay. Check availability and environmental practices at the individual campground you’re considering. 1. Kampgrounds of America KOA provides the largest system of independently owned and operated campgrounds. With over 500 locations across North America, KOA offers a broad range of options for an extended stay. Level sites and full-hookup options complement clean bathrooms and consistent service standards. Select campgrounds offer KampK9® dog parks, while knowledgeable staff can help you discuss extended-stay availability and rates. Key Features Full hookups Extended stay options Pet-friendly sites 2. Equity LifeStyle Properties Equity LifeStyle Properties operates RV resorts and campgrounds through Thousand Trails and Encore. Both brands offer longer-stay options, with full-hookup RV sites available through Encore. The portfolio includes lakeside and coastal settings, as well as inland destinations, offering varied surroundings to consider. Its properties also host activities and events, which may appeal if you’d like opportunities to meet fellow campers. Key Features Extended stays Varied destinations Organized activities 3. Sun Outdoors If you prefer a resort-style base, Sun Outdoors offers seasonal and annual stay options. Amenities vary by property, with pools and organized events among the possibilities. Check how the resort’s operating season aligns with its agreement length, since the months you can use the site may differ. That distinction matters when choosing between an occasional getaway base and a longer, continuous visit. Key Features Seasonal stays Resort amenities Organized events Frequently Asked Questions Site suitability and environmental practices deserve attention alongside the full cost of your stay. Q: What should I look for in a long-term RV campground? A: Prioritize level ground with enough clearance for your vehicle and utility connections that match your setup. Confirm wastewater disposal arrangements, then check where you’ll find bathrooms and laundry facilities. Q: How can you tell if an RV campground prioritizes sustainability? A: Clearly explained recycling and water conservation practices provide specific measures for evaluation. Ask how those systems work during your visit and what guidance the campground provides for protecting wildlife. Q: Do long-term RV rates offer better value than nightly rates? A: Monthly or seasonal rates may offer better value, depending on your dates and the services included. Evaluate the full quote, including any additional charges and the facilities available during your stay. Find the Right Long-Term RV Home Base for You A comfortable extended stay starts with a campground that fits your vehicle and makes daily routines manageable. Clear conservation practices give you ways to care for the place while you’re there. With your dates and priorities in hand, contact the providers that interest you. Their campground-specific details can help you choose a base that suits your budget and aligns with your environmental values. The post What to Look for in a Long-Term RV Campground: Examining Sustainability, Facilities and More appeared first on Happy Eco News .

The night didn’t tell just one story, it told 10 different ones. Just for the governors, but it told a lot of stories just across the board. One that stood out to me, and one that will definitely end up in the history books, is that Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia became the first Black woman ever elected governor of any US state. And in 200 years of gubernatorial elections, it had never happened. Her election was very inspirational. I believe her great-grandfather was a slave. We’ve made so much progress, so it’s still so closely… It’s not that far away, too, and we’re still— Arielle: Yeah, that past is not as far away as a lot of us like to think. Karissa: Yeah, exactly. Of course, Texas was the biggest upset of the night across the board, and that was very inspirational to see as well. Democrat Gina Hinojosa beat incumbent Greg Abbott, and it made her the first Latina governor and the first Democrat to win that race in over 30 years. It was just good to see so many different people be elected to these positions across the United States. And it just feels like we’re shaking things up a bit, and having some more accurate representation of what our country looks like. Dermatologists weigh in on the eat-your-skincare TikTok trend Karissa: Well, moving on to the next solution, we have “Dermatologists weigh in on the eat-your-skincare TikTok trend.” Before I go on, Arielle, have you heard about this trend? Arielle: I’ve seen little YouTube Shorts or my sisters will send me reels about, like, this special carrot salad that’s like you eating your retinol or something, ’cause I’m in my 30s now, so they’re just sending me all this stuff. But I, yeah, I wonder if it really does work. So this article definitely caught my attention. Karissa: If you’ve been on this eat-your-skincare side of TikTok or the internet, this is for you, but it’s also for anyone who’s been kind of skeptical about it. It turns out that dermatologists say it’s both real and over-hyped at the same time, but the nuance is actually pretty interesting. So the core thing is that food can fill the tank, but it can’t overfill it. So it means that eating more vitamin C doesn’t make your collagen-making work faster or anything. It just makes sure it’s not running low. And one aspect this article talked about is the eat your sunscreen angle of it all. It sounds kind of wild, but it actually has science behind it, which I did not know. Certain carotenoids and polyphenols have been studied for UV protection, but dermatologists are very clear that these are an extra layer and not a replacement for actual physical SPF. The foods that actually show up in dermatologists’ recommendations are ones that you would probably expect. It’s salmon, avocado, walnuts, eggs, dark chocolate. So this is kind of a vindicating solution if you’re already eating that way. It’s helping you out. It’s not gonna do a million things more for your skin, but it’ll definitely help you out. Arielle: Yeah. Okay, that’s kind of what I thought. I think food, in terms of skincare, will support the overall system, but there’s so many products. I try not to have too complicated of a skincare routine, ’cause I know that too many products is also not ideal for your skin. So if you can combine the serums, the moisturizers, the creams that work for you with a really good nutritious diet, then I think that’s gonna help you glow from the inside and the outside. Karissa: 100%. Took the words right out of my mouth. Electric ferries that fly above water are arriving in the US Karissa: The next solution is “Electric ferries that fly above water are arriving in the US.” We’ve talked about this a little bit before on The Optimist Daily. There’s these really cool electric ferries that fly. They’re kinda like skimming across the water a bit. And so the technology is that they use underwater wings to lift the hull out of the water, and that will cut the drag by 66%, makes it a lot faster, and it’s finally what makes long range electric boats practical. Over in Europe and Canada, I believe they’ve already been kinda using these for transportation. But San Francisco is about to spend half of a billion dollars converting their whole ferry fleet over to these electric ferries. The problem with electric boats has been that the drag has been bad, and so they haven’t been so quick. Water resists a vessel much more than air resists a car, so batteries couldn’t hold enough charge to make it very useful. Hydrofoils solve that by just getting the boat out of the water a bit. I’m excited to see these over in the US, and San Francisco is close to me, and though I don’t really use ferries when I’m visiting the cities, maybe I’ll have to check it out the next time I’m over. Fall activities for you and your dog: a trainer’s guide Karissa: Okay, well, this solution is another lifestyle one, and it’s “Fall activities for you and your dog: a trainer’s guide.” So this solution is a cute and fun one, but it’s essentially a permission slip to take your dog somewhere fun this fall, whether that’s the farmer’s market, pumpkin patches, corn mazes, hiking trails. We have tips from a dog trainer named Sassafras Patterdale who breaks down what to bring, what to watch for, and how to make these trips actually good for the dog and not just all about the photos. Arielle, I thought about you and Tink. Have you done anything autumn-like with her? Arielle: She’s usually off leash, and she loves sniffing around, so we do take her out on, I guess you can call them hikes or just, like, really long walks. I haven’t really taken her to farmer’s markets, which is one of the tips here. Tink is kind of… She doesn’t like kids. Karissa: So. Well, that could be a little— a little hard at the farmer’s market ’cause there usually tends to be a lot of families. And in this article, they’re kinda talking about taking your dog to the farmer’s market, aiming it at, like, younger dogs because it can be a really good training opportunity with all the people and the smells and foot traffic. So it’s kind of like a good place for younger dogs to just get more of that exposure and more practice for calm leash behavior, helping them get used to that. So maybe Tink is a little bit past that. Arielle: Yeah, she’s a bit too old for that, set in her ways. But your dog is also… Is your dog a senior dog? Karissa: Oh, yes, he is a very senior dog now, so he’s not really out on the leash in public anymore, unfortunately. But we used to take him to the farmer’s market, and I think we took him to some kind of, like, fall pumpkin patch thing at some point, and we definitely have a lot of good photos over the years of him with a cute pumpkin. So yeah, it’s just a good time of year to get your pup out there. One consistent thread and important reminder for all the activities that are mentioned in this article is to call ahead or research ahead to make sure dogs are allowed to be wherever you’re going if it’s somewhere, uh, out in public. Brazil releases the world’s first fossil fuel phaseout roadmap Karissa: “Brazil releases the world’s first fossil fuel phaseout roadmap.” This first global roadmap is all about phasing out coal, oil, and gas. It’s a voluntary roadmap, and it has no legal teeth, and it came out during COP30 last year, which notably ended without mentioning fossil fuels in the final text at all. The roadmap exists because Brazil decided to just do it anyways, and it’s being brought back up now that COP31 is happening as we speak. Just kind of jumping back to last year, what happened at COP30, Saudi Arabia and Russia killed the fossil fuel language, and Brazil’s response was to publish this independently and bring it into COP31 this year, which opened, uh, this week. The plan is a three-phase plan through 2033, and it explicitly says there’s no universal solution. Countries are supposed to tailor it to their own situation, which makes it harder to dismiss, but also harder to hold anyone to. Arielle: I think it is encouraging that countries are creating plans, or at least Brazil is creating a plan even though it’s not legally required of them. There’s no external motivation other than the fact that they want to help our environment survive uh, and thrive. And I think that shift from asking or requesting people to commit to the change to just giving them an example of how they can actually make the change is a good kind of reframe. Karissa: 100%. Prince Bashangezi turned personal loss into peer tutoring for refugee students Arielle: The next solution is a Local Changemakers feature. It’s titled “Prince Bashangezi turned personal loss into peer tutoring for refugee students.” This Local Changemaker story is really quite moving. Prince grew up at Tongogara Refugee Camp in Zimbabwe, a camp of more than 17,000 people near the Mozambique border, home to families displaced by conflict across Central and Eastern Africa. He lost his own family to war before ending up there, and he was 17 or 18-ish when COVID hit. While that was happening, he was trying to finish his A-Levels, and when schools closed, he and a small group of fellow students just started teaching the younger kids themselves, ’cause, of course, there was a lack of schooling during that time. And this eventually turned into a program called TWEENS, which stands for Together We Educationally Empower Non-privileged Students. He’s now at Pomona College in California, studying computer science and economics, and the program he built in that camp is actually still running, so it’s now been, uh, over half a decade. The Optimist who nominated Prince for the Local Changemaker series said, “Prince’s work is a reaction to his incredible loss,” and that he turned his personal tragedy into loving service for others. And that framing says everything about what TWEENS is. This peer model works in a refugee context in a way outside volunteers can’t really replicate. These tutors live in the camp. They went through the same disruptions. They understand what it means to build a future from inside a displaced population, so their credibility comes from proximity and not credentials. TWEENS has expanded to include an A-level program, a girls’ book club, and ongoing homework support alongside the original peer tutoring. If you’re interested in helping out, then the GlobalGiving campaign is still active, and I can put a link to where you can donate to this project, uh, in the show notes. This is a great story that Optimists can actually do something about right now, so if you feel compelled to learn more or to give, then I would highly recommend just checking out the article. The dermatologist guide to a skin-friendly shower routine Arielle: The next solution is another skin solution. It’s titled “The dermatologist guide to a skin-friendly shower routine.” Three dermatologists are out here saying that showering every day might be working against your skin. They’re not saying it in, like, a soft, “Well, maybe,” kind of way. They’re actually pretty direct about it. This piece breaks down who actually needs daily showers, who doesn’t, and what the signs are that you’ve overdone it, because that squeaky clean feeling after a hot shower, you might think, “Oh, yeah, I got everything. I’m, like, completely clean.” But that’s not necessarily a good sign. Karissa, are you a shower every day type of person? Karissa: I mean, I definitely am, and I do a lot of heated workouts where I’m sweating a lot, so I definitely need my daily shower, but I’m so intrigued of the argument against it. What about you, Arielle? Arielle: I used to be a shower every day when I was living under my mom’s, uh, watchful eye, and definitely whenever I live in a tropical place, that’s, like, multiple showers a day ’cause I’m sweating, and it’s, like, kind of grimy, and you get sand and everything everywhere. But now I have to say I don’t shower every single day. If I don’t work out that day, and I don’t really do anything strenuous, then chances are, I’m probably gonna skip the shower. Karissa: Yeah. Arielle: Okay, so this article makes a key distinction. Hygiene and skin health are not the same thing. So daily washing serves hygiene, but when you think about it, if you’re not super active, then only your underarms, your groin, your feet, and the skin folds that, like, trap a lot of, I guess, like, perspiration and stuff, that’s what needs soap every day. The rest of your body, you can usually skip. The signs that your skin is asking for a break are quite specific. So if your skin feels super tight after the shower or if you’re experiencing persistent nighttime itchiness or ashiness or flaking on your shins, that’s what a stripped skin barrier looks like. All the listeners out there, you guys should just check those things out and see if any of that applies to you. There’s something about age here as well, ’cause age actually changes the whole game when it comes to showering. Babies, like, they can’t be showered all the time. Their skin is too sensitive, so twice a week is good for babies, whereas teens, on the other hand, they’re going through a lot of hormonal fluctuations. They’re going through puberty. They need more showers, for sure. And then older adults often need less showers because the skin produces fewer surface oils over time, and you just have to kind of use your own judgment. Uh, this is not a one-size-fits-all solution. There are some key tips that I’m glazing over right now, but you can find everything in the article. After a decade of community pressure, LA bans oil drilling for good Arielle: The next solution is titled “After a decade of community pressure, LA bans oil drilling for good.” Los Angeles just became the first major US city to ban oil extraction entirely, and what makes this story different from most environmental news is the decade of community advocacy that actually got it done. This wasn’t a top-down policy decision. People who are actually living next to oil wells pushed for this for more than 10 years. The neighborhoods where these wells sit are working-class communities of color. Residents have been living with benzene and hydrogen sulfide and higher rates of respiratory illness for generations. Wendy Miranda, one of the lead advocates, has asthma, and so does her mother. The city actually tried this back in 2022, but they just passed an ordinance. Oil companies challenged it in court, and they won. So California then passed legislation giving local governments more power, and this vote is what came out the other side. Environmental justice has shifted from an advocacy framework to a legal one, and these days, communities have better tools than they did 10 years ago. And then I also noticed that in the article, the communities expressed that they’re not necessarily anti-oil. They’re anti-drilling next to our kids’ school. And this framing could resonate more broadly than just the pure climate messaging, so they’re also positioning themselves in a much more strategic way. This isn’t just an environmental issue. It’s a health issue, and it’s a human rights issue. Karissa: I’m glad to see this pass in LA because, yeah, I don’t think anyone should have to live right next to a oil drilling well. The next challenge is going to be removing these oil wells because I don’t think there’s, like, a great legal framework for holding oil companies accountable for either paying for that cleanup or removing them. They’ve had a couple of oil wells in the area that have just, like, sat there for years, and getting those out of the way is also the next step here. Why spiders show up in your home every fall, and what to do about it Arielle: The next solution is very seasonal. It’s titled “Why spiders show up in your home every fall, and what to do about it.” Karissa: Oh, I need this solution. I think I have, like, two spider bites on my ankles, so. Arielle: Oh, you have actual bites? I just have so many spiders, like up in the corners of my… Well, basically all the rooms in my house. So yeah, this article gets into it, and if you are like me and Karissa and you’ve been seeing more spiders lately, there’s a simple biological reason. Fall is mating season for spiders, and a lot of them are coming inside to find mates and somewhere quiet to lay their eggs. And the reassuring thing an entomologist from Oregon State said is that most of them are minding their own business. They’re also eating your gnats and all those other insects that might be bothering you in your home. I found it unexpected that of the 3,700 spider species in the United States, only 0.3% are dangerous to humans. The ones showing up in your house are almost certainly not in that category, thankfully. The entry points are pretty mundane. You could probably guess. Your worn garage door weather strip, cracks in your foundation, gaps around window frames are all entry points for spiders and other critters. And if your house already has like a lot of gnats or flies, then the spiders are just following the food. Karissa: Yeah. That makes sense. Arielle: The most effective seasonal fix is clearing wood piles or compost heaps and old boards from around the perimeter of your house because that’s where spiders can shelter before they come into your home. There’s fall decluttering content everywhere right now, and this article gives it a practical reason beyond just aesthetics. But there’s also a maybe just leave them kind of framing at the end of this article, and it’s part of a broader shift towards coexisting with nature rather than trying to eliminate it. Because the spiders are cold, they just wanna get cozy, they wanna find a mate. It’s cuffing season for them as well, I guess. I used to be super scared of spiders, but I think they’ve… I don’t know. We don’t have like really juicy-looking spiders here in the Netherlands. They’re all kind of like spindly, and they look really fragile. Ah. I don’t know, maybe in Northern California it’s a bit of a different story. Karissa: Yeah. They’re pretty small. Like, obviously you won’t ever want one around. I did see a pretty juicy one though the other day on the wall, and it was a little bit scary. But usually the ones that end up in my house here are not too bad. But yeah, I think there’s some kind of one that like bites, ’cause every once in a while I’ll just have like this giant, like welt from… That’s what I’ve heard, read. I never see the spider doing it, but yeah, my ankle currently has a bite, so it’s a little bit annoying, but it’s nothing like poisonous of course. I guess I’ll take this advice and this solution to let them coexist. How two Princeton graduates built the world’s first microplastics removal system Arielle: All right. The last solution that I’m going to be sharing with all you Optimists this week is titled “How two Princeton graduates built the world’s first microplastics removal system.” There is now a wastewater treatment plant in Atlantic City, New Jersey, that removes microplastics before they reach the ocean, and it’s the first one in the entire world. The two people who built the technology are architects who basically looked at how certain wetland plants trap microplastics naturally, and then scaled it up. There’s, again, no law that’s requiring this, but they just did it anyway. The design philosophy is explicitly about simplicity. The founders wanted something like an iPhone approach to a complex problem. Minimal material, low energy, but big results. It’s a pretty big problem, these microplastics. They’ve already turned up in human bloodstream, in brain tissue and other organs. And the Atlantic County plant manager said it pretty plainly, “We’re discharging to the ocean. If we’re not removing the plastic, we’re putting it back in.” And yeah, it’s just like the, the Brazil, uh, phase out fossil fuels roadmap. There’s no law that’s requiring this. It’s the municipality doing it because it’s the right thing to do, not because they have to. Karissa: Yeah. This is so awesome, and it’s very intriguing that it’s the first in the world to do this. I know we’ve written on The Optimist Daily about a lot of solutions that can filter out microplastics and being developed, but I guess we haven’t really seen them deployed so much. So this is a great, uh, article describing how this is actually being put into action now. And the fact that they don’t have to, they’re doing it to better their municipality is, uh, is great news. Arielle: All right. Well, those were all the solutions that we had to share with everyone this week. But as usual, we leave you off with a positive quote. Karissa: This week we have, “If they don’t give you a seat at the table, bring a folding chair.” And that’s from Shirley Chisholm. I really like this one, and I was inspired to add it just from all the great progress in the United States we saw in this past week of people getting a seat at the table. So I’m excited to see what those seats will produce. Arielle: Well, Karissa and I wish everyone a wonderful, restful weekend. Uh, we will be back next week with more solutions. But in the meantime, stay positive and optimistic. Karissa: Absolutely. Have a great weekend, everyone. Bye! The post Podcast Transcript November 13th, 2026— This midterm’s historic governor firsts, flying electric ferries, and eat-your-skincare first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.descriptionOriginal: The advice for eating in a warming world is by now familiar: more beans, fruit and vegetables; less meat and dairy. But it seems the same plate could also help with an entirely different planetary problem. Two new studies in mice suggest that high-fiber diets help nanoplastics, the tiny plastic particles strewn through oceans and soils, and found in the food we eat, pass through the gut without being absorbed. High-fat diets, by contrast, appear to make the body hold onto more of them. Millions of tons of plastic waste enter the environment each year. This waste slowly degrades into microplastics and nanoplastics that find their way into farms, plants, ocean life, and even the Amazon—where they were recently found in the blood of wild tapirs and anteaters . Once ingested with food, these tiny particles percolate into the human brain, lungs, liver, kidneys, placenta, and testes , where they cause inflammation, oxidative stress, DNA damage, and other cellular injuries. Nanoplastics are even found in the atherosclerotic plaques of our coronary arteries , where they increase the risk of heart attack, stroke, or premature death by more than 4-fold. The two new studies looked at how diet influences the absorption and effects of nanoplastics in mice. One study found that in the first 24 hours after consuming nanoplastics, mice eating medium- or high-fiber diets accumulated two to seven times less plastics in their intestinal tract than those on regular diets. Mice fed nanoplastics for 28 days experienced inflammation and breakdown of their intestinal barriers—setting the stage for nanoplastics to enter the rest of the body; but these negative effects were absorption of nanoplastics by 2.8-fold compared to regular diets. That finding is especially worrisome, given that fast foods and takeout foods, both rich in fat, are often served in containers laced with plastics. In the two new studies, dietary fiber may have exerted its protective effects by shaping the intestinal microbiome, coating the nanoplastic particles, and speeding up their elimination through poop—allowing the intestinal lining to avoid excessive exposure. These new insights come at a time when scientists are already proposing higher-plant and lower-animal diets that could improve worldwide health while also reducing the environmental impacts of the global food system , such as greenhouse emissions, water pollution, and land use. Human studies are needed to confirm these newest results. But for the moment, they suggest that sustainable diets could also reduce another nasty problem: nanoplastics. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News A Year In, Networks for Nature is Reconnecting Cheshire’s Wild Spaces Reading Time: 3 minutes Chester Zoo’s Networks for Nature community project planted 14,000 trees and restored and created 13 ponds in its first year, putting it well on its way to its five-year goals. Networks for Nature started with a simple idea. Wildlife does better when habitats connect, and so do communities. One year in, about 8,700 people across northwest Cheshire, England, have put that idea to work. Chester Zoo launched the project with a £4.4 million grant from The National Lottery Heritage Fund. It covers about 60 square miles, from Ellesmere Port to Chester, and runs through 2028. The Westminster Foundation and individual supporters also help fund it. The project builds on the zoo’s earlier Nature Recovery Corridor. That effort improved more than 62 hectares for wildlife and engaged over 12,000 people. Connection is the core of the approach. Small, isolated habitat patches leave plants and animals stranded. Hedgerows, ponds, and green corridors help them move, feed, and breed across a wider area. Hannah Brooks leads the project as Chester Zoo’s Senior Community Participation and Engagement Manager. She says connectivity is how species grow and thrive. In her view, the project works the same way, relying on landowners, community groups, and individuals working together. Networks for Nature’s first-year numbers show that cooperation in action. Volunteers and partners planted 14,000 trees and created or restored 13 ponds. They also established or restored 1.6 kilometers of hedgerow. Those figures put the project well on track. Over the full five years, it aims for 20 ponds and nearly 3,000 meters of hedgerow. In year one, it reached about two-thirds of the pond target and more than half of the hedgerow goal. Woodland work added nearly 7 hectares of new or improved habitat, roughly the size of 10 soccer fields. Teams also removed 269 tonnes of invasive plants and animals from the water. These species crowd out native wildlife and can choke waterways. One cleanup stands out. The project cleared 500 cubic meters of illegally dumped rubbish from a single community green space. That is enough to fill about seven large shipping containers. Each site has its own focus. At Gowy Meadows Nature Reserve near Ellesmere Port, work has improved public access. In Lache, a neglected space called The Backies has reopened as an enhanced community green space. Along the Shropshire Union Canal, teams have cleared invasive species. The Canal and River Trust is also monitoring water quality there. Meanwhile, The Land Trust is creating a wetland at Countess of Chester Country Park. Getting people to nature matters as much as restoring it. The project built 1,090 meters of new pathways so residents can reach green spaces more easily. Cheshire West and Chester Council is also planting wildflower meadows and improving five public parks for wildlife. Local participants did much of the hands-on work, from planting and clearing to laying footpaths. Others joined bug hunts, bird box building, and garden makeovers that brought wildlife closer to home. Some participants have gone further and trained as Wildlife Champions. They learn practical skills to keep improving outdoor spaces in their own neighborhoods. Brooks sees this long-term local leadership as central to the project’s value. Young people have played a central role. In year one, 83 young people joined hedgehog awareness campaigns, built bird and bat boxes, and improved allotments. They also completed leadership skills courses, nearly reaching the project’s five-year goal of 90. Schools are the next big focus for Networks for Nature. The project aims to reach 4,500 students through a year-long program to improve school grounds for wildlife. Local pupils have already joined in through wildlife clubs. Through Networks for Nature, Sutton Green Primary pupils joined the City Nature Challenge, using tablets to log the plants and animals they found outdoors. Photo courtesy of Chester Zoo . The project also links nature with health. Through green social prescribing, doctors can refer patients to outdoor, nature-based activities instead of, or alongside, medicine. Western Avenue Medical Centre in Blacon and Great Sutton Medical Centre in Ellesmere Port take part. Research suggests that time in green spaces can boost mental and physical wellbeing. Restoring parks and ponds close to home makes that benefit easier for residents to reach. Helen Featherstone, Director, England, North at The National Lottery Heritage Fund, praised the project’s community-led approach. She says it shows how communities and conservation groups can protect natural heritage together for the long term. Year one has focused on completed work, such as planting trees and restoring ponds. The bigger test will be whether wildlife responds. Ongoing monitoring, including water quality checks on the canal, will help show those results over time. The first year shows what community involvement adds. Thousands of residents turned a funded plan into trees in the ground, cleaner green spaces, and new local leaders. With four years still to go, Networks for Nature is only beginning to grow. Schools, community groups, landowners, and volunteers can learn more on Chester Zoo’s Networks for Nature page. Opportunities to train and take part continue to expand. The post A Year In, Networks for Nature is Reconnecting Cheshire’s Wild Spaces appeared first on Happy Eco News .

The town of Lahaina, which holds a deep place in Hawaiian history and once served as the capital of the Hawaiian Kingdom, suffered the greatest devastation: Most of its buildings were destroyed, and thousands of residents were displaced. The disaster exposed vulnerabilities that had been building long before the flames, from a shortage of affordable housing and dependence on tourism to questions around land use, water access and food security. items.descriptionOriginal: Grief has a way of ambushing us in ordinary places. It was in the middle of an Ikea store, surrounded by display of sofas and couples building lives together, that a recently widowed woman sat down and wept. A passing stranger stopped, pressed a packet of tissues into her hands, rested a palm on her shoulder, and waited in silence until a nod signaled she was steadier. Then, she simply walked on. That wordless exchange, offered without expectation or introduction, cracked something open: "I knew then that a relationship was possible, because there are good people in the world." What followed, over the next decade, was a new love, a rebuilt life, and a quiet personal ritual -- the widow now carries tissues wherever she goes and has pressed them into the hands of four strangers crying in restaurants and bars. Kindness, it turns out, doesn't just comfort; it teaches, and those who receive it often become its most faithful carriers.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Living with the Wild Documentary Confronts What Coexistence Actually Looks Like Reading Time: 3 minutes A five-part Living with the Wild documentary series explores what coexistence really looks like as elephants, lions, and rural communities increasingly compete for the same shrinking landscapes. Living with the Wild documentary from the International Fund for Animal Welfare (IFAW) arrives at a moment when human-wildlife conflict has become one of conservation’s most pressing and least resolved challenges. Across Africa’s great ecosystems, growing human populations, expanding agriculture, and shifting climate patterns push people and wildlife into ever-closer proximity, often with deadly consequences for both. Nowhere is this tension more visible than in Kenya’s Amboseli ecosystem, a landscape spanning the shadow of Mount Kilimanjaro where more than a thousand elephants roam alongside tens of thousands of Maasai pastoralists and their livestock. The documentary draws heavily on landscapes like this, where elephants raiding crops can destroy an entire family’s harvest overnight, and where retaliatory killings of wildlife remain a persistent, painful reality. IFAW has worked in Amboseli for years, partnering with the Amboseli Ecosystem Trust and Kenya Wildlife Service to mitigate conflict and secure migratory corridors elephants depend on. The organization’s multi-year commitment to securing tens of thousands of acres as wildlife dispersal land reflects a core premise underlying the Living with the Wild documentary: coexistence requires physical space, not just goodwill. That space-based approach extends well beyond Amboseli through IFAW’s broader Room to Roam initiative, which works to secure safe migratory corridors for African elephants across multiple countries. In Zimbabwe, the initiative has leased tens of thousands of acres between Victoria Falls and Hwange National Park, creating no-poaching territory that benefits elephants and more than a dozen other migratory species sharing the landscape. The Living with the Wild documentary connects to IFAW’s Room to Roam initiative, which secures tens of thousands of acres of safe migratory territory for elephants and other species across Southern Africa, demonstrating how physical space underpins genuine coexistence. Photo by Gil DAIX on Pexels. The Living with the Wild documentary captures a central truth about modern conservation: protecting iconic species increasingly means addressing the needs of the people living alongside them, not treating human and wildlife welfare as competing priorities. Communities bordering protected areas often bear disproportionate costs from wildlife presence, losing crops, livestock, and sometimes lives, while receiving comparatively little benefit from the tourism revenue wildlife generates elsewhere. Addressing this imbalance requires solutions extending beyond fences and patrols. IFAW’s work supporting human-wildlife conflict mitigation has included deploying tracking collars on elephants to better predict and prevent dangerous encounters, funding infrastructure improvements benefiting local communities, and developing early warning systems that help people and elephants avoid confrontations before they escalate into tragedy. The Living with the Wild documentary arrives as momentum builds to treat coexistence as an achievable policy rather than a distant aspiration. Organizations including the Elephant Protection Initiative increasingly bring communities, governments, and conservation groups to the same table, recognizing that sustainable solutions require buy-in from everyone sharing a landscape, not interventions imposed from outside. This shift matters because conventional conservation approaches, focused narrowly on anti-poaching enforcement or protected-area boundaries, often fail to address why conflict happens in the first place. When communities lose half their crops to wildlife and receive no compensation or support for alternative livelihoods, tolerance for coexistence erodes, no matter how much international attention a species receives. The Living with the Wild documentary suggests that genuine coexistence depends on reframing wildlife not as a burden communities must endure, but as a shared resource whose benefits and costs are distributed more equitably. Corridors that allow elephants to migrate safely also reduce crop-raiding incidents. Conflict mitigation infrastructure protects both human livelihoods and animal lives. Community-based conservation models increasingly demonstrate that when local people have genuine stakes in wildlife survival, coexistence becomes self-reinforcing rather than externally enforced. As climate change intensifies pressure on already-strained landscapes and pushes wildlife and communities into more frequent contact, the questions raised throughout the Living with the Wild documentary will only grow more urgent. The series offers no simple resolution, because none exists. Instead, it offers a clear-eyed look at what sharing a planet with megafauna requires: space, compromise, and sustained investment in solutions that work for both the elephants crossing ancient migratory routes and the families whose homes and farms lie along the way. The post Living with the Wild Documentary Confronts What Coexistence Actually Looks Like appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Daniel Te, an American artist living in London, has set his sights on sketching distinctive landmarks at the city’s 272 active Tube stations. The 27-year-old recently completed all 16 stops on the Victoria Line in a 10-hour sketching marathon, beginning with Brixton and concluding with Walthamstow Central. He spent about half an hour at each stop drawing something near the station. Daniel Te / SWNS “I think drawing landmarks helps create a more distinctive sense of what a place is exactly,” he told SWNS. “Seven Sisters was the most memorable, and I really like the origin story — it’s the symbol of the place, just seven trees in a circle.” Te said he was surprised by what he discovered, not having researched the stations in advance. For example, at Highbury & Islington, he spotted a green plaque marking where George Orwell used to live. “And that’s something that I never knew,” he remarked. Daniel Te / SWNS When he got to the final stop at Walthamstow Central, it was getting dark and hard to see what he was sketching. “I felt relieved, hungry, tired, and satisfied,” Te said. “It was fulfilling, and I really liked the journey.” And despite increasing costs of transport, his day of traveling cost him less than $10. Daniel Te / SWNS Te moved to London from Portland, Oregon, in July, inspired to explore European city planning. “One of the reasons why I started doing Tube sketching is that I wanted to see more of London and have an excuse to go out and about,” he explained, adding, “I really do love the process of just exploring every single destination.” He has visited many cities, including Amsterdam, Vienna, and Prague, and has completed drawings of Berlin’s S7 S-Bahn and the Palace of Culture and Science in Warsaw. Whenever he sketches, he likes that people come and talk to him, share their own art, or simply watch him in action. Daniel Te / SWNS Next up? Te is inviting fellow Londoners to join him at Farringdon Station at 11 a.m. tomorrow to begin sketching the Circle Line. And further down the line (pun intended), he plans to turn the sketches into a book or expand his work to cover other locations. This article was originally written by Tahira Amini for SWNS — the U.K.’s largest independent news agency, providing globally relevant original, verified, and engaging content to the world’s leading media outlets.

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM For decades, wastewater treatment plants have been filtering out bacteria, chemicals, and biological waste before discharging treated water back into the environment. Microplastics have been going straight through. This week, a plant in Atlantic City, New Jersey, became the first in the world to do something about that, installing a system built specifically to capture microplastics before they reach the ocean. As of this moment, no law requires this. PolyGone Systems , a startup founded by two former Princeton University graduate students, built it anyway. Why microplastics are hard to remove Plastics don’t biodegrade; they break down into tinier and tinier fragments called microplastics, which don’t go away and build up in living organisms over time. Standard wastewater treatment removes a lot, but it wasn’t designed for particles this small or this plentiful. They get into the water from industrial discharge, stormwater picking up particles shed from car tires, and washing machines releasing microfibers from synthetic clothes. By the time water arrives at a treatment plant, the microplastics are already in it. “We’re discharging to the ocean,” said Matt DeNafo, president of the Atlantic County Utilities Authority. “So, if we’re not removing the plastic that’s in our wastewater, we’re putting it back into the environment. It’s getting into the fish that we’re eating, even the water that we’re bathing. So, it really becomes an issue for human health.” Microplastics and nanoplastics have already turned up in human bloodstream, brain tissue , and other organs. Some researchers have linked exposure to a higher risk of heart attack or stroke, though scientists are still working out exactly what harm these particles cause at different levels of exposure. How the technology works PolyGone’s founders, Nathaniel Banks and Yidian Liu , trained as architects, and the technology they built shows it. Their system, called Polypods, doesn’t try to filter microplastics out of water the conventional way. Instead, it replicates the surface of ultrahydrophobic plants found in wetlands, which microplastics cling to naturally. Scale that up, and you can pull microplastics out of a water stream with very little material and minimal energy. The lab numbers are strong: more than 98 percent of microplastics removed. There’s no commercial data yet, but Banks and Liu say the Polypods work best on the smallest particles, which are also the hardest to catch by other means and the ones most easily absorbed by living tissue. Liu on the design philosophy: “We really like how some sleek products such as the iPhone were able to resolve very complex problems with very simple but sleek-looking designs. And we want to really emphasize that in how we design the Polypods.” “I think this really marks a new era for treatment innovation, where we’re able to build very large, scalable systems that use a very small amount of material and very low energy to treat very challenging contaminants,” Banks said. “And, having the first system in the world for that in Atlantic County, it’s quite unusual.” Where PolyGone goes from here A similar installation is already running at a wastewater plant in California, and PolyGone is developing a residential version. The Atlantic City system was fully funded by a federal grant, and both the technology and the funding route could give other municipalities a path to act without waiting on a mandate.
